- Character creation, experience thresholds, single-class levels 1–20, classes, subclasses, backgrounds, species, feats, equipment, and spellcasting present in the SRD. Multiclassing remains explicitly excluded from Alpha 3.
- Spell acquisition, preparation, casting time, range, components, concentration, duration, targets, areas, saving throws, attack rolls, damage, healing, conditions, summoning, transformations, and ongoing effects.
- Rules glossary terms.
- Gameplay toolbox material used by the product, including travel pace, environmental effects, traps, fear, mental stress, poison, and encounter guidance where included.
- Magic item categories, attunement or activation behavior, charges, curses, resilience, crafting support if implemented, and individual items in the licensed manifest.
- Monster stat-block fields, action economy, traits, movement modes, senses, immunities, resistances, vulnerabilities, reactions, legendary or similar structures when present, and encounter use.

Each category has one of five statuses: Not Started, Structured, Engine Implemented, Conformance Tested, or Production Approved. **Production Approved is a per-rule readiness state, not a Phase 6/7 release state.** A rule reaches Production Approved after its normalized source record, deterministic conformance tests, applicable boundary/adversarial cases, and ordinary independent QA player-visible scenarios pass on the current frozen candidate. The later Independent QA Judge re-challenges sampled/full rule evidence during hardening/release but is not required to grant the initial Production Approved status.

**QA bootstrap rule:** a rule-dependent control may be exposed in the **Local Arena certification runtime** once every rule required by that control is at least **Conformance Tested**, specifically so Builder and ordinary independent QA can exercise the real rendered player path needed to decide Production Approved. That pre-approval exposure is a certification state, not authorization for a hosted milestone or player release. The control becomes eligible for an ordinary player-facing Public Milestone or Launch Production surface only after its required rules are Production Approved. Future rules that the screen does not depend on do not block it. No separate mock control or QA-only replacement UI is permitted; QA exercises the same production code path that will remain after approval. **Readiness status is candidate-bound certification/evidence metadata, not a runtime feature flag whose promotion rewrites source, rules behavior, or the frozen artifact.** Promoting Conformance Tested to Production Approved records QA approval against the exact tested candidate hash; it does not create a new candidate merely by changing the certification label.

## 6.3 Defined-term discipline

Rules terms must be modeled as explicit concepts rather than loose strings. “Action,” “attack,” “Attack action,” “weapon attack,” “spell attack,” “target,” “creature,” “object,” “occupied space,” “visible,” “within range,” “concentration,” and “reaction” must not be treated as interchangeable unless the licensed rule says they are.

The engine must distinguish:

- A command from an action in the fiction.
- An action economy resource from an ordinary-language action.
- An attack roll from an effect that deals damage without an attack roll.
- A creature being seen by the player from being visible to the acting character.
- A selected graphical token from a legal target.
- A point in space from a creature or object.
- A spell being known, prepared, available, and castable.
- A rule permission from a narrative description.

Every rules record must list the terms it consumes and produces. Rule tests must include common-language ambiguity designed to catch accidental string matching.

## 6.4 Character creation rules contract

Character creation must be a guided, reversible workflow that produces a legal level-one character under the approved SRD options. The workflow must never present a final “Create” action while required decisions remain unresolved.

The character builder must:

- Explain whether the campaign uses standard arrays, point buy, rolled abilities, or a host-approved method.
- Apply legal minimums, maximums, costs, and prerequisites deterministically.
- Show the effect of each selection immediately.
- Prevent incompatible selections rather than accepting them and failing later.
- Show class, background, species, feat, proficiency, language, equipment, and spell decisions in an ordered checklist.
- Provide a review page that identifies source category, mechanical effect, and unresolved choices.
- Calculate hit points, Armor Class, initiative, passive values, saving throw proficiencies, skill proficiencies, speed, senses, attacks, spellcasting statistics, and starting resources from rules data.
- Store the exact choices and derivation trail rather than only final numbers.
- Support keyboard, screen-reader, reduced-motion, and low-vision use.
- Save a draft after every confirmed step.
- Permit the player to leave and resume without creating duplicate characters.

The builder must not use the AI Game Director to decide legal selections. AI may explain an option, compare play styles, or suggest a build, but the player must confirm every character-defining choice.

## 6.5 Character-sheet derivation and audit

Every derived value must be recomputable. The character sheet must expose a “Why is this number?” control for important values. The explanation must list base value, modifiers, conditions, equipment, temporary effects, and rule identifiers.

The system must detect and quarantine impossible sheets, including negative resource maxima, duplicate exclusive choices, unknown content identifiers, invalid proficiency combinations, orphaned spells, attributes outside allowed bounds, or features from a rules version not enabled in the campaign.

A character version transition must never flatten the sheet into unexplained totals. If a feature changes across rules-engine releases, the version transition record must say what changed and why.

## 6.6 Experience awards and level advancement

### 6.6.1 Sole advancement authority

Experience Points are the only advancement currency in Alpha 3. Milestone advancement, manual owner level grants, Director-authored level mutations, hidden level buttons, and client-authored XP are prohibited.

The deterministic progression service owns:

- XP award validation.
- XP award idempotency.
- Current XP total.
- Current class level.
- Next threshold.
- Level availability.
- Pending level-up choices.
- Derived-statistic recomputation.
- Final level-up commitment.
- Level-cap enforcement.

The Game Director may recommend an award category or explain why XP was earned. It cannot write the character record, choose a number outside the approved award policy, skip a threshold, or grant a level directly.

### 6.6.2 Experience award events

Every XP award is a canonical event containing:

- Character and owner identifiers.
- Campaign, scene, encounter, quest, discovery, or approved source identifier.
- Award policy and rules-manifest version.
- Base amount and any approved deterministic allocation rule.
- Party-sharing method where applicable.
- Prior and resulting XP totals.
- Prior and resulting level-availability state.
- Idempotency key.
- Server commit time.
- Player-visible mechanical notice.

Retries, reconnects, worker replacement, duplicate WebSocket delivery, and repeated UI activation cannot duplicate an award. A negative XP mutation, unexplained manual edit, or attempt to remove XP for convenience fails closed unless a verified corruption-recovery event restores already-established truth.

### 6.6.3 Threshold crossing and level availability

When XP reaches or exceeds the next approved threshold, the character enters `LEVEL_UP_AVAILABLE`. Excess XP carries forward. Crossing multiple thresholds does not skip choices or combine levels into one opaque mutation; the character completes each level sequentially until current level matches the highest legally reached threshold.

A level-up cannot begin while the character has:

- An unresolved command.
- A pending roll or reroll chain.
- An open Reaction or Decision Window.
- An active compound-action node.
- An unresolved death or revival transition.
- A state-recovery freeze.
- A pending ownership or authentication incident.

Campaign policy may require a rest, scene boundary, or safe intermission before level-up choices become available only when that requirement is explicitly supported by the approved rules and campaign configuration. The system cannot invent such a delay from narrative convenience.

### 6.6.4 Single-class progression

Every Alpha 3 character has one class selected during creation and advances only in that class through level 20.

The interface and server must not expose or accept:

- Multiclass selection.
- Level allocation into another class.
- Multiclass prerequisites.
- Mixed class spell-slot calculations.
- Mixed hit-dice progression.
- Cross-class feature acquisition.
- A partially implemented multiclass feature flag.
- AI suggestions that present multiclassing as available.

A future architecture may add multiclassing only through a separately approved blueprint revision, rules-manifest expansion, version transition plan, and full conformance suite. Alpha 3 code must not contain a secret or dormant user-accessible multiclass path.

### 6.6.5 Transactional level-up workflow

A level-up operates as a durable transaction with preview, player confirmation, server validation, canonical commit, projection rebuild, mechanical notices, and resumable completion.

The preview identifies:

- Prior and new class level.
- Prior XP, threshold crossed, and remaining XP toward the next threshold.
- Hit Point change and approved method.
- Class and subclass features gained.
- Proficiency Bonus and scaling changes.
- Spell slots, prepared spells, known spells, cantrips, replacement choices, and spellcasting changes.
- Feat or Ability Score Improvement choices where applicable.
- Weapon Mastery, resource, movement, sense, resistance, and recharge changes.
- Effects on attacks, saves, DCs, Armor Class, initiative, passive values, inventory capacity, and other derived statistics.
- Any unresolved required choice.

No final statistic is accepted from the client. The server recomputes the complete character projection from source choices and the approved rules manifest. The transaction either commits all required changes once or commits none.

The workflow is resumable across refresh, reconnect, browser closure, and worker replacement. A stale submission is rejected with a refreshed preview. Repeated submission with the same idempotency key produces the original result. A character cannot play at the new level until the level-up event commits and the new projection is published.

### 6.6.6 Level cap and invalid advancement

Level 20 is the maximum. XP may remain recorded for campaign history if product policy permits, but it cannot create level 21, a hidden prestige level, an invented feature, or a Game Director exception.

The system rejects:

- Leveling below the required threshold.
- Skipping a level.
- Selecting features from another class.
- Selecting unapproved or unlicensed options.
- Duplicating a feature already granted.
- Applying the wrong proficiency, cantrip, spell-slot, or class-feature scaling.
- Completing with unresolved mandatory choices.
- Direct database edits that cannot be reproduced from source choices and canonical XP events.

### 6.6.7 Progression QA harness

The Local Arena must include a server-authorized Progression QA Harness for disposable QA fixtures. The harness calls the same canonical progression services used by hosted play, but the harness endpoint/capability itself must be absent or fail closed in Milestone and Launch Production. It may:

- Create a level-1 fixture for any supported class.
- Set a fixture to one XP below a threshold through a typed test setup event.
- Award the exact XP needed to cross one threshold.
- Award enough XP to cross multiple thresholds and require sequential level completion.
- Place a fixture into a pending level-up state.
- Generate a validated level-N fixture by replaying canonical progression choices and services.
- Reset a fixture to a named progression checkpoint.
- Simulate duplicate, stale, interrupted, and concurrent XP and level-up operations.
- Attempt level 21, milestone advancement, and multiclassing and prove rejection.

The harness may manipulate test inputs and fixtures but must invoke the same production XP, level-up, derivation, event, projection, and notice services. It may not stamp a level number or directly write final Hit Points, features, spell slots, ability scores, or derived values.

Every operation requires a valid QA capability, a disposable fixture marker, an allowlisted operation, a test-run identifier, and an immutable audit event. The exact character-name prefix `QA ` may make fixtures easy to identify but grants zero authorization.

### 6.6.8 Advancement conformance

The permanent progression suite must:

- Advance at least one character of every supported class sequentially from level 1 through level 20.
- Exercise every subclass and every level-dependent choice exposed in Alpha 3.
- Independently recompute each changed value from the rules manifest.
- Test targeted boundaries at levels 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, 17, 19, and 20.
- Verify cantrip, spell-slot, class-feature, proficiency, resource, attack, save, and DC scaling at applicable boundaries.
- Verify reconnect and resume at every level-up stage.
- Verify duplicate prevention and stale-preview rejection.
- Verify ordinary accounts cannot invoke QA progression operations.
- Verify milestone and multiclass requests are absent from ordinary UI and rejected server-side.

A polished level-up screen is not proof. Certification requires source choices, XP events, level-up events, resulting projections, mechanical notices, visible UI, reconnect evidence, QA player use, and independent recomputation. Human review is required only when the level-up experience is part of an explicit Section 25 human gate.

## 6.7 Modes of play and transitions

The engine must represent at least four modes: Free Exploration, Structured Exploration, Social Exchange, and Encounter. A mode controls timing, available UI, batching, and response expectations. It does not remove rules.

**Free Exploration** allows natural conversation and broad movement without turn-by-turn enforcement when no immediate hazard or competition requires precision.

**Structured Exploration** introduces ordered declarations, movement costs, time pressure, detection checks, or hazard resolution without presenting a full combat interface unless needed.

**Social Exchange** tracks active speakers, NPC attitudes, known information, promises, deception attempts, and consequences while preserving player agency. A high roll cannot force a player character to feel or believe something.

**Encounter** enforces initiative, action economy, reactions, precise position, durations, and end-of-turn processing.

Transitions must be visible and narrated. The system must not silently start combat because a player used an aggressive verb. It must confirm hostile intent when ambiguity would have major consequences. Leaving encounter mode requires completion or explicit suspension of pending reactions, durations, and turn-end effects.

## 6.8 D20 Test pipeline

Every D20 Test must follow one traceable pipeline:

1. Identify the requested fictional objective.
2. Determine whether the outcome is uncertain and consequential.
3. Determine whether a roll is required or whether the action automatically succeeds or fails.
4. Select the relevant test type and ability.
5. Apply proficiency or expertise-like modifiers only from approved features.
6. Apply advantage and disadvantage sources, including cancellation behavior.
7. Determine the target number or opposing process.
8. Expose the material stakes before the roll when doing so does not reveal hidden information.
9. Generate and preserve the random result server-side.
10. Calculate the baseline result.
11. Allow a bounded Director ruling only where judgment is permitted.
12. Commit the final event and narrate the actual result.

The Director may decide that a creative approach changes the ability used or grants advantage when the fiction supports it. The Director may not change a revealed die result, fabricate proficiency, or conceal a resource cost.

## 6.9 Difficulty, hidden information, and fairness

The exact target number may be hidden when disclosure would reveal secret information. The system must still store it before the roll or derive it from a rule that was fixed before the result. The Director cannot wait to see the roll and then invent a target to force the desired outcome.

When the Director uses a contextual difficulty rather than a fixed rule, the event record must store a reason code and a bounded difficulty category. QA must be able to detect favoritism, systematic inflation, and post-roll manipulation.

The player-facing explanation should describe relevant factors without exposing secrets. After the secret no longer matters, a campaign audit may reveal the original target and sources if the host has enabled transparent rulings.

## 6.10 Randomness integrity

All authoritative random results must be generated server-side by an approved cryptographically secure random source or a reviewed deterministic generator seeded server-side for replayable test environments. Client animations are presentations of already committed random results; they are not the source of truth.

Each roll record must contain:

- Roll identifier.
- Dice expression or table selection.
- Individual die faces.
- Kept and discarded dice.
- Static and temporary modifiers.
- Advantage or disadvantage sources.
- Timestamp and acting entity.
- Command identifier.
- State version.
- Visibility class.
- Whether the roll was public, private to the actor, private to the Director, or delayed reveal.

A retry caused by network failure must return the existing result. It must never roll again unless the original command was definitively rejected before a roll was created.


### 6.10.1 Player-triggered authoritative roll interaction

A roll for a present player character uses the following interaction sequence unless secrecy or a mandatory interrupt requires an automatic server roll:

1. The rules engine determines that a roll is required and freezes the roll context: actor, action, targets, expression, modifiers, advantage or disadvantage, visibility, and state version.
2. The interface displays a context-specific prompt such as **Roll Attack**, **Roll Dexterity Save**, or **Roll Death Save**. It does not display a bag of selectable dice.
3. The player may continue using table chat before clicking. The action cannot progress to outcome commitment until activation or a documented timeout path occurs.
4. The player activates the Roll control once. Repeated clicks, keyboard activation, touch duplication, reconnect, and retry share one idempotency key.
5. The server generates or retrieves the authoritative result and records every die face and modifier.
6. The client receives the authoritative faces and plays a short presentation animation. The animation does not determine physics or randomness.
7. The interface settles on the exact server result, exposes the breakdown according to visibility rules, and continues the deterministic and Director pipeline.

The system chooses the correct dice automatically. Players cannot add dice, remove dice, change modifiers, choose advantage, type a result, or substitute a physical roll. Where a feature permits a legitimate choice—such as which inspiration-like resource to spend—the choice occurs in a separate validated preview before the roll is created.

Default visual timing is short enough to preserve table energy. Standard presentation targets 500–900 milliseconds after result receipt; Fast presentation targets 150–400 milliseconds; reduced-motion presentation has no tumbling motion. A dramatic-roll treatment may extend to 1.5 seconds only for rare configured events such as a final death save and must remain skippable.

Secret checks, NPC rolls, environmental rolls, initiative batches, and rolls whose existence would reveal hidden information resolve automatically on the server. Player-facing text must never falsely claim that the player rolled when the server resolved a hidden roll.

Required QA includes double click, key repeat, touch repeat, tab close after activation, reconnect before animation, duplicate WebSocket delivery, animation disabled, reduced motion, screen reader, stale prompt, two devices, and attempts to modify the displayed expression through client tools. Every scenario produces at most one authoritative roll.


## 6.11 Turn economy

The engine must represent turn resources as explicit state rather than infer them from narration. At minimum, the turn state tracks movement remaining, action availability, bonus-action availability, reaction availability, free interactions governed by the rules, concentration, ongoing effects, and any feature-specific once-per-turn limits.

The UI must show what has been spent and what remains. Selecting an action previews resource use before commitment. The system must prevent a second use when a resource has been spent, even if the player changes devices or retries a command.

Rules that trigger at the start or end of a turn must be processed in a stable order. When multiple effects are controlled by the same creature and the rules permit a choice of order, the player receives a consolidated choice panel. The AI may suggest an order but may not silently choose an irreversible harmful order for a player character.

## 6.12 Movement and position

Movement is a server-authorized path, not a client coordinate update. A movement command contains the intended ordered square path, movement mode, expected state version, and optional declared interactions. The engine validates adjacency, terrain cost, the actor’s complete footprint, occupied spaces, barriers, corners, hazards, opportunity triggers, movement remaining, forced movement, and destination legality.

The client may display a predicted path, but the server recomputes the path cost and may return a corrected path or interruption point. The committed event records each traversed square when intermediate position matters. Teleportation, jumping, climbing, swimming, flying, burrowing, crawling, standing, mounting, dismounting, dragging, carrying, and squeezing use separate reviewed rule primitives rather than one generic distance subtraction.

### 6.12.1 Sole tactical topology

All exact tactical horizontal position uses a square grid. Each square represents five feet by five feet. Each cell uses integer `column` and `row` coordinates inside a versioned map coordinate space. Elevation is stored separately in feet or approved five-foot increments and cannot be inferred from screen pixels.

The production rules engine implements one native square topology. Gridless scene presentation may be used for conversation, travel, montage, downtime, and other scenes where exact position is not mechanically relevant. The moment exact movement, range, cover, line of sight, hazards, or area placement matters, the scene uses the square tactical model.

### 6.12.2 Adjacency and movement cost

Under the default SRD-compatible grid standard, an orthogonally or diagonally adjacent square normally costs five feet to enter. Difficult terrain and other modifiers change the cost of entering a square according to the rules manifest. The engine calculates the actual traversed path, not only the distance between endpoints.

The path validator must prevent diagonal corner cutting when the mover’s footprint cannot physically pass between blocked edges or occupied geometry. A one-square creature cannot pass diagonally between two blocking corners merely because the destination is adjacent. A larger creature must be tested across its full swept footprint at every step.

Campaigns may not silently enable an alternate diagonal rule. Any future optional diagonal convention requires a separately versioned rules module, visible campaign setting, version transition analysis, template revalidation, complete regression suite, and product approval. It is outside Alpha 3.

### 6.12.3 Creature footprints

A creature’s occupied space is canonical data, not a radius around a token center and not only an anchor coordinate. The reviewed defaults are four Tiny occupancy slots per five-foot square, one-by-one for Small and Medium creatures, two-by-two for Large creatures, three-by-three for Huge creatures, and four-by-four for Gargantuan creatures, with explicit exceptions stored in the creature record.

A Tiny creature uses a containing square plus one deterministic occupancy slot such as northwest, northeast, southwest, or southeast. The slot exists for sharing, selection, rendering, and collision; ordinary grid movement still occurs in five-foot square entries rather than invented two-and-a-half-foot steps. A square cannot hold more Tiny occupants than allowed, and sharing with non-Tiny creatures follows the reviewed creature-space rules. Area effects, range, line of sight, and hazards normally evaluate the containing square, while token selection and overlap controls distinguish individual Tiny occupants.

Every movement, placement, summon, teleport, transformation, forced movement, spawn, and return-from-disconnect operation must validate all destination squares and any required Tiny occupancy slot. The system must also validate the swept footprint along the path where intermediate collision matters.

A creature cannot enter a doorway, corridor, bridge, stair, landing, or gap narrower than its legal footprint unless a reviewed squeezing rule applies. Squeezing is explicit state with cost and consequences; it is not an invisible collision bypass.

### 6.12.4 Movement preview and commitment

The preview must identify:

- Ordered path.
- Cost per step.
- Total movement cost.
- Remaining movement before and after the command.
- Difficult terrain and known hazard exposure.
- Required door or object interactions.
- Known reaction opportunities without exposing hidden entities.
- Elevation changes.
- Squeezing or alternate movement mode.
- Illegal step and reason when the path fails.

The client sends intent, never an authoritative final position. The server validates from the current projection version and returns the committed path. The token animation follows the committed path and cannot choose a visually shorter route that would avoid a hazard or reaction.

### 6.12.5 Range and distance

Grid range uses the reviewed SRD square-grid measurement policy and the shortest legal square route or rule-specific measurement primitive. The engine must not mix Euclidean pixel distance, Manhattan distance, and grid-step distance unpredictably. Every rule record states which distance primitive applies.

Vertical distance must be included when mechanically relevant. A two-dimensional preview that omits elevation must display that limitation and cannot be used as the final authority.

### 6.12.6 Unknown space and hidden blockers

Movement previews through unexplored or partially known space must not reveal hidden walls, creatures, traps, or doors through snapping, path shape, timing, error text, or sound. The server may stop movement at the first newly discovered obstruction or resolve the applicable surprise consequence. The player-facing explanation reveals only what the character becomes entitled to know.

### 6.12.7 Movement conformance failures

QA must fail the implementation if:

- Endpoint distance is legal but the traversed path is not.
- A large token validates only its anchor square.
- A diagonal crosses a blocked corner.
- Difficult terrain is charged inconsistently between preview and commit.
- A rejected move leaves the token visually committed.
- A reconnect places the token from browser memory.
- A spell, effect, or hazard tests pixel overlap rather than canonical squares.
- Coordinates outside the approved row, column, edge, footprint, and elevation schema appear in an active command, event, projection, database document, or client state.

### 6.12.8 Cinematic Final-Step Adjustment

“Cinematic latitude” is not a free-form permission and may not be represented by a generic collision override, `ignoreRules` switch, off-grid pixel offset, temporary noclip state, hidden teleport, or narrator-triggered correction. The only Alpha 3 movement primitive for a cinematic final step is the **Cinematic Final-Step Adjustment**.

The compact Director Adjudicator may propose this adjustment only before the final event commits and only when every condition below is true:

- The player already confirmed a voluntary movement intent through direct controls or the Intent Intercept.
- The deterministic baseline reaches a legal endpoint but falls short of the desired destination by exactly one orthogonally or diagonally adjacent tactical square.
- Entering the additional square has an ordinary base cost of five feet. The square is not difficult terrain and does not require a special movement mode, jump, climb, swim, flight, burrow, teleport, squeeze initiation, object interaction, door operation, or additional action.
- The standard path validator approves the additional entry using the actor’s complete swept footprint. All shared-edge barriers, occupied spaces, blocked corners, elevation rules, movement-mode restrictions, hazards, opportunity triggers, and destination legality remain active.
- The destination is already represented in canonical scene geometry and is not hidden, unexplored, or inaccessible to the acting character. The adjustment cannot discover a secret passage, cross a locked or closed barrier, enter an unrevealed room, or use server rejection behavior to infer concealed geometry.
- The adjustment does not move another creature, deny another player an already committed choice, create a duplicate turn benefit, or avoid a mandatory trigger. Standard reactions and consequences caused by the additional entry still resolve.
- The adjustment is one-time for the command unless separately approved as a visible campaign precedent. It cannot chain with another movement allowance or be recursively applied.
- The player sees the proposed extra square, any known trigger, and the final movement cost or allowance in the pre-commit confirmation.

The event records the baseline endpoint, the additional destination square, the Cinematic Final-Step Adjustment category, Director reason code, affected footprint, triggered consequences, and precedent scope. The projection contains only the final committed square position. Animation may depict a slide, vault, stumble, or dramatic reach, but its endpoints and collision path must remain the canonical square path.

The post-commit Narrator cannot propose, infer, or create this adjustment. If generated prose places the character beyond the committed square, narrative validation repairs or replaces the prose; state does not change.

QA must fail the implementation if any “cinematic” field disables the standard path validator, permits pixel-authoritative position, crosses an illegal edge, avoids a reaction, enters concealed geometry, grants more than one ordinary square, or causes the Narrator’s prose to mutate movement after commitment.


### 6.12.9 Orthogonal-clearance and swept-vertex algorithm

The canonical path validator represents walls, doors, ledges, and other boundaries as edge records rather than merely marking destination cells blocked. For an orthogonal step, every face crossed by every occupied footprint cell must be open under the movement mode. For a diagonal step, the validator evaluates both adjacent orthogonal clearance cells, all touched boundary vertices, and the swept union of the mover's footprint.

A diagonal step is legal only when both orthogonal clearance channels are traversable for the complete footprint and no blocking edge or full-space obstacle occupies the swept corner. It is not enough that one L-shaped route would eventually reach the same destination. The rule prevents a token, mount, grapple pair, or large footprint from passing through a geometric gap that does not physically admit it.

Pathfinding, preview, server validation, token interpolation, forced movement, cinematic movement, and replay use the same transition primitive. A pathfinding library's default corner-cutting option, post-processing smoother, or line simplifier cannot override it. The committed event records the ordered transitions and the Grid Adjudication Standard version.

## 6.13 Attacks and defenses

An attack action flow must validate attacker capability, action economy, target legality, range, line of effect, cover, weapon or spell properties, ammunition, disadvantage or advantage, and any once-per-turn effects before the roll.

The system must distinguish melee, ranged, weapon, spell, unarmed, and special attacks. It must model reach, normal and long range, adjacent hostile creatures affecting ranged attacks where the rules require it, cover, invisibility or unseen interactions, critical behavior, damage types, resistances, immunities, vulnerabilities, temporary hit points, and concentration consequences.

Damage cannot be committed from prose. The engine resolves damage components individually so resistance or immunity applies correctly. The interface must show a concise damage ledger such as base roll, bonus, resistance, temporary hit points absorbed, and final hit point change.

## 6.14 Saving throws and area effects

Area effects use deterministic continuous geometry linked to the canonical square map and a versioned Grid Adjudication Standard. The caster or player selects only the choices the rule allows, such as origin, target point, direction, orientation, length, width, radius, height, or legal affected creatures. The preview must show legal coverage without revealing hidden creatures that the acting character cannot perceive.

### 6.14.1 Dual representation

Every area has two synchronized representations:

1. **Continuous visual geometry:** the accurate circle, cone, line, square, rectangle, wall, aura, cylinder footprint, or other top-down shape shown to the player.
2. **Affected-square set:** the deterministic server-calculated cells used for occupancy and target resolution.

The visual shape may be smooth and attractive, but the affected-square highlight must be unambiguous. Particle effects, textures, bloom, smoke, and animation do not define mechanical reach.

### 6.14.2 Default square-inclusion standard

Unless an approved rule contains a more specific instruction, a square is included when the center point of that square lies inside or on the boundary of the continuous top-down geometry. Boundary equality uses deterministic fixed-precision math and a published tolerance so different clients and server runtimes cannot disagree.

This center-point standard is a digital adjudication policy, not a claim that every edge case is expressly resolved by the SRD. It must be identified as such in the rules manifest and explained through the rules panel.

A creature is affected when at least one square in its canonical footprint is included, unless the effect’s rule explicitly uses another target standard. The server evaluates the creature once even when several occupied squares are included.

### 6.14.3 Shape requirements

The effect engine must support at minimum:

- **Sphere or circular radius:** a circle in top-down space with height behavior stored separately where relevant.
- **Cylinder:** a circular footprint plus base, height, and vertical inclusion.
- **Cone:** a directional sector or reviewed cone geometry beginning from the legal origin, with orientation controlled continuously or in documented increments.
- **Line:** a rectangle with defined length and width, not a one-pixel ray.
- **Cube:** a square top-down footprint with defined side length and vertical extent.
- **Rectangle:** a width-by-length region used by walls, terrain, and special effects.
- **Emanation:** a region extending from the origin creature’s complete footprint or another specified source boundary, not merely from its anchor square.
- **Wall:** one or more connected segments with legal length, thickness, height, placement surface, and corner behavior.
- **Aura or persistent zone:** a canonical area entity that is recomputed when its source moves if the rule requires it.

### 6.14.4 Origin, rotation, and placement

The UI must show the legal origin domain before placement. A player cannot place an effect beyond range and rely on the server to quietly pull it closer. Shapes that may rotate must have keyboard, pointer, and accessible controls. Rotation precision must be consistent between preview and server calculation.

For shapes originating from a creature, the rules record identifies whether origin is the creature, a point in its space, the edge of its footprint, a visible point, or another legal source. Multi-square creatures must not gain or lose reach accidentally because the client used the anchor square.

### 6.14.5 Walls, cover, and line of effect

Area inclusion and line of effect are separate checks. A square may geometrically fall inside a shape but be protected by total cover or an opaque barrier where the effect’s rules require a clear path. The server evaluates barriers from canonical edges and elevation.

Wall-like effects must define whether they occupy cells, edges, a thin rectangle, or another reviewed geometry. Visual art must align with the canonical wall segments. A wall cannot look open while mechanics block passage, or look closed while mechanics permit it.

### 6.14.6 Target resolution plan

Before random rolls are created, the server stores an immutable resolution plan containing the effect version, origin, orientation, affected-square set, known and hidden affected entities, required rolls, resource cost, concentration relation, and expected state version. The client receives only the authorized portion.

Each target receives its own saving throw, attack resolution, damage, healing, or condition result as required. A technical retry reuses the stored plan and existing rolls. The transaction design must commit the complete effect atomically or resume from the recorded plan without rerolling, retargeting, or charging the resource twice.

### 6.14.7 Director discretion

The deterministic geometry and target set form the baseline ruling. The Game Director may make a bounded ruling in a genuine ambiguity—such as whether a precarious creature at an exact boundary is grazed—only through the normal Director-ruling envelope and before final commit. It may not secretly resize an effect, reveal an unseen target, exclude a disliked player, or alter a revealed placement after seeing saves.

A valid adjustment records the baseline set, final set, reason, affected entities, and player-facing explanation. Repeated equivalent cases within the same scene should follow the established ruling unless the fiction materially changes.

### 6.14.8 Area-effect QA failures

QA must fail the implementation if:

- Client and server calculate different visible squares without an explicit correction.
- A hidden creature changes preview count, snapping, cursor state, timing, or sound.
- A multi-square creature is resolved more than once.
- A rotated shape renders differently from the server’s target set.
- A retry creates new saves or charges a second slot.
- A visual particle reaches squares that the UI presents as mechanically affected when they are not.
- An effect ignores total cover because its circle overlaps a blocked square.
- Area behavior bypasses the approved square and three-dimensional geometry contracts.


### 6.14.9 Canonical Area Origin Anchor Registry

Every placement-capable area rule points to a versioned anchor policy. The server enumerates legal anchors from the map coordinate space and current state. The client renders and describes those anchors but does not construct authoritative coordinates from pointer pixels.

The default fixed lattice uses integer half-cell coordinates so both five-foot grid vertices and exact square centers are representable without floating ambiguity. Elevation uses the approved fixed-precision vertical unit. Every command stores the anchor ID, coordinate-space version, fixed coordinates, elevation, anchor class, and rule-policy version.

The rules manifest may restrict an effect to:

- The source creature or object's reference anchor.
- A point in or on a source footprint.
- Grid vertices.
- Square centers.
- Registered surface anchors.
- Object, portal, or feature anchors.
- A reviewed subset of the lattice.

Free-floating browser coordinates are never accepted. Client and server use the same visible anchor set. Hidden entities and secret geometry do not alter snapping, cursor resistance, available orientation, target count, accessibility labels, or request timing.

Orientation is also deterministic. Every effect declares an angular policy such as fixed cardinal directions, approved increments, segment endpoints, or a server-normalized fixed-angle value. Raw client floating-point rotation is not canonical.

### 6.14.10 Effect Propagation Profiles and around-corner routing

Every area effect has both a geometry profile and a propagation profile. The server selects the algorithm from the reviewed rules manifest; the client cannot infer it from an animation.

For direct effects, candidate target points require the registered direct line-of-effect relation. For an effect that spreads around corners, the server performs a bounded shortest-path propagation over a three-dimensional navigation volume built from open canonical cell faces, portals, door states, shafts, stairs, and other approved transitions. The propagation cannot cross sealed total-cover boundaries, but it may pass through an open doorway and reach space that lacks a straight origin-to-target ray when the rule permits spreading.

The propagation budget is the effect's registered distance or volume limit. Graph transitions use the approved fixed distance policy and may include vertical cost. The engine first creates the continuous candidate volume, then applies the propagation relation, barriers, and effect-specific exclusions. It does not flood the entire connected map and clip afterward.

A propagation plan stores the topology version, origin anchor, candidate nodes, traversed faces or portals, shortest authorized distances, unreachable regions, final reachable volume, and affected target identities. Retries reuse the plan. Player-facing inspection may show the approved visible propagation contour without revealing hidden doors or creatures.

### 6.14.11 Three-dimensional solid evaluation

A top-down circle is only the horizontal projection of a sphere. The server evaluates the actual registered solid.

Coordinates are converted to deterministic fixed-precision world units. Sphere inclusion uses squared three-dimensional distance from the canonical origin. Cylinder inclusion tests horizontal radius plus bounded base and height. Cube, cone, wall, and custom volumes use their registered three-dimensional equations or reviewed decomposition. Boundary tolerance is fixed and versioned.

Each tactical entity has a canonical vertical reference and occupied elevation band appropriate to the map and rules representation. The Grid Adjudication Standard defines the target reference points or occupied prisms used by each effect family. The same policy applies to players, monsters, objects, hazards, summons, and persistent zones.

The default cell inclusion test remains center based, but the center is three-dimensional: horizontal square center plus the cell or entity's canonical reference elevation. An effect-specific record may use occupied-volume intersection or another reviewed rule when the licensed text requires it. The engine never substitutes a two-dimensional distance followed by unlimited vertical extrusion.

Floors, ceilings, walls, and vertical total cover participate in propagation and line-of-effect tests. A sphere may reach a lower floor through an open shaft while being blocked by a sealed floor. A cylinder may affect stacked elevations inside its height even when a sphere of the same radius would not.

### 6.14.12 Geometry inspection and conformance evidence

The placement inspector must expose, without leaking secrets:

- Anchor class and fixed coordinates.
- Elevation and orientation.
- Shape and propagation profile.
- Three-dimensional dimensions.
- Visible candidate squares or elevation slices.
- Visible blocking faces and portals.
- Final authorized affected squares and entities.
- Grid Adjudication Standard version.

QA must compare client preview, server resolution plan, semantic scene graph, mechanical event, and replay. A one-pixel pointer move between the same anchors cannot change mechanics. Different zoom, device scale, browser, camera, or antialiasing cannot change the chosen anchor or target set.

## 6.15 Conditions and ongoing effects

Conditions and ongoing effects must be typed records with source, start event, duration model, save timing, removal conditions, stacking rule, visibility, and mechanical modifiers. A condition name alone is insufficient.

The engine must support durations based on rounds, turns, absolute time, concentration, rest, scene end, save success, damage taken, movement, line of sight, or specific triggers. Start-of-turn and end-of-turn saves must occur exactly once. Reconnects and server replacement must not skip or duplicate them.

The character sheet and token must show player-relevant conditions. Hidden effects may remain concealed, but their mechanical consequences must be applied consistently and later auditable.

## 6.16 Concentration

Concentration must be modeled as a single exclusive relation between a concentrating creature and an active effect unless an approved rule explicitly changes that relation. Casting or activating a new concentration effect must show which existing effect will end before commitment.

Damage-triggered concentration checks must be generated from committed damage events. Multiple damage instances remain distinguishable. A disconnect, narration delay, or animation cannot postpone the check beyond the rules timing.

When concentration ends, dependent effects, zones, summons, and visual indicators must end through one causal event chain. No orphaned magical zone may remain because its particle effect outlived its rule record.

## 6.17 Spellcasting rules model

Each spell record must contain structured fields for level, school if included, casting time, range, components, duration, concentration, ritual capability where applicable, target model, area geometry, attack or save model, damage or healing formulas, scaling, conditions, movement, summoned entities, persistent zones, and special clauses.

The engine must separately validate:

- Whether the character has access to the spell.
- Whether it is known or prepared as required.
- Whether the correct slot or resource exists.
- Whether components are available and whether a focus or pouch satisfies them.
- Whether costly or consumed components are present.
- Whether the caster can provide verbal, somatic, and material components under current conditions.
- Whether casting time is compatible with the current turn and state.
- Whether concentration is available.
- Whether target, range, line of effect, and visibility requirements are met.
- Whether the selected slot level is legal.
- Whether the spell has an unresolved choice.

The spell button must never be a decorative list item that simply sends the spell name to AI. It must open an action panel grounded in the structured spell record.

## 6.18 Spell preparation, slots, and recovery

Spell lists, preparation limits, known spells, and slot progression must derive from approved class and character records. The sheet must clearly distinguish a spell the character knows from one prepared for use and from one currently castable.

Resource recovery during rests must be deterministic. A rest cannot be applied while unresolved encounter events would make the state ambiguous. The Director may interrupt a rest through a structured event before recovery is committed, but it cannot revoke resources after the rest has already committed merely for drama.

## 6.19 Reactions and interrupts

Reactions are exact rule-timed interrupts, not optional user-interface conveniences and not prose suggestions. The SRD defines a Reaction as an instant response to a trigger and places it immediately after the trigger unless the Reaction says otherwise. The engine must therefore represent triggering actions as staged resolution frames rather than one indivisible batch.

A triggering command cannot skip from declaration to final effect when any legal Reaction can occur between those moments. The rules manifest defines the exact checkpoint for every supported Reaction. Examples include:

- A creature begins casting a perceptible spell, before that spell resolves.
- An attack roll is determined to hit, before damage and hit-dependent effects resolve.
- A creature is about to leave another creature's reach, immediately before the triggering movement step completes.
- A creature begins to fall, before the fall is fully resolved where a supported Reaction uses that trigger.
- A creature takes damage, succeeds or fails a save, enters a square, leaves a square, or performs another event when a reviewed feature explicitly names that event as its trigger.

The implementation must never approximate all Reactions as “after the action.” It also must never open a Reaction before the rule's trigger has actually occurred. Shield-style defenses need the hit result but precede damage. Counterspell-style interruption needs a perceptible casting declaration but precedes the spell's effect. Opportunity Attacks occur immediately before the creature leaves reach. Each supported feature record must identify its trigger checkpoint, information disclosure, eligibility predicate, costs, target model, timeout behavior, and resume rule.

### 6.19.1 Resolution frames and hard interrupt boundaries

Every action capable of creating an interrupt is decomposed into ordered resolution frames. A frame has one mechanical purpose, one entry condition, one immutable input state version, and one allowed next transition. Typical attack frames are:

1. Attack declaration and target validation.
2. Pre-roll modifiers and any reactions whose trigger occurs before the roll.
3. Authoritative attack roll.
4. Hit-or-miss determination.
5. After-hit/before-damage Reaction window.
6. Authoritative damage roll when a hit remains valid.
7. Damage and hit-dependent effect commitment.
8. After-damage triggers and Reactions.
9. Mechanical result publication.
10. Narration request.

Typical spell frames are:

1. Casting declaration, target or area selection, component validation, and proposed resource cost.
2. Spell-cast Reaction window for eligible observers.
3. Resolution of any nested interrupt, including another Reaction responding to the first Reaction when rules permit it.
4. Confirmation that the original spell remains unresolved and legal.
5. Attack roll, saving throw, or direct effect resolution.
6. Additional timing windows explicitly created by the spell or feature.
7. Final spell effect and resource commitment according to the licensed rule record.
8. Mechanical publication and later narration.

A frame in `WAITING_FOR_REACTION` status is a hard server-side barrier. The parent frame cannot apply damage, finish movement, create an area, spend a later contingent resource, begin final spell animation, request final narration, or advance the turn until the Reaction window reaches a terminal state.

The browser is not the lock owner. The durable resolution record and its deadline survive disconnect, worker replacement, tab closure, reconnect, or another device taking over the same account session. No database transaction remains open while waiting for a human response.

### 6.19.2 Reaction Opportunity record

Every opportunity is represented by a typed durable record containing at least:

- Opportunity identifier.
- Parent resolution-frame identifier.
- Triggering event and rule-source identifiers.
- Trigger checkpoint enum.
- Eligible account, seat, character, or AI-controlled entity identifiers.
- Recipient-specific visible trigger facts.
- Legal Reaction option identifiers.
- Cost and availability snapshot.
- Projection version and event sequence used for eligibility.
- Opening and expiration timestamps.
- Current status: offered, viewed, selected, passed, expired, invalidated, resolving, or resolved.
- Deterministic fallback, normally Pass.
- Resulting child-frame identifiers.
- Audit evidence showing why each option was or was not eligible.

The client never supplies a new Reaction option name, target, cost, die expression, or rule interpretation. It selects one server-offered option or Passes. The server revalidates eligibility and state version before acceptance.

A reaction-use submission is idempotent. Repeated clicks, retries, reconnect replay, or duplicate WebSocket messages cannot spend the Reaction twice, consume two spell slots, create two attacks, or resolve the parent action more than once.

### 6.19.3 Reaction prompt UX

The Reaction prompt must appear above ordinary chat and action controls without visually covering the triggering map area. It must:

- Clearly state that play is paused for a Reaction decision.
- Identify the perceivable trigger without exposing hidden information.
- Display the exact legal options the character currently has.
- Show Action-economy and resource cost.
- Explain the immediate mechanical purpose in plain language.
- Provide a prominent Use control and an equally accessible Pass control.
- Show a visible countdown and the timeout result.
- Remain keyboard accessible and announced through a dedicated assertive live region that does not reread the entire combat log.
- Preserve focus safely when it opens and restore focus when it closes.
- Avoid an animation or sound delay before the player can respond.

The prompt must not claim the triggering outcome is final. It may say “The attack would hit” or “A visible creature begins casting a spell,” but it cannot say “You take 8 damage” before the defensive window closes. A pre-resolution suspense sentence may be shown only when it contains no committed-outcome claim.

The default live-play timer is twelve seconds. Campaign owners may select an approved range from eight to thirty seconds during campaign setup; accessibility preferences may request the campaign's longer approved setting but cannot secretly pause the table forever. Expiration defaults to Pass. A player can Pass immediately. Alpha 3 does not allow another player or host to choose the Reaction for the owner.

A disconnected player may still answer if the connection returns before the deadline. If the deadline expires, the opportunity Passes. No AI guesses whether that player “probably would have” spent a slot. A player may configure deterministic prompt-suppression or auto-Pass rules, but Alpha 3 does not auto-spend a scarce resource or take an offensive Reaction on the player's behalf.

### 6.19.4 Nested and competing Reactions

A Reaction can itself create another trigger. The system represents this as a parent-child resolution-frame tree, not as free-form recursive model conversation. The newest valid child interrupt resolves before its parent resumes. After each child resolution, the server recomputes the parent from canonical state; it does not assume the original outcome still applies.

When multiple creatures can respond to the same trigger, ordering follows the reviewed SRD rule record. If the SRD leaves a genuine simultaneous-order choice to the Game Master, the Director receives a typed ordering decision request with only legal candidates and returns one ordered identifier list. It cannot change the available options or outcomes.

The implementation must detect cycles caused by defects or malformed content. A safety threshold may stop and quarantine an impossible repeated frame pattern, but it cannot silently discard a legitimate chain merely because many creatures are involved. A stopped chain creates a visible rules-system incident, preserves all committed history, blocks further mutation of that action, and requires audited correction rather than guessing.

### 6.19.5 Visibility and information disclosure

Reaction eligibility and prompt content are recipient-specific. The server discloses only what the triggering rule and the character's senses permit.

- A spell-cast prompt does not reveal the spell's identity, target, slot level, hidden caster feature, or secret objective unless another rule or successful knowledge event established it.
- A hidden NPC's potential Reaction is never sent to player clients before it is used.
- A Reaction prompt shown to one player does not expose that player's private inventory, prepared spells, or tactical preferences to others.
- A shared “waiting” indicator may state that an interrupt is resolving without naming secret options.
- The presence or absence of model latency must not reveal that a hidden creature has a Reaction. NPC reaction decisions use prevalidated tactical policies or a compact bounded decision path with a fixed visible cadence and timeout-to-Pass behavior.

Every final narrative receives the settled frame tree and may describe only Reactions that were committed or publicly observable. It cannot retroactively invent a missed interrupt or imply that a player declined an option they were never legally offered.

### 6.19.6 Reaction-specific state and turn economy

The character projection must show whether the Reaction is available, spent, restored, suppressed, or conditionally unavailable. The Reaction indicator updates from committed events, not from prompt-local state.

When a Reaction changes armor class, position, damage, a spell's existence, or another downstream value, all affected later frames recompute from the committed Reaction event. A defensive Reaction that turns a hit into a miss prevents the damage frame from opening. A Reaction attack that stops or incapacitates a mover forces the remaining movement plan to revalidate. A countered spell never advances to its target-resolution frames.

Restoration of a Reaction at the start of the creature's turn creates a canonical mechanical notice. A player must never discover that their Reaction was unavailable only after clicking an option that the UI should have known was illegal.

### 6.19.7 Reaction acceptance failures

The QA agent must fail the implementation if any of the following occurs:

- Damage commits before an eligible after-hit defensive Reaction closes.
- A spell effect appears before a legal spell-cast interrupt resolves.
- A moving token visually or canonically exits reach before an Opportunity Attack checkpoint.
- The Narrator states a final result while the frame is waiting.
- A player is prompted for an option they cannot legally afford or use.
- A legal option is absent because the AI did not think of it.
- A timeout causes an automatic resource spend.
- A duplicate response spends a Reaction twice.
- A reconnect opens an already resolved opportunity again.
- Hidden information leaks through the prompt, shared log, timing, telemetry exposed to clients, or accessibility text.
- A local client flag, animation callback, or chat response advances the parent frame without a canonical terminal opportunity event.

## 6.20 Hit points, defeat, death, and recovery

Hit points, temporary hit points, healing, damage overflow, death saves, stabilization, and death must be explicit state transitions. The system must prevent current hit points from exceeding the legal maximum or dropping below the internal bound used for death calculations.

At 0 hit points, the interface must change to a focused survival view. It must explain what the player can still do, show death-save state when visible, and avoid celebratory or punitive language. Death saves use preserved server rolls and cannot be rerolled on reconnect.

The Director may choose a nonlethal narrative consequence when the rules and campaign tone allow, but it may not secretly erase a lethal result after showing it as final. A rescue, capture, bargain, or miraculous intervention must be a visible Director ruling with a cost, permission, or campaign rule supporting it.


### 6.20.1 Death state, memorial beat, revival, and continued player participation

When the rules engine commits character death, the system freezes ordinary living-character commands and creates an immutable Character Death Event linked to the causal events and preserved rolls. Death does not grant a host, player, retry, recap edit, or prose generator authority to restore the character. Restoration can occur only through a subsequently committed, rules-valid revival effect or a narrow audited correction for a verified implementation defect.

When fiction permits, the player receives one optional **Final Beat** prompt. It may contain a last line, gesture, memory, curse, joke, or instruction that does not change mechanics, transfer an item, reveal unknown facts, attack, cast a spell, or extend consciousness beyond the committed result. The player may skip it. The prompt times out safely so the table is not trapped.

The Narrator then produces a memorable memorial scene from committed facts and approved memories. It should acknowledge the character's defining choices and table history rather than output a generic death paragraph. Tone follows the player's saved memorial preference and current scene: Epic, Historical, Defiant, Darkly Funny, Tender, or Contextual. Humor is optional and never imposed because a session-level humor target exists.

The live table receives a concise mechanical death card and streamed narration. The campaign chronicle stores a memorial entry, portrait, level, defining moments selected from canonical events, cause of death at the permitted visibility level, remains status, and any Final Beat. The narration must use language such as **dead**, **fallen**, or **lost for now** according to the fiction; it must not claim permanent retirement or impossibility of revival unless the canonical eligibility record supports that conclusion.

The player remains a table participant and text-chat member. The interface offers spectator mode and in-product creation of another eligible character for later narrated entry. Creating another character does not transfer, delete, or permanently retire the dead character.

A revival attempt is a new forward-moving command. It validates the specific effect, elapsed fictional time, target identity, remains, material components, caster resources, location, effect restrictions, and any soul-consent choice. The original death and memorial events remain immutable. A successful revival creates a new living-state transition and return narration; it never rewrites history as though the death did not happen.

Permanent retirement is separate from death. It requires the account owner, explicit irreversible confirmation, and an eligibility summary explaining that retirement prevents future play and revival in this campaign. The campaign owner and Game Director cannot retire another player's character.

## 6.21 Rest, time, travel, and resource clocks

The campaign must maintain a canonical game clock separate from real-world time. Travel, spell durations, rests, environmental effects, and scheduled events consume game time through events.

The AI Director may summarize uneventful travel, but the system still accounts for elapsed time, movement pace, resources, watches, conditions, and encounter checks that the campaign uses. Players must be told when a summary will advance significant time and given an opportunity to state preparations.

A long or short rest request opens a preview of expected recovery and unresolved risks. Rest completion is a committed event, not a sentence in narration.

## 6.22 Social interaction and agency

NPC attitudes, goals, fears, knowledge, promises, and leverage must be structured enough to prevent the AI from granting arbitrary success. Social rolls affect NPC behavior within plausible boundaries; they do not mind-control ordinary creatures unless a rule explicitly creates such an effect.

Player-versus-player persuasion, deception, intimidation, charm, theft, or hostile action requires campaign consent rules. A player cannot roll to control another player character’s beliefs, emotions, or choices. The affected player decides their character’s internal response.

## 6.23 Hiding, perception, and secret information

The engine must distinguish what exists, what a character can perceive, what the player is allowed to see, and what the Director knows. Hidden creatures and objects remain in canonical state but are excluded from player projections.

Searches and perception checks must not leak success through UI timing, target highlighting, sound, network payload size, or error messages. The same response shape and similar timing should be used for “nothing found” and “not found” where practical.

When a hidden entity becomes perceived, one reveal event updates map visibility, token rendering, narrative context, and any newly legal actions.

## 6.24 Inventory, equipment, and encumbrance

Inventory entries must identify quantity, ownership, container, weight if used, equipped state, attunement or activation state where applicable, charges, durability only if an enabled rule requires it, and provenance.

Transferring an item between players is a two-party transaction when the recipient is online and a pending offer when they are not. The system must prevent duplication during retries. Equipping an item must update derived values and legal actions through deterministic recalculation.

The Director cannot create permanent treasure through prose. Treasure is proposed, validated against campaign authority and content availability, then committed as item records.

### 6.24.1 Equipment, hand, and weapon-state truth

Equipment state is mechanical state. Every carried object has a canonical location and availability status such as equipped in a named hand, worn, stowed in a reachable container, carried but inaccessible, dropped in a square, lodged, consumed, destroyed, transferred, or otherwise unavailable. The system must not reduce inventory to an unordered list of names.

The character aggregate records at least:

- Main-hand and off-hand occupancy where hands matter.
- Worn armor and shield state.
- Readied spellcasting focus, component pouch, tools, ammunition source, and relevant containers.
- Stowed and dropped item locations.
- Weapon kind, properties, mastery property, and whether the character has the required mastery feature for that kind.
- Current grip mode for Versatile or Two-Handed use where mechanically relevant.
- Ammunition, loading, charges, attunement, and consumable counts.
- Any effect that ends when an item is dropped, stowed, released, or no longer held.

The SRD rule manifest—not the Narrator—controls when an Attack action permits equipping or unequipping a weapon, how Light and thrown weapons interact with attacks, when a free hand is needed for spell components, and which mastery property applies to the weapon actually used. Each equip, unequip, draw, stow, drop, pick-up, hand-transfer, grip change, ammunition use, and item consumption is a typed proposed step and, when legal, a committed event.

A weapon's Mastery property is available only when all of the following are true:

1. The character has a feature granting mastery for that weapon kind.
2. The canonical item used for the attack has that mastery property.
3. The weapon is legally equipped or drawn at the required frame.
4. The attack, hit, miss, damage, target, size, frequency, and timing predicates of the property are satisfied.
5. Any choice or follow-up roll is resolved at the correct checkpoint.

The engine must not keep a generic “active mastery” toggle independent of the weapon. Changing weapons changes the eligible property set immediately through canonical projection.

### 6.24.2 Equipment actions inside compound turns

A natural-language statement such as “I sheathe the sword, draw my bow, move to the doorway, and fire” is not flavor. It becomes a sequential action plan whose equipment nodes are checked against the SRD action and interaction economy at the exact attack frames where they occur.

An equip or unequip step may be permitted before or after an attack when the applicable rule says so. It cannot be inserted retroactively after the player learns a result merely to make an otherwise illegal attack possible. Movement between attacks, Extra Attack sequencing, Light weapon use, mastery triggers, and hand availability must all re-evaluate after each committed step.

When a later equipment step becomes illegal, earlier committed attacks and movement remain committed. The plan stops and returns control if the turn is still open. The system does not silently drop a shield, invent a third hand, move a focus into a pocket, or treat a stowed bow as already wielded.

### 6.24.3 Narrator equipment-claim boundary

The Narrator receives a typed equipment snapshot and a list of committed equipment events relevant to the described moment. It is prohibited from describing a state-bearing equipment action unless that event is present.

State-bearing verbs include, but are not limited to, drawing, sheathing, stowing, dropping, picking up, handing over, reloading, consuming, breaking, donning, doffing, equipping, unequipping, gripping with one or two hands, switching weapons, producing a component, and freeing a hand.

The post-generation claim validator compares equipment assertions in prose with the committed equipment events and final projection. If a sentence implies an uncommitted change, the server must:

1. Remove or rewrite the sentence into mechanically neutral flavor.
2. Revalidate the repaired sentence.
3. Use concise fallback narration if repair fails.
4. Record the mismatch for model-quality review.

Neutral description may characterize motion without changing state—for example, “you square your stance” or “the blade catches the torchlight”—but may not imply possession, readiness, item location, or a different weapon than canonical state supports.

The visual token badge, action tray, character sheet, attack options, mastery badge, hand indicators, and narration all derive from the same projection. A player cannot see a bow in prose, a sword in the hand indicator, and a crossbow attack in the action tray.

### 6.24.4 Equipment-truth QA failures

The implementation fails if:

- A stowed or dropped weapon can attack without a legal equip event.
- A mastery property remains active after switching to another weapon.
- The prose changes held gear without a committed event.
- The token image or hand indicator leads or lags canonical equipment state.
- A spell requiring a free hand or component is offered despite incompatible hand state.
- Ammunition or a consumed component changes only in local UI.
- Reconnect restores inventory counts but not exact held/stowed/dropped state.
- A multiattack sequence uses mutually incompatible weapons without legal intermediate equip or unequip steps.
- A narrator repair silently creates the missing equipment event.

## 6.25 Monsters and NPC mechanics

Every combat-capable NPC or monster must have an approved stat block or a generated stat block that has passed deterministic validation before it enters an encounter. The AI cannot invent an attack bonus or damage expression during narration.

Generated encounter entities must satisfy schema, challenge budget policy, hit point bounds, Armor Class bounds, action completeness, damage sanity checks, movement and sense validity, and content-rating rules. The encounter planner may adjust composition before reveal, but cannot silently rewrite an enemy’s core statistics after players make decisions based on them.

Dynamic difficulty must use encounter design, reinforcement timing, morale, objectives, terrain, and Director rulings—not retroactive hit point manipulation tied to player connection count.

## 6.26 Rule bending contract

The baseline engine calculates the licensed default. The Game Director may then issue a structured ruling inside the approved envelope. A ruling must state:

- The flexible rule or ambiguity involved.
- Fictional justification.
- Mechanical adjustment.
- Magnitude.
- Duration.
- Beneficiary and affected entities.
- Cost, complication, or tradeoff if any.
- Whether the ruling is one-time, scene precedent, or campaign precedent.
- Visibility to players.

Permitted examples include a small advantage for excellent preparation, allowing an improvised environmental action that passes the deterministic potency comparator, converting a binary failure into partial success with a meaningful cost, or applying the exact Cinematic Final-Step Adjustment defined in Section 6.12.8. A phrase such as “rule of cool,” “cinematic,” “comparable,” or “minor” has no mechanical authority by itself.

Prohibited examples include changing a revealed roll, inventing a missing spell slot, transferring character ownership, exposing hidden information, ignoring consent, duplicating an item, bypassing safety policy, granting an unbounded permanent feature, switching off collision, creating off-grid position, inventing an absence location, or passing free-form mechanical instructions from one AI role to another.

A valid ruling becomes the authoritative result. State mutation, visual effects, narration, logs, and subsequent precedent must all reflect it.

### 6.26.1 Improvised action reference requirement

Every improvised action with mechanical consequences must cite exactly one approved **reference profile** before the Director may adjust it. A reference profile is either:

- A rules-manifest action the acting character could legally choose at that moment using the proposed action economy and resources.
- A reviewed universal action appropriate to the actor, such as an ordinary attack, shove-like contest, object interaction, or ability check.
- A canonical environmental interaction profile attached to the exact object, hazard, terrain feature, or scene element involved.

The reference must be currently available, not merely present somewhere on the character sheet. A spent spell slot, unequipped weapon, unavailable feature, silenced spell, unreachable object, concealed hazard, or action already consumed cannot supply the potency ceiling. If the improvisation spends a limited resource, that resource and its tier are explicit in the Intent Intercept. If it spends no limited resource, its ceiling is an at-will or ordinary-action reference.

The Director may choose among eligible references, but the server validates eligibility. The model cannot supply an arbitrary numeric ceiling or cite an unavailable high-level feature to inflate the result.

### 6.26.2 Improvised Action Potency Profile and comparator

The server constructs a potency profile for both the proposed improvisation and its reference. At minimum, the comparator evaluates:

- Action, Bonus Action, Reaction, movement, interaction, and setup cost.
- Limited-resource tier and whether the resource is actually spent.
- Attack roll, ability check, saving throw, automatic effect, and failure behavior.
- Number of targets and whether targets are selected, adjacent, line-based, area-based, or indiscriminate.
- Range, reach, area dimensions, and required line of effect.
- Damage dice expression, static modifiers, expected damage, maximum possible damage, damage type, and whether damage repeats.
- Healing or temporary-hit-point magnitude where applicable.
- Forced-movement distance and direction restrictions.
- Condition severity, duration, repeat saves, escape method, concentration, and immunity interactions.
- Object, terrain, cover, visibility, and environmental prerequisites.
- Repeatability, setup dependence, self-risk, ally risk, and opportunity cost.

The proposed action must not exceed the reference in any potency dimension unless an exchange is explicitly allowed by a reviewed conversion table. Alpha 3 does not permit the Director or an implementation subagent to invent exchange rates. Increasing one dimension does not automatically justify increasing another. Full reference damage plus an additional full-strength control effect is prohibited unless the reference itself contains both.

The following ceilings apply even before a more detailed conversion table exists:

- The proposed damage dice expression, expected damage, and maximum damage cannot exceed the strongest eligible reference that is currently legal and actually paid for.
- An at-will improvisation cannot use a limited-resource spell or feature as its ceiling.
- A single-target reference cannot become an area effect.
- A non-damaging reference cannot gain damaging dice merely because the narration describes impact or fire.
- A reference without forced movement cannot add more than the reviewed minor rider, and the Alpha 3 default minor rider is at most five feet with a successful contest or save and no prohibited collision.
- A reference without a condition cannot add a severe condition. Any allowed minor condition rider must come from an approved table, use a save or contest where required, and expire no later than the end of the affected creature’s next turn unless the reference supports longer duration.
- Stunned, Paralyzed, Unconscious, Dominated, Petrified, instant defeat, permanent impairment, resource restoration, extra turns, and equivalent high-severity outcomes require an explicit rules-manifest or environmental reference that already authorizes them.
- The action cannot be more repeatable, longer ranged, longer lasting, safer, broader, and stronger than its reference merely because the fictional setup is clever. Creativity may improve the chance, positioning, or tradeoff inside the envelope; it does not erase the envelope.

A failed comparator returns the exact exceeded dimensions and allowed alternatives. The fixed player intent and any already generated random result are preserved. The Director may submit one bounded repair or the engine uses the legal baseline.

### 6.26.3 Environmental improvisation truth

Environmental power must come from canonical scene data. A dusty room, hanging chandelier, unstable bridge, oil pool, collapsing shelf, burning brazier, or loose boulder has no extraordinary mechanical potency unless the scene contains an approved interaction or hazard profile describing its location, prerequisites, affected region, checks or saves, damage or control bounds, persistence, and resulting object state.

The Director may recognize a plausible ordinary interaction with an unprofiled object, but the result is capped by the eligible ordinary-action reference and cannot create a large explosion, broad area, severe condition, or high-tier spell analogue. Throwing a torch into scenery that merely looks dusty does not become a third-level area spell because the paragraph was enthusiastic.

Creating or upgrading an environmental profile is a map-authoring or campaign-preparation operation subject to validation and provenance. It is not an in-turn narration side effect.
