Each generated asset record must preserve the anchor version, complete request, model and model version, seed or equivalent reproducibility data when available, source references, generation date, reviewer, originality result, accessibility review, intended placement, and replacement history.

No prompt may use a living artist’s name, a commercial franchise, a copyrighted character, or instructions to imitate a recognizable protected style. Reference images require provenance and usage authorization. Failed originality or style-consistency review places the asset in quarantine rather than allowing a developer to “temporarily” ship it.

### 8.17.4 Cohesion and visual-quality gates

A candidate build fails visual certification when any of the following occurs:

- A screen introduces an unregistered visual language or resembles a different genre.
- Map, portrait, token, spell effect, and interface appear to belong to unrelated products.
- Tactical readability is sacrificed for atmosphere.
- The same mechanical state uses different visual semantics in different screens.
- Generated assets visibly change a recurring character’s identity without a canonical transformation.
- A component bypasses design tokens with a local literal or arbitrary stacking value.
- A visual-regression snapshot is updated solely to make a failure disappear.
- Decorative art causes text, focus, targets, templates, warnings, or hit areas to become unclear.

Phase evidence must include a visual-cohesion contact sheet showing the landing page, character creator, campaign gate, exploration scene, combat scene, spell effect, character sheet, chronicle, modal, error state, loading state, and reduced-effects mode together. QA must inspect the set as one product, not as isolated screenshots. Phase 6/7 deep challenge independently samples the full-product visual set.


### 8.17.5 Opening identity sequence and title transition

The opening identity sequence is part of the Design System Manifest and has its own named motion, typography, sound, performance, and fallback tokens. It is not an independent microsite and may not establish a second visual language.

#### 8.17.5.1 Required visual progression

The approved progression is:

1. The usable landing page begins loading beneath a near-black Obsidian Chronicle presentation layer.
2. Subtle stone, parchment, mist, or map texture becomes perceptible without hiding the skip control or title semantics.
3. Fine lines, edges, or fragments suggest a dungeon map, archway, path, or remembered place forming from incomplete information.
4. The geometry briefly misaligns, refracts, or dissolves in a restrained manner that supports the word “Hallucinated” without producing visual chaos.
5. Controlled light and color collect near the focal area without obscuring the title, skip control, or underlying page.
6. The fragments resolve into the exact title **Hallucinated Dungeons**.
7. The title settles without a permanent neon glow, the presentation layer blends into the actual landing composition, and the authentication or invitation state is already ready or visibly loading underneath.

The exact animation may evolve through reviewed prototypes, but it must preserve this emotional rhythm: emergence, slight uncertainty, confident resolution, immediate usability.

#### 8.17.5.2 Frequency and bypass rules

The full sequence appears at most once per browser session for an anonymous or signed-out landing-page visit. A non-authoritative local preference may suppress repeated presentation, but absence of that preference cannot affect account, invitation, or campaign state.

The full sequence is bypassed for:

- Authenticated deep links into a campaign or dashboard.
- Invitation continuation after authentication.
- Reconnect and state resynchronization.
- Active-session resume.
- Browser Back and Forward navigation.
- Internal route transitions.
- Automated accessibility or low-graphics preference where the full sequence adds no value.

A returning landing-page visitor may receive the abbreviated title resolve, but no repeat visitor must wait through the complete sequence to reach a form they have already used.

#### 8.17.5.3 Interaction and accessibility

From the first interactive frame:

- A visible or accessibly named **Skip intro** control is available.
- Escape, Enter, Space, pointer activation, and touch may dismiss the sequence without accidental form submission.
- Focus is never trapped behind or beneath the presentation layer.
- Screen readers encounter one correctly structured page title and do not hear every decorative fragment.
- Reduced-motion mode renders a static or brief fade-based title.
- High-contrast and forced-colors modes preserve the title and skip action.
- The sequence contains no required information unavailable after dismissal.
- The title does not replace the semantic page heading.

The presentation layer may intercept decorative pointer events only while visible. It must release all pointer and keyboard ownership atomically when skipped or completed.

#### 8.17.5.4 Performance and failure behavior

The sequence must not depend on a large autoplay video. It uses manifest-approved lightweight assets and rendering methods that degrade cleanly.

Certification requires:

- No blank screen while the sequence bundle loads.
- No layout shift that moves the sign-in form after the title resolves.
- No blocking wait on optional sound or generated art.
- Immediate static fallback after animation error, asset failure, unsupported rendering, or reduced-effects activation.
- The ability to submit authentication as soon as the underlying page is ready after skipping.
- Frame-time and responsiveness evidence on every supported desktop browser and certified tablet class.
- No replay after reconnect or campaign resume.

#### 8.17.5.5 Optional non-musical sound

Opening sound is disabled unless site sound was previously enabled and the browser permits playback without a new disruptive prompt. The sound design is brief, original or properly licensed, non-musical, and mixed below ordinary game effect peaks.

Approved categories include low stone movement, soft air movement, parchment or map texture, muted resonance, and one subtle title-settle accent. Prohibited categories include orchestral stings, songs, rhythmic musical beds, synthetic spoken taglines, jump-scare impacts, and loud sub-bass intended to startle.

#### 8.17.5.6 Cinematic asset manifest

The opening sequence has one versioned **Cinematic Asset Manifest**. It lists every programmatic module and file that can participate in the sequence, including:

- Stable asset identifier.
- Asset class.
- Local hosted path.
- Content hash.
- Original or licensed provenance.
- License restrictions.
- Visual or sound role.
- Required or optional status.
- Compressed and decoded size.
- Supported browser formats.
- Accessibility behavior.
- Reduced-motion behavior.
- Failure fallback.
- Review status.
- Manifest version first approving the asset.
- Replacement or deprecation record.

No unregistered asset, remote hotlink, data fetched from a design workspace, generative request, or developer-local file may appear in a certified sequence. An asset referenced by source but absent from the release fails the asset-manifest check before deployment.

Programmatic paths and particles are equally governed. “Generated in code” does not exempt a motion system from visual review, performance measurement, reduced-motion replacement, deterministic seeding where needed for reproducible screenshots, or the Design System Manifest's accessibility/readability/color-coherence contract.

The semantic title is ordinary accessible text. A vector wordmark may visually overlay or mask it, but failure of the vector cannot remove the page name, heading structure, browser title, or assistive-technology label.

#### 8.17.5.7 Asset loading and cache behavior

The landing shell does not wait for optional cinematic files. Asset acquisition follows this order:

1. Render the semantic landing shell, title, legal links, skip control, invitation state, and authentication readiness.
2. Determine reduced-motion, low-graphics, visit-frequency, and sound preferences without treating them as account authority.
3. Begin the highest permitted presentation mode whose required local assets are already available or can load inside the nonblocking budget.
4. Downgrade immediately when an asset fails, arrives too late, decodes incorrectly, violates integrity, or exceeds a runtime performance threshold.
5. Never upgrade mid-sequence in a way that restarts or lengthens the intro.

Cached assets must be content-addressed or versioned. A stale cached title, texture, or audio file cannot be combined silently with a new manifest. Cache mismatch produces a clean fallback or fetch of the matching release asset; it does not produce a hybrid visual composition.

Optional sound loading begins only after the page is usable and only when prior site-sound consent or preference permits it. Failure to decode audio is silent and does not create a toast, retry loop, or blocked title.


### 8.17.6 Original logo and responsive brand-mark system

The product requires a complete original identity family, not only a generated title image.

Required deliverables:

- Primary horizontal wordmark.
- Compact emblem or monogram.
- Favicon and browser-tab mark.
- Square social and campaign-invite mark.
- Monochrome light and dark variants.
- Small-size and reduced-detail variants.
- Motion-safe title treatment for the opening sequence.
- Accessible text equivalent and semantic page title independent of image loading.
- Clear-space, minimum-size, color, contrast, misuse, and background rules.

The mark must remain recognizable on the landing page, dashboard, game header, loading state, legal pages, error pages, screenshots, and reduced-effects mode. It cannot depend on any glow, gradient, or single color for legibility.

Final logo construction uses reviewed vector geometry and proofread text. Raw generated lettering is concept material only. The logo requires originality, trademark, visual-similarity, accessibility, and cross-size review.

### 8.17.7 Ambient motion and looped visual-life contract

Where appropriate, the visual stage should feel alive through restrained, repeatable motion such as:

- Torch and firelight variation.
- Drifting mist, dust, snow, rain, ash, insects, or embers.
- Water, smoke, foliage, banners, clouds, or distant environmental movement.
- Gentle magical-zone pulsing.
- Token breathing, stance, hover, or selection motion that does not change position.
- Dialogue portrait focus and subtle environmental parallax.
- Door, trap, spell, projectile, impact, damage, healing, condition, and defeat animations tied to committed events.

Ambient loops are decorative state described by the Visual Scene Manifest. They cannot originate from AI prose, alter mechanics, hide a token, or imply an uncommitted event.

Motion requirements:

- Use seamless loops without a visible snap or accumulating drift.
- Pause or reduce loops when the tab is hidden, the scene is offscreen, the user selects reduced motion, the device enters a reduced-effects tier, or the frame budget is exceeded.
- Avoid synchronized flashing, rapid luminance changes, continuous camera motion, or movement behind text that harms reading.
- Never encode a hazard, target, turn, or condition only through animation.
- Limit concurrent effects through a central budget and degrade decorative effects before tactical cues.
- Preserve deterministic or seedable checkpoints for visual QA.
- Ensure looping assets do not trigger repeated sounds. Audio follows separate scene-zone and Presentation Cue Plan authority.

A static alternative must preserve mood using approved art, lighting, and composition rather than collapsing to a blank surface.

### 8.17.8 Visual coherence across every player-facing screen

The Design System Manifest and Art Direction Prompt Anchor apply to:

- Logo and login.
- Legal and conditional eligibility/affirmation pages.
- Dashboard and invitations.
- Character builder and quick-start templates.
- Character vault.
- Campaign setup and session zero.
- Social, exploration, travel, rest, and combat screens.
- Chronicle, Party Chat, Rules Desk, and Action Composer.
- Error, reconnect, outage, unsupported-browser, and recovery screens.
- Memorial, revival, advancement, and campaign-continuation experiences.

A screen cannot be exempted as “administrative” and ship as an unrelated default component library page. Trust and polish must survive the entire lifecycle.

## 8.18 Interaction language contract

The interface must use one stable vocabulary. The same concept cannot be called “action,” “move,” “command,” and “event” interchangeably in player-facing controls. Technical terms may exist in logs, but player language must remain consistent.

Required player-facing terms include:

- **Do This:** opens or confirms a chosen character action only where the exact action name is already visible.
- **Confirm:** commits a previewed action.
- **Cancel:** discards an uncommitted preview.
- **End Turn:** declares no further voluntary action in the current turn.
- **Step Away:** begins a temporary absence.
- **Leave Session:** records durable departure intent. Outside active Initiative it may begin legal Departure Handling; during active Initiative it marks the player absent while the character remains under `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` until Initiative ends.
- **Reconnect:** attempts technical resynchronization.
- **Ask Why:** explains a result or restriction.
- **Request Review:** invokes the ruling review process.

Generic labels such as Submit, Continue, OK, Proceed, or Execute may be used only when context is unmistakable. Destructive actions name the object and consequence.

## 8.19 Feedback timing

Every player input must receive immediate local acknowledgment without pretending it has committed. The interface distinguishes:

- Selected.
- Previewing.
- Awaiting confirmation.
- Sent.
- Accepted by server.
- Resolving.
- Waiting for another player or reaction.
- Committed.
- Rejected.
- Corrected.

These states use text and iconography, not color alone. A player must never click repeatedly because the button appears dead while the server is working.

### 8.19.1 Canonical Mechanical Notice Feed

The live table must include a distinct Mechanical Notice Feed generated from committed events and recipient-safe projection deltas. It is not part of AI narration, cannot be delayed by model generation, and cannot be edited by the Narrator.

The feed communicates rule-relevant changes such as:

- A condition begins, changes, suppresses another effect, or ends.
- Concentration begins, is tested, is maintained, or is lost.
- A spell, feature, light source, hazard, zone, resistance, temporary benefit, or penalty changes duration or expires.
- A Reaction is spent or restored.
- An Action, Bonus Action, movement allowance, attack, charge, ammunition, spell slot, item, or other tracked resource changes.
- A weapon is equipped, unequipped, drawn, stowed, dropped, consumed, or made unavailable.
- Armor Class, speed, reach, senses, cover, visibility, or targeting eligibility changes for an observable reason.
- A door, obstacle, environmental source, persistent zone, or interactable object changes state.
- A death save, stabilization state, defeat state, or other survival threshold changes.
- Initiative, active turn, round, or interrupt ownership changes.

Every notice includes a controlled category, salience, source event, affected visible entity, plain-language message, icon, timestamp or game-time marker, and link to the relevant sheet, map location, or event details when authorized.

Critical notices cannot be collapsed, suppressed by narration, or hidden behind chat scrolling. High-salience examples include concentration loss, expiration of a major buff, newly unavailable Reaction, light loss that changes visibility, weapon-state change that invalidates an action, dropping to 0 Hit Points, and a turn beginning with materially different capabilities.

Low-salience repeated notices may group into one expandable entry, but grouping cannot conceal the exact final value or event count. The feed is filterable by personal, party, combat, resource, condition, and environment categories. Filters affect presentation only; they do not prevent a critical alert.

### 8.19.2 Persistent status surfaces

Decision-relevant ongoing state must also remain visible outside the scrolling feed:

- Conditions and concentration appear as labeled chips with source and remaining duration where the character is allowed to know it.
- Light and vision show current radius and source.
- Reaction availability is visible near turn economy.
- Active spell and feature durations show the relevant remaining rounds, turns, or game time.
- Weapon and hand state appear beside available attacks.
- A selected target's visible conditions and effect zones appear in the target panel.

When an effect expires, the chip changes state and disappears only after a brief accessible transition paired with the canonical notice. The interface must not simply remove Bless, extinguish a torch radius, or restore a Reaction with no explanation.

### 8.19.3 Turn Delta Summary

At the beginning of a player's turn, and after reconnect or return from a backgrounded tab, the interface presents a compact **What Changed Since You Last Had Control** summary when material changes occurred. It is derived from event sequence ranges, not from AI memory.

Examples include:

- “Bless ended at the start of this round.”
- “Your Reaction is available again.”
- “The torch went out; your visible area is smaller.”
- “You are now Slowed until the start of the ogre's next turn.”
- “Your bow is stowed and your longsword is in hand.”
- “The northern door is open.”

The summary cannot reveal hidden events or private changes belonging to another character. It is informational and does not pause the turn unless a required choice is pending.

### 8.19.4 Mechanical notice accessibility and reliability

Critical notices use a concise live region separate from streaming prose. Screen-reader announcements must not duplicate the same event through the map, feed, toast, and chat. Reduced-motion mode removes floating-number travel while retaining text, icon, and final value.

Every notice is replayable after reconnect using event sequence identifiers. Duplicate delivery is deduplicated by notice identifier. A client may acknowledge that a notice was seen, but acknowledgment is not required for the state change to remain valid or for the table to continue.

### 8.19.5 Silent-state failure conditions

The implementation fails if:

- A duration reaches zero without a visible canonical notice.
- A concentration effect disappears only from backend state.
- A player's available action changes without the action tray and status surface updating from the same projection.
- Narration is the only indication of a resource or equipment change.
- A reconnect skips important changes that occurred while disconnected.
- A hidden NPC attitude or unseen effect leaks into the notice feed.
- A client computes an expiration from its own timer and mutates UI before the server event.
- A narrative timeout suppresses mechanical notices.

## 8.20 Confirmation policy

Confirmation dialogs are reserved for actions that are irreversible, costly, socially consequential, or ambiguous. Routine movement and common attacks should use a compact preview plus one confirmation, not multiple modal layers.

Mandatory confirmation includes:

- Spending a rare or nonrenewable resource.
- Ending concentration to begin another effect.
- Leaving while active responsibilities exist.
- Deleting or transferring content.
- Starting hostile player-versus-player action.
- Accepting a permanent bargain or campaign consequence.
- Applying a Director interpretation whose impact is materially different from the player’s stated intent.

The confirmation must state the consequence in plain language. Dark patterns and preselected consent are prohibited.

### 8.20.1 Universal Decision Window UX

The interface must use a common interaction pattern for all deterministic Decision Windows. The pattern includes:

- A concise trigger statement.
- The exact option owner.
- Legal options with mechanical consequences.
- Resource costs.
- Current deadline or timing boundary.
- A visible default outcome when the player does nothing.
- A rules explanation link that does not close the window.
- Keyboard, touch, and screen-reader controls.

Decision Windows are prioritized above ordinary chat and narrative but below critical safety and account alerts. They do not stack as independent modals. Nested windows appear as a visible resolution stack showing what is paused and why.

A player may keep text chat open and talk trash while deciding. Chat does not count as a response. The UI must never interpret natural-language banter as acceptance of a mechanical option.

The following decisions must use the shared system rather than bespoke prompts: authorized rerolls, Temporary Hit Point replacement, nonlethal defeat, simultaneous ordering, readied-action release, optional once-per-turn bonuses, revival consent, and compelled-choice selection.

### 8.20.2 Roll-chain presentation

When a rule-authorized reroll or replacement becomes available, the dice surface displays the initial result as locked history, the feature that opened the option, the cost, and what the new result will do. If the new roll must be used, that fact appears before confirmation.

The replacement animation is brief and visually linked to the original roll. It must not resemble an undo or delete the prior result. The mechanical log shows both rolls and identifies the operative result.

### 8.20.3 Simultaneous ordering presentation

When the active chooser must order simultaneous effects, the UI presents compact effect cards with source, visible consequence, and timing. Dragging is optional; keyboard movement and numbered controls are required. The server validates the returned order against the original candidate set and state version.

### 8.20.4 Compelled-choice presentation

A compelled character remains visibly account-owned. The interface states the effect-imposed constraint and enables only legal choices. It does not display another player as controlling the character.

Mandatory behavior with no choice is announced before execution when visibility permits. Hidden effect details remain concealed; the player receives enough information to understand the legal restriction without learning secrets.

## 8.21 Error-message standard

An error message must answer:

- What did not happen?
- Why, at the level safe to reveal?
- Was anything spent or changed?
- What can the player do next?
- Is the issue temporary?

Examples of acceptable structure include “Your spell was not cast. The target moved out of range before the command resolved. No slot was spent. Select another target or choose a different action.”

Internal exception names, raw provider responses, and security-sensitive details are never shown to players.

## 8.22 Help without leaving play

Contextual help must open within the site and preserve table state. Rules explanations, control help, glossary entries, and accessibility shortcuts must not replace the live page or lose an action preview.

Help content is versioned with the product and rules manifest. Search results must identify whether an entry is a rule, control explanation, campaign precedent, or troubleshooting article.

The AI may answer help questions, but the answer must be grounded in approved help and rule records. When confidence is insufficient, it links to the relevant in-product source rather than improvising.

## 8.23 Tutorial design

Tutorials must teach the actual production interaction path. A tutorial cannot use special controls, hidden automation, fake rules, or a separate map engine that makes the real game feel broken afterward.

Tutorial progression includes:

1. Identify character and table.
2. Understand scene and objective.
3. Move token.
4. Select and resolve an action.
5. Read result and resource changes.
6. Respond to a reaction or prompt.
7. Ask for a rule explanation.
8. End turn.
9. Step away and return.

Players may skip, replay, or reset tutorials. Tutorial state is a preference, not a gate on character ownership or campaigns.

## 8.24 UX copy review

All player-facing copy must be reviewed for clarity, tone, and accuracy. AI-generated copy does not bypass review merely because it sounds polished.

Critical copy includes authentication, ownership, resource spending, safety, policy refusal, errors, connection state, absence, death, deletion, reporting, and payment if introduced.

Copy must not shame the player for an illegal move, slow connection, accessibility need, or misunderstanding. It should distinguish character failure from user error.


### 8.24.1 Product voice and wit review

The UX copy review must classify every player-facing string by purpose and humor eligibility.

Approved purpose classes include:

- Mechanical instruction.
- Safety or consent.
- Account or security.
- Connection and recovery.
- Rules explanation.
- Ordinary guidance.
- Empty state.
- Loading or waiting.
- Success acknowledgment.
- Recoverable player error.
- Irrecoverable or support-required failure.
- Atmospheric flavor.

Safety, consent, security, data integrity, accessibility failure, payment if later introduced, and serious support messages are not humor targets. Mechanical and rules messages may use one restrained line of wit only when the factual explanation remains immediate and unmistakable.

A compliant ordinary error follows this structure:

1. State what did not happen.
2. State the safe-to-reveal reason.
3. State whether anything changed or was spent.
4. State the next legal action.
5. Optionally add one short, non-mocking atmospheric or witty phrase.

The optional phrase may never be the only explanation. It may not ridicule the player, imply incompetence, turn accessibility needs into a joke, or make a service failure sound like an intentional game consequence.

Loading and empty-state wit must rotate from a reviewed pool, avoid repetition during reconnect loops, and never imply progress that is not occurring. A stalled process cannot continue serving increasingly whimsical messages while hiding that it has failed.

Recurring copy receives Builder/QA repetition testing for clarity, tone, frequency, accessibility, and cumulative annoyance. Product Owner review is batched into the explicit Phase 1, Phase 5, or Phase 7 experience gate when the copy belongs to that gate; ordinary copy edits do not create a new human checkpoint. A line that is charming once may still fail when seen twenty times during an outage.

## 8.25 Supportability

Every recurring player-facing failure must have a stable error identifier that support can use without exposing internals. The help center maps identifiers to safe troubleshooting steps.

Support tools may inspect account, session, campaign, and event metadata only according to role. They must not impersonate a player or edit state invisibly. A player-authorized diagnostic package may include browser capability, connection timeline, relevant correlation identifiers, and sanitized logs. It is not a gameplay export and contains no portable character or campaign state.

## 8.26 UX release metrics

A core flow is not certified solely because it can be completed. The phase must record:

- Task completion rate.
- Time to first meaningful action.
- Error and backtrack rate.
- Number of unexplained blocked actions.
- Use of help.
- Turn abandonment.
- Disconnect recovery success.
- Player ability to correctly describe the outcome.
- Accessibility task completion.
- Difference between novice and expert completion.

Any core task with repeated silent confusion remains a launch blocker even when automated tests pass.

# 9. VISUAL STAGE, MAPS, TOKENS, AND IMAGERY

## 9.1 Stage modes

The visual stage supports:

- Illustrated scene view.
- Tactical square-grid map.
- Dialogue portrait composition.
- Travel route.
- Investigation board.
- Rest or camp scene.

The Game Director selects a proposed mode, but the client uses deterministic scene metadata to render it.

## 9.2 Map art and collision data are separate

A map image is never authoritative for movement. Every tactical map requires structured layers:

- Walkable squares.
- Blocked squares and blocked cell edges.
- Difficult terrain.
- Elevation.
- Doors.
- Interactable objects.
- Hazard zones.
- Cover.
- Opaque boundaries.
- Spawn zones.
- Secret regions.
- Lighting.
- Ambient sound zones.

If generated art and collision data disagree, collision data wins and the discrepancy is logged for correction.


### 9.2.1 Player-safe map-art and secret-asset delivery

Fog of war cannot secure a secret that the browser has already downloaded.

The canonical map bundle distinguishes:

- **Player-safe base art:** terrain and architecture that may be known or visible without revealing secret spaces.
- **Explored or currently visible tiles and overlays:** authorized per seat and projection version.
- **Secret geometry and art:** unrevealed rooms, hidden doors, traps, creatures, objects, labels, portraits, lighting, and annotations retained server-side until disclosure is authorized.
- **Director-only or system-only layers:** never delivered to ordinary player clients.

A single full-map image containing unrevealed rooms may not be sent to a player and concealed with WebGL fog, CSS, clipping, alpha, or a shader. Approved strategies include player-safe base art plus authorized tile or region delivery, server-produced audience-specific composites, or separate reveal overlays whose absence does not expose the hidden shape.

Secret assets require audience-bound URLs or authenticated delivery, private cache policy, non-guessable identities, seat and projection authorization, and logout or seat-switch cleanup. Browser cache, service worker, prefetch, source maps, scene-graph export, accessibility tree, image-generation prompt, asset manifest, filename, dimensions, and timing must not reveal undiscovered content.

Once a player legitimately observes a region, the campaign may preserve that knowledge according to exploration rules. The system cannot make the human forget it, but a later seat or different account on a shared browser must not inherit the prior seat's secret cache.

QA must inspect browser network traffic, cache storage, memory-visible asset manifests, source maps, and disabled-fog rendering. If an unrevealed room or entity can be reconstructed from delivered assets, fog security fails even when the screen looks dark.

## 9.3 Token legibility

Every token must have:

- Distinct silhouette.
- Name or short label.
- Selection ring.
- Ownership marker.
- Hit Point/health state when visible and mechanically appropriate.
- Condition markers.
- Elevation marker when relevant.
- Current-turn marker.
- Connection or automation marker when relevant.

Color alone may not communicate ownership or danger.


### 9.3.1 Avatar, portrait, and token identity contract

“Avatar” is the player-facing visual identity spanning the character portrait, compact party portrait, token art, initiative portrait, dialogue portrait, memorial image, and accessible description.

Each character stores one approved visual specification and asset family. Requirements include:

- Consistent face, body, species traits, age presentation, hair, clothing, equipment, palette, scars, and symbols across derivatives.
- Distinct silhouette at tactical scale.
- Token crop that remains readable at minimum supported zoom.
- Non-color ownership and turn cues.
- Original art and rights metadata.
- A safe curated fallback that matches class and role without impersonating another character.
- Stable asset IDs so reconnect does not randomly replace a face.
- Player review before a generated portrait becomes canonical.
- Clear differentiation between player characters, NPCs, summons, enemies, objects, and disconnected states.

An avatar may not display equipment the character never possessed in a way that misleads tactical decisions. Artistic simplification is allowed, but canonical weapon, shield, form, and major transformation state receives an approved overlay or alternate representation when player comprehension requires it.

## 9.4 Character portrait creation

Players may:

- Choose from curated original portraits.
- Generate a new original portrait from controlled descriptors.
- Upload an image with rights attestation.
- Edit non-sensitive visual traits through safe controls.

Portrait generation must forbid:

- Real-person likeness requests.
- Franchise names.
- Artist-style imitation.
- Sexualized young-looking characters.
- Hate symbols.
- Third-party logos.
- Deceptive documentary appearance.

Generated portraits must be labeled as AI-assisted in asset details.

## 9.5 Scene imagery

Scene images exist to establish place, mood, and visible facts. They must not introduce critical objects that are absent from game state.

If an image shows a bridge, door, creature, or treasure that is not interactive or present in structured state, the interface must avoid implying otherwise. The asset prompt and scene validator should use the same scene manifest.


### 9.5.1 Minimum visual content by stage mode

Each stage mode has a minimum visual package:

- **Illustrated scene:** original location image, active speaker or NPC portrait arrangement, time and lighting treatment, and at least one appropriate ambient-life layer when effects are enabled.
- **Tactical map:** validated image-backed terrain, square-grid calibration, player and NPC tokens, fog or visibility treatment, interactive-object art, and tactical overlays.
- **Dialogue composition:** location backdrop, visible participants, speaker focus, relationship or attitude cues available to the viewer, and text that never covers every face.
- **Travel route:** illustrated regional context, current route, known destinations, progress, hazards or weather, and party marker.
- **Investigation board:** original evidence imagery or icons, explicit discovered relationships, unknown slots that do not leak hidden answers, and accessible text equivalents.
- **Rest or camp:** party presence, environment, time-of-day treatment, resource summary, and optional subtle looped fire, weather, or ambient motion.

A scene without its minimum package may use an approved degraded fallback during an outage, but it cannot be certified as the completed visual experience.

## 9.6 Image-generation failure

When image generation fails, is blocked, times out, or exceeds quota:

- Use a curated original fallback.
- Preserve scene text and gameplay.
- Do not repeatedly retry without a backoff.
- Do not expose provider error text to players.
- Mark the asset for asynchronous regeneration only when the player is not waiting on it.
- Never block a turn on decorative imagery.

## 9.7 Fog of war

Fog of war is calculated server-side per seat. A client receives only the visibility projection it is authorized to render.

The server must not broadcast the full hidden map and rely on a client overlay. That would make hidden information available to browser inspection.

Fog states:

- Unseen.
- Previously seen.
- Currently visible.
- Revealed by party sharing.
- Revealed by a temporary effect.
- Host-visible.

## 9.8 Camera behavior

Camera controls include:

- Follow my character.
- Free pan.
- Fit party.
- Focus active target.
- Return to action.
- Reduced-motion movement.
- Keyboard panning.
- Zoom bounds.

The camera must not automatically whip across the map during another player’s action when reduced motion is enabled.

## 9.9 Generated map acceptance checks

A generated tactical map is not playable until validation confirms:

- Every player spawn is walkable.
- Required objectives are reachable.
- No critical corridor is narrower than token rules allow.
- Doors align with boundaries.
- Opaque edges match visible walls.
- No unreachable enemy is required for victory.
- Escape routes exist where the scenario expects retreat.
- Text labels are not baked into the image unless intentionally localized.
- Contrast remains sufficient beneath grid and tokens.
- No prohibited or third-party content is visible.

---

## 9.10 Visual production standard

The visual stage is a game interface first and a fantasy illustration second. Every decorative choice must preserve tactical truth. Art may enrich a wall, but collision data defines the wall. A glowing hazard may look irregular, but its affected spaces must be visibly and mechanically exact.

Every scene must pass three views:

- **Beauty view:** art, lighting, atmosphere, portraits, environmental effects, and cinematic framing.
- **Tactical view:** grid, boundaries, elevation, cover, hazards, movement costs, targets, and effect areas.
- **Accessible view:** high-contrast geometry, labels, patterns, text alternatives, reduced motion, and keyboard-readable spatial relationships.

Players may switch between these views without changing canonical state. Tactical overlays must never be hidden behind paid cosmetics or advanced settings.

## 9.11 Map construction contract

A playable map is a bundle of coordinated layers, not one generated image. Each map must contain:

- Background art.
- Grid geometry and world scale.
- Walkable and blocked spaces.
- Doors, passages, windows, and interactable barriers.
- Elevation and vertical connections.
- Terrain costs.
- Cover and concealment sources.
- Opaque boundaries for line of sight.
- Light sources and darkness zones.
- Hazards and triggers.
- Spawn regions.
- Objective regions.
- Sound zones.
- Art-anchor points for effects and tokens.
- A navigation mesh or equivalent legal-movement graph.

Generated art cannot infer its own collision authority at runtime. A map-generation pipeline may propose geometry, but deterministic validation and human or test-agent review must approve it before production use.

Doors require explicit states such as open, closed, locked, barred, broken, hidden, or destroyed. The visible art, line of sight, pathfinding, cover, and interaction menu must all derive from the same door state.

### 9.11.1 Rendering and z-order hierarchy

The visual table uses one **Render Layer Registry** shared by the PixiJS/WebGL stage and the surrounding DOM interface. The registry defines named layers, ordering, clipping, opacity limits, input behavior, visibility rules, and accessibility equivalents. No component may introduce an arbitrary stacking value, private portal root, or emergency `z-index: 9999`-style override.

The required bottom-to-top order inside the WebGL stage is:

1. **World background:** void color, panorama, parallax plane, or scene backing that contains no tactical authority.
2. **Terrain art:** floor, ground, water, cliffs, architecture, and approved decorative decals.
3. **Grid and spatial reference:** grid lines, coordinates when enabled, scale, elevation boundaries, and navigation reference marks.
4. **Structural and interactable underlays:** doors, traps known to the viewer, floor switches, containers, low furniture, cover outlines, and object footprints.
5. **Hazards and persistent zones:** difficult terrain, fire, magical areas, environmental triggers, auras, and other canonical ground-space effects.
6. **Ground markers and token shadows:** destination rings, footprints, selection feet, shadow planes, and occupied-space markers.
7. **Tokens and world entities:** player characters, creatures, summons, movable objects, projectiles currently in travel, and interactable entity art.
8. **Token information:** names, ownership rings, health presentation allowed to the viewer, conditions, elevation markers, concentration markers, active-turn state, and selection state.
9. **Overhead environment:** tree canopies, arches, roofs intentionally revealed or faded, smoke, weather, falling debris, and environmental particles. Overhead material must use bounded opacity and may never make an actionable token or template unreadable.
10. **Visibility and fog-of-war mask:** the player-specific visibility projection, explored-space treatment, darkness, and concealment mask. This layer must hide unauthorized tokens, labels, zones, and effects rather than merely dimming them.
11. **Action previews and tactical templates:** proposed paths, ranges, cones, lines, bursts, target indicators, danger warnings, and pending destination ghosts. These overlays may appear above fog only where clipped to information the player is authorized to know. They may not expose an unseen wall, creature, hazard, room shape, target count, or collision response.
12. **Canvas interaction affordances:** cursor markers, drag handles, keyboard focus cell, measurement endpoints, and approved developer diagnostics that are disabled outside authorized environments.

The required bottom-to-top order for DOM surfaces is:

1. **Stage host and noninteractive frame.**
2. **Persistent table HUD:** scene header, party strip, character rail, action dock, connection state, and safety control.
3. **Drawers and sheets:** character sheet, inventory, spell browser, chronicle expansion, rules explanation, and campaign panels.
4. **Anchored popovers:** selectors, context menus, dropdowns, target details, and tooltips.
5. **Time-sensitive prompts:** reactions, confirmations, turn warnings, connection-recovery choices, and cost disclosures.
6. **Ordinary modals:** settings, creation flows, review dialogs, and nonemergency blocking tasks.
7. **Critical system overlays:** safety pause, authentication expiration, canonical-state integrity failure, forced resynchronization, account-security warning, and fatal unsupported-state message.

Toasts and nonblocking notifications use a dedicated manifest location that does not cover the active token, action confirmation, reaction prompt, critical warning, or screen-reader live region. A toast may never become the only record of a mechanical result.

### 9.11.2 Canvas and DOM input ownership

The topmost visible interactive layer owns pointer input. Decorative layers must not intercept input. When a DOM drawer, menu, prompt, or modal is active, the canvas cannot steal keyboard focus, pointer capture, wheel input, or escape handling from that surface.

The input contract requires:

- A modal to trap focus and make lower surfaces inert until it closes.
- Escape to cancel only the highest cancelable interaction, never several stacked states at once.
- A reaction prompt to remain reachable even when a character sheet or chronicle drawer is open.
- Canvas drag to begin only on an authorized selectable entity and only when no higher layer owns the gesture.
- Touch panning, browser zoom, map zoom, token dragging, and drawer swiping to have nonconflicting gesture thresholds.
- Weather, particles, lighting, and decorative effects to be noninteractive.
- Tooltip and context-menu placement to remain inside the viewport and above the triggering surface.
- Screen-reader order to follow semantic task order rather than visual stacking accidents.

Every named layer must have an automated hit-test scenario. Phase QA must prove that the intended control receives input while covered, overlapped, zoomed, or displayed with a prompt. Screenshot evidence alone is insufficient because a visually correct layer can still capture the wrong pointer events.

### 9.11.3 Layer-registry enforcement

If numerical layer values are required by the implementation, they are assigned centrally by the Render Layer Registry and never authored directly in a feature component. The registry must leave controlled gaps for future named layers without encouraging arbitrary escalation.

A visual-layer defect is fixed by correcting layer ownership, portal placement, clipping, or registry order. Raising a component above everything else without analyzing the full stack is prohibited. Any registry change requires visual regression across exploration, combat, fog, weather, targeting, reactions, drawers, modals, connection loss, and safety pause.

### 9.11.4 Square-grid construction and coordinate contract

Every tactical map uses one square-grid coordinate system. The grid is part of the map’s canonical data bundle even when the player temporarily hides the grid lines.

Each map revision must define:

- Coordinate-space identifier and schema version.
- Number of columns and rows.
- Five-foot world scale per square.
- Pixel-to-world transform used only for presentation and input conversion.
- Canonical origin and axis direction.
- Square identifiers or deterministic derivation from column and row.
- Cell elevation or surface reference where applicable.
- Cell terrain and movement-cost metadata.
- Cell-edge walls, doors, windows, barriers, and one-way restrictions.
- Occupancy permissions and maximum supported footprint.
- Light, visibility, cover, sound, hazard, spawn, and objective data.
- Art alignment metadata and calibration points.

Coordinates are integer data. Floating pointer positions are converted into a candidate square through one centralized transform, then validated. Screen size, zoom, pan, device pixel ratio, animation, and art cropping cannot change canonical coordinates.

#### Cell edges and corners

Walls and doors normally attach to explicit cell edges rather than being inferred from filled cells. This permits a wall to separate adjacent squares without consuming an entire five-foot space. Each edge has one canonical record shared by both neighboring squares so contradictory one-sided walls cannot exist.

Corner behavior must be deterministic. Diagonal movement, line of sight, effect placement, and projectile travel cannot each invent a different corner rule. The map validator checks for impossible slivers, overlapping doors, zero-width passages, visual gaps in blocking walls, and corner configurations that create accidental peeking or movement exploits.

#### Token anchoring and footprints

A token projection includes an anchor square, optional Tiny occupancy slot, size category, explicit footprint dimensions or footprint mask, elevation, facing only when a rule requires facing, and occupancy state. The anchor is used for identity and rendering; collision, range origins, emanations, opportunity rules, and target inclusion use the complete footprint.

The visual token art may extend beyond the occupied squares for silhouette, wings, weapons, or dramatic pose, but the occupancy overlay must remain available and the artwork cannot imply a different legal footprint. Selection and hit testing must resolve to the canonical entity even when art overlaps neighboring cells.

#### Grid rendering

Grid lines must remain readable without overwhelming map art. The Design System Manifest defines line weight, opacity, active-square highlight, legal path, illegal path, selected footprint, target footprint, coordinate labels, and high-contrast mode.

Players may hide ordinary grid lines for atmosphere, but the interface must automatically reveal sufficient geometry during movement, targeting, measurement, and placement. Hiding the grid cannot hide legal information or change input snapping.

#### Map art alignment

Generated or uploaded art must be calibrated to the square bundle through multiple anchor points, not a single guessed scale. Doors, corridors, walls, stairs, bridges, furniture, hazards, and objective art must be reviewed against the mechanical layer.

A room may contain decorative curves and irregular stonework, but its legal spaces and boundaries must be clear. A visible passage that cannot be entered, or an invisible passage that can, is a map defect unless deliberately represented as an illusion and supported by structured state.

#### Square-map validation

Before a tactical map becomes playable, automated validation and test-agent review must prove:

- Every required spawn footprint fits entirely, including available Tiny occupancy slots.
- Every required objective is reachable by at least one intended legal route.
- Pathfinding and direct player path validation agree on step cost.
- A Medium token cannot pass through blocked corners.
- Large and larger tokens cannot pass through undersized openings unless squeezing is intentionally supported.
- Doors change movement, visibility, cover, and art together.
- No wall edge is contradictory, orphaned, or visually displaced beyond tolerance.
- Every known hazard highlights the same affected squares used by mechanics.
- Fog and line of sight reveal only authorized squares and entities.
- Area-template calibration matches server geometry at the map’s scale.
- Keyboard and screen-reader movement can identify row, column, nearby barriers, terrain, occupants, elevation, and legal destinations.
- Every active map payload contains only approved row, column, edge, footprint, and elevation fields.

### 9.11.5 No dual-topology implementation

The renderer, map schema, command schema, event schema, projections, rules engine, and tests may not expose a generic topology switch during Alpha 3. Abstraction is allowed where it improves clarity, but an abstraction cannot conceal an untested second engine.

A future request for a different tactical topology must begin as a separate product decision with its own licensed-rules analysis, UX research, geometry specification, version transition plan, performance budget, accessibility model, and complete duplicated conformance suite. It cannot be added by reactivating quarantined code.

## 9.12 Token interaction and ownership cues

A player token must communicate ownership, selection, turn status, health state, conditions, elevation, and connection state without requiring portrait recognition.

The owning player sees a consistent ring and name label. Other players see party-appropriate identification but not private statistics. A selected token has a clear focus state that does not rely only on color. The active-turn token receives a stronger state plus a textual turn announcement.

Dragging a token is a request to preview movement. The token remains canonically in its original space until the player confirms and the server commits. During preview:

- Legal path spaces are shown.
- Movement cost accumulates.
- Opportunity or hazard warnings appear without exposing unknown threats.
- The destination label announces coordinates or relative location accessibly.
- The player may edit the path.
- The player may cancel without sending a command.

A click-to-move and keyboard path-building alternative must provide equivalent capability.

## 9.13 Spell and ability effect taxonomy

Spell effects must be driven by mechanical effect records, not by spell-name string matching. Each ability may request one or more visual primitives:

- Projectile.
- Beam or ray.
- Cone.
- Line.
- Sphere or burst.
- Cylinder.
- Cube.
- Wall.
- Persistent zone.
- Aura.
- Shield or ward.
- Weapon enhancement.
- Healing pulse.
- Teleport departure and arrival.
- Summoning or manifestation.
- Transformation.
- Condition application.
- Environmental alteration.
- Dispel or effect removal.

The visual-effects registry maps approved rules content to these primitives with timing, scale, attachment point, duration, and accessibility metadata. Effects must not be generated freely by the AI during combat.

## 9.14 Strict state-to-UI binding, effect timing, and mechanical truth

No local UI component may own, independently mutate, or silently cache canonical game data. Tokens, health bars, resource counters, conditions, spell slots, inventory quantities, doors, hazards, concentration, turn state, ownership, presence, visibility, objectives, and scene status must render from immutable server-produced projections associated with a projection version and event sequence.

A client-side component may request an action. It may not decide that the action happened.

### 9.14.1 Canonical and ephemeral state boundary

Allowed local ephemeral state includes:

- Pointer hover and keyboard focus.
- Which drawer or tooltip is open.
- Unsubmitted text entry.
- A selected action before commit.
- A proposed path, target, area template, or destination ghost.
- Local camera position and zoom preference.
- Animation interpolation time.
- A visibly labeled pending-command indicator.
- Temporary accessibility announcements and tutorial progress that do not change mechanics.

Forbidden local canonical state includes writable copies of:

- Token location, facing when mechanically relevant, elevation, or occupied space.
- Current or maximum hit points and temporary hit points.
- Conditions, concentration, durations, death-save state, or ongoing effects.
- Action, Bonus Action, Reaction, movement, spell-slot, charge, ammunition, item, currency, or rest resources.
- Turn order, active turn, encounter mode, objective completion, or time progression.
- Character ownership, campaign membership, seat authorization, absence handling, or connection presence.
- Door, wall, cover, hazard, light, fog, hidden-object, creature-visibility, or line-of-sight state.
- Roll outcomes, difficulty values, target eligibility, damage, healing, or Director rulings.

A component may derive display formatting from a projection, but it may not become a second source of truth. Derived values must be reproducible from the same projection version and rules manifest. If a derived display cannot be explained from those inputs, it is not allowed to appear as a mechanical fact.

### 9.14.2 Command and projection sequence

The standard interaction sequence is:

1. The player selects an action using the current read-only projection.
2. The client creates an ephemeral preview without changing the canonical rendering.
3. The client sends a command containing the expected state version and an idempotency identifier.
4. The UI shows the command as pending and preserves the last confirmed projection.
5. The server authorizes, validates, resolves, and either rejects the command or commits events.
6. A new player-specific projection arrives with a higher sequence or an explicit rejection arrives tied to the command.
7. The UI renders the new projection and runs presentation effects associated with the committed event identifiers.
8. Narration and the mechanical summary reference the same committed event set.

The client cannot convert “pending” into “committed” using elapsed time, animation completion, model narration, or a successful network send. Only an authoritative event or projection may do that.

### 9.14.3 Movement truth

Dragging or clicking a token creates a destination ghost or path preview while the canonical token remains in its confirmed location. After the server commits movement, the rendered token may animate from the old projected location to the new projected location. If the server rejects the command, the ghost disappears and the rejection explanation appears; there is no canonical rollback because the canonical token never moved locally.

Animation interpolation is cosmetic. If a newer projection arrives during animation, the component must reconcile to the newest canonical position, shortening, redirecting, or ending the animation without inventing intermediate occupancy. Collision, reactions, hazards, line of sight, and targeting always use server state rather than the token’s in-between pixels.

### 9.14.4 Health, resource, and condition truth

A health bar may animate between old and new projected values, but the accessible value, mechanical summary, targeting logic, and subsequent command validation use the newest canonical value immediately. The animation must never suggest negative health, healing beyond the projected maximum, or a condition ending before its event.

Resource buttons remain disabled or enabled according to the current projection. A pending spend may show a reservation indicator, but the displayed canonical quantity changes only after commit. Rejection removes the reservation. A reconnect must rebuild reservations from server-recognized pending commands rather than browser memory.

Conditions and persistent effects are added and removed by event identity. Re-rendering, reconnecting, receiving a duplicate network frame, or replaying an animation cannot apply or remove them twice.

### 9.14.5 Visibility-safe rendering

The client receives only the player-specific projection needed to render authorized information. It must not receive a complete hidden state and rely on local CSS, alpha, clipping, or fog to conceal it.

Action previews, pathfinding feedback, snapping, hover states, sound cues, loading behavior, and error messages must not reveal hidden entities or geometry. A preview that crosses unknown space may show only information the character can legitimately infer. Rejection language must not disclose whether an unseen creature, trap, door, or wall caused the restriction unless the rules outcome reveals it.

### 9.14.6 Projection version and resynchronization

Every canonical projection must identify its campaign, scene, viewer, rules version, schema version, event sequence, and projection version. A client receiving an out-of-order, duplicated, incompatible, or gapped projection must not merge it into local state heuristically.

On a detected gap or mismatch, the client must:

1. Mark the view as synchronizing without erasing the last confirmed state.
2. Block new consequential commands while allowing safe inspection and communication where possible.
3. Request the missing delta or a complete authorized snapshot.
4. Replace the affected projection atomically.
5. Reconcile pending commands by server status.
6. Resume only after sequence continuity is established.

The UI must not ask the player to refresh as the default integrity strategy. Refresh is a last-resort recovery path and must reconnect to the same authorized seat without duplicating presence or commands.

### 9.14.7 Effect timing and event binding

The mechanical result is resolved before the client displays a final effect outcome. Presentation may begin with a pre-cast windup after command acceptance, but it must not show a hit, failed save, death, healed wound, removed condition, destroyed object, opened door, spent slot, or completed movement until the corresponding authoritative event exists.

The standard effect sequence is:

1. Player selects and previews ability.
2. Server validates command.
3. Player confirms resource spend if needed.
4. Command is accepted and locked.
5. Cast or activation anticipation may begin.
6. Authoritative rolls, Director ruling, and outcomes are committed.
7. Outcome-specific animation is triggered from committed event identifiers.
8. Projection-bound indicators update.
9. Narration arrives or streams in alignment with the same result.
10. A concise mechanical summary remains available after animation ends.

An effect consumer must remember which committed event identifiers it has presented so a component rerender or duplicate frame does not replay a damaging, alarming, or misleading effect. Reconnect may summarize missed effects rather than replay a long queue. The canonical chronicle remains the durable record.

If narration is delayed, the effect and mechanical summary still complete. If narration contradicts committed state, the narration repair process applies and the projection remains authoritative. If an effect asset fails, a geometric fallback and text log communicate the result without changing timing or mechanics.

### 9.14.8 Architecture and QA failure conditions

The implementation fails architecture review if:

- A token component exposes a writable canonical position setter used before server commit.
- A health, resource, condition, inventory, visibility, or ownership component stores an independently mutable canonical value.
- An animation completion callback changes game state.
- A model response directly updates a rendered canonical value.
- A client calculates a final affected target set and displays it as committed without server confirmation.
- A rejected or timed-out command leaves a canonical-looking visual change in place.
- A reload or reconnect can replay an effect as a second mechanic or duplicate a command.
- A stale client merges its local state over a newer projection.
- A hidden fact is present in the player payload but merely concealed visually.

QA must inspect both the visible result and the command/event/projection evidence. QA must fail any state-to-UI claim supported only by a screenshot, because a beautiful wrong token is still wrong. A required deep independent challenge samples these claims separately.

### 9.14.9 Mechanics-first delivery does not authorize optimistic canonical state

The mechanics-first experience contract does not weaken Canonical Projection Binding. The client may immediately acknowledge input, show a pending command, play an outcome-neutral windup, reserve chronicle space, and prepare assets. It may not display a final target result until an event or authoritative projection identifies that result.

The implementation must maintain separate visual types for:

- Unsubmitted local preview.
- Submitted but unaccepted request.
- Accepted and resolving command.
- Committed mechanical outcome.
- Narrative still streaming for a committed outcome.
- Rejected, expired, or superseded request.

These states must not share styling that causes a pending destination, tentative damage estimate, or AI interpretation to look final. Automated UI tests must inspect the rendered labels and accessibility semantics at every stage.

A state library, cache, animation layer, or component hook fails architecture review if it converts elapsed time, network success, an AI stream chunk, or a provider completion callback into canonical mechanics. Only the command/event/projection pipeline may advance the mechanical state.


### 9.14.10 Semantic Scene Graph export

The tactical renderer must maintain a versioned semantic representation of the player-authorized scene in parallel with the PixiJS display tree. This representation is not a second source of mechanical truth. It is a read-only description generated from the same authorized projection and renderer state so QA, accessibility tooling, diagnostics, and recovery can inspect what the canvas is attempting to display.

Each relevant node must expose, as applicable:

- Stable visual-node identifier.
- Canonical entity, event, effect, map-object, or UI-source identifier.
- Authorized viewer and projection version.
- Node type and semantic role.
- Parent node and registered render-layer identifier.
- Numeric `zIndex`, sibling order, and DOM-versus-canvas surface ownership.
- Local and world transforms.
- Grid coordinate, elevation, world-space bounds, and screen-space bounds.
- Anchor point, pivot, scale, rotation, and camera transform.
- Visible, renderable, culled, clipped, and interactive state.
- Local alpha, world alpha, blend mode, tint token, and approved semantic color role.
- Mask, filter, shader, and relevant reviewed uniform identities.
- Texture, atlas, generated-effect, or fallback asset identity and content hash.
- Hit area, pointer behavior, keyboard equivalent, focus relation, and accessible label reference.
- Fog, hidden-information, line-of-sight, and audience authorization classification.
- Animation event identity, start state, target state, progress, and reduced-motion substitute.

The export must be deterministic at defined checkpoints and available through a restricted testing and diagnostics interface. Production players may receive only the accessible and debug information already authorized to them. A QA-only elevated export must never be embedded in the public client bundle, enabled by a guessable query parameter, or capable of revealing another viewer's fog or hidden entities.

### 9.14.11 Rendered-output certification

Structured scene data does not prove that the GPU produced a usable frame. Every critical tactical checkpoint must therefore support actual rendered-output evidence, including:

- Browser screenshot capture after a deterministic render-settled signal.
- Perceptual or pixel-difference comparison against reviewed baselines where stable rendering permits it.
- Region assertions proving that the map is not wholly black, wholly transparent, unexpectedly uniform, or covered by one oversized node.
- Layer-specific captures for map, grid, tokens, fog, action previews, spell effects, weather, HUD, popovers, and modals.
- WebGL initialization, shader compilation, texture upload, mask, filter, blend-mode, framebuffer, and context-loss errors.
- Tests with failed textures, failed shaders, lost contexts, low-graphics mode, reduced motion, high zoom, and browser-specific compositing.
- Cross-check of visible rendered nodes against the semantic graph and authorized canonical projection.

A baseline update requires a linked requirement or documented intentional visual change plus QA review of the rendered result. Product Owner review is required only when the update materially changes an art direction already approved at a Section 25 human gate. Builder cannot replace a failing baseline merely because its new output is internally consistent.

### 9.14.12 Human visual review and evidence triad

Builder and QA visual review is required for every new render layer, map mode, fog behavior, major spell-effect family, responsive tabletop layout, and browser certification. Product Owner visual review is batched at the explicit Section 25 visual gates rather than performed per component. The reviewer must inspect:

- Whether tokens, paths, targets, hazards, and notices are understandable at normal play speed.
- Whether fog, weather, particles, glows, and spell effects obscure tactical information.
- Whether DOM prompts and modals appear above the correct canvas layers.
- Whether color and contrast comply with the Design System Manifest.
- Whether animation conveys the committed event without inventing a different result.
- Whether the scene remains coherent in reduced-motion and low-effects modes.
- Whether any output plainly appears clipped, blank, black, flickering, overexposed, or displaced despite passing data checks.

A visual claim passes only when the semantic graph, actual rendered output, and the required reviewer agree. During ordinary implementation the required reviewer is QA; at an explicit Section 25 visual gate it also includes the Product Owner. When they disagree, the candidate fails until the discrepancy is understood and corrected.

### 9.14.13 Scene-graph and visual-evidence failure conditions

QA must fail the build when:

- A visible tactical node lacks a canonical or approved presentation source.
- Scene-graph coordinates or layers disagree with the authorized projection.
- The graph claims visibility while the rendered node is fully obscured, clipped, transparent, or outside the viewport without an approved reason.
- A hidden node appears in a player-authorized graph, screenshot, accessibility tree, hit area, or animation.
- A screenshot passes while the graph maps the wrong entity, stale projection, or incorrect layer.
- The graph passes while actual rendered output is blank, black, corrupted, or materially misleading.
- A visual baseline changes without reviewed evidence.
- Test-only introspection leaks into production authorization.


### 9.14.14 Presentation Cue Plan observability

The Semantic Scene Graph and visual-evidence capture must include the active Presentation Cue Plan without exposing hidden information. For each rendered cue, QA can inspect the source event, recipient scope, target visual nodes, scheduled milestone, actual start and completion timestamps, asset identity, mute or reduced-effects fallback, and deduplication key.

A cue that lacks a committed event source, plays before its authorized milestone, targets an unauthorized node, or is triggered by narrative text fails certification. Rendered-output tests must verify that sound-correlated visual milestones exist even when audio is muted, unavailable, or prohibited by browser autoplay rules.

## 9.15 Area-template UX

A player casting an area spell or using an area ability places the correct continuous template directly on the square map. The interface enforces allowed origin, range, orientation, shape, size, elevation, and line-of-effect prerequisites before confirmation.

The visual template and affected-square overlay must be displayed together. The smooth shape communicates fantasy and direction; the square overlay communicates exact mechanics. Neither may obscure the other.

The preview must:

- Show the origin point or origin footprint.
- Show continuous boundary, direction, dimensions, and height when relevant.
- Highlight each mechanically included visible square.
- Show affected visible creatures once, including their complete footprints.
- Mark allies and enemies distinctly without assuming the player’s intent.
- Distinguish guaranteed targets, conditional targets, blocked squares, and illegal placement.
- Display cover, total-cover, obstruction, elevation, and line-of-effect warnings.
- Avoid revealing unseen creatures through target counts, snapping, cursor changes, path resistance, performance differences, accessible labels, or sound.
- Allow keyboard movement, rotation, resizing, and confirmation where the rule permits those choices.
- Provide a numeric and textual summary such as “20-foot radius; 14 visible squares; 2 known creatures.” The square count must omit information that would reveal hidden geometry.
- Announce affected known targets and friendly-fire risk to screen readers.
- Explain whether the caster or source footprint is included.
- Show action, slot, material, concentration, and other resource costs.
- Preserve the chosen placement while a confirmation or reaction prompt is open unless canonical state invalidates it.

For common shapes, the interaction must feel natural:

- A radius snaps its center to legal points or squares as defined by the spell record and expands as a true circle.
- A cone pivots from its origin with a visible direction handle and exact affected squares.
- A line exposes width and length, not only a thin ray.
- A cube or rectangular region shows exact side lengths in squares and may rotate only where rules permit.
- An emanation visibly originates from every edge of the source footprint.
- A wall uses connected segments, remaining-length feedback, legal corners, and immediate collision preview.

The client sends the chosen geometry parameters, expected projection version, and command identifier. It does not send an authoritative target list. The server recomputes continuous geometry, affected squares, barriers, and targets. If the server result differs from the visible preview, commitment pauses and the corrected overlay is shown for reconfirmation unless the difference is solely hidden information that the rules resolve without disclosure.

A template cannot be confirmed while its visual geometry, square set, cost, or target summary is stale. A camera pan or zoom cannot change placement. Reconnect restores a pending placement only when the server recognizes the pending command or the action remains unsubmitted local draft state.

## 9.16 Persistent spell zones

A persistent spell zone is a canonical entity with geometry, source, owner, duration, concentration link if any, trigger timing, and visual profile. It must remain synchronized for all clients and after reconnect.

The zone must show:

- Exact affected area in tactical view.
- Remaining duration when knowable.
- Whether entry, start of turn, end of turn, or another trigger matters.
- Whether it blocks movement, sight, or targeting.
- The source character or creature.
- A reduced-motion presentation.

When the zone ends, one event removes mechanics, visual effect, target overlays, and associated sound. Cosmetic fade-out may continue briefly, but it cannot appear mechanically active.

## 9.17 Summons and transformations

A summon is created only after an approved creature record and placement are validated. The interface must show who controls it, when it acts, its duration, and whether it requires concentration. A disconnected summoner does not orphan control; campaign disconnect policy applies.

Transformation must preserve the original entity identity while applying a form layer. The sheet must clearly show which statistics, senses, actions, resources, and conditions come from the current form and which remain from the underlying character. Ending the transformation recalculates legal state from recorded values rather than relying on AI memory.

Visual transitions must avoid flashing and must have an instant reduced-motion alternative.

## 9.18 Visual effect accessibility and safety

Every effect must have a reduced-motion variant. Rapid flashes, high-frequency strobing, violent camera shake, uncontrolled zoom, and full-screen white frames are prohibited.

Information conveyed by color must also use geometry, pattern, icon, or text. Damage types may use color as a secondary cue but must be named in the result ledger.

Players can independently set:

- Overall effect intensity.
- Camera motion.
- Screen shake.
- Particle density.
- Persistent-zone animation.
- Damage-number display.
- Blood and injury detail within campaign limits.
- Automatic camera focus.

The most restrictive local setting wins for that player’s rendering without changing other players’ mechanics.

## 9.19 Camera and attention management

The camera may suggest attention but cannot steal control repeatedly. Automatic focus is permitted for encounter start, a player’s own turn, a newly revealed threat, a reaction opportunity, or a major resolved event. The player can cancel the movement immediately.

The camera must not jump while the player is placing a template, reading a rule, composing a command, or reviewing a confirmation. Off-screen urgent events create edge indicators and accessible alerts.

Cinematic close-ups are optional and never hide tactical state during a decision window.

## 9.20 Portrait and token consistency

A character portrait, tabletop token, initiative portrait, and narrative illustration must depict the same approved identity. The asset system stores a character visual specification covering face, body type, skin tone, hair, clothing, equipment, symbols, palette, and prohibited deviations.

Regeneration requires player confirmation when it would materially change identity. The AI Director cannot alter a player character’s appearance through narrative unless a validated game effect or player choice causes the change.

## 9.21 Scene image generation and approval

Generated scene imagery is never placed directly into a live session without checks. The pipeline must validate policy, originality, dimensions, content rating, text artifacts, visual clarity, and consistency with known scene facts.

For latency-sensitive play, the Director chooses from preapproved scene motifs, maps, props, and effects. New generation may occur between scenes or asynchronously. The system must prefer a stable approved image over making players wait for a prettier loading spinner.

## 9.22 Visual quality gates

A visual feature fails release if:

- Players cannot identify their token within three seconds.
- A legal target appears illegal or vice versa.
- An effect area differs from the server calculation.
- Fog reveals hidden geometry or tokens.
- Animation implies a different outcome than the event log.
- Reduced-motion mode removes essential information.
- Text becomes unreadable at supported scaling.
- Optional art failure blocks play.
- A map contains inaccessible legal spaces or visible but noninteractive doors without explanation.
- A player must infer turn state from animation alone.


## 9.22.1 Whole-screen graphical completeness gate

Visual acceptance occurs at the complete-screen level, not by approving assets one at a time.

The reviewer must inspect the login screen, dashboard, character builder, quick-start selection, campaign setup, social scene, exploration scene, tactical combat, spell targeting, reaction prompt, rest, travel, advancement, death and memorial, reconnect, outage, recovery, and legal surfaces as one product.

The candidate fails when:

- The center stage is a blank or monochrome grid during normal play.
- Most meaningful events are represented only by Chronicle text.
- Map art, grid, collision, and fog appear misaligned.
- Avatars change identity across screens.
- Tokens are generic circles after approved art should exist.
- A palette change makes persistent surfaces visually confusing or unreadable.
- Motion is absent from every eligible scene or excessive in a way that distracts from play.
- Effects obscure tactical truth.
- Fallback art becomes the default because production assets never completed.
- The login page looks unrelated to the game screen.
- The logo resembles another product or fails at small sizes.
- Accessibility mode removes all atmosphere instead of adapting it.

The applicable Section 25 visual gate requires a cross-screen contact sheet, short deterministic capture of motion states, browser matrix, reduced-motion comparison, low-effects comparison, and Product Owner review against the Art Direction Manifest. Ordinary component work uses Builder/QA review and does not stop independently.

# 10. ACTION UX AND PLAYER INTENT

## 10.1 Three ways to act

Players can act through:

- **Context controls:** Select token or object and choose a legal action.
- **Action palette:** Browse abilities, items, interactions, and common actions.
- **Natural language:** Describe intent in plain language.

All three produce the same structured command pathway.

## 10.2 Command preview

Before a consequential command is committed, show:

- Acting character.
- Action.
- Target.
- Range.
- Path.
- Cost.
- Expected roll type.
- Known risks.
- Whether the action ends the turn.
- Any ambiguity.

Noncanonical interface/navigation actions that create no gameplay event may execute immediately when unambiguous. **Canonical gameplay actions are never made 'reversible' merely to skip confirmation**; consequential or ambiguous gameplay follows the required preview/Intent Intercept/confirmation rules.

**Canonical confirmation and resource-order law:** preview/Intent Intercept confirmation expresses player intent but does not itself spend a resource. After confirmation, the server performs the command-acceptance transaction against the current identity, Timing Authority, state version, targets/path, and resource availability. A stale/illegal acceptance spends nothing and returns a corrected preview where appropriate. Once accepted, any rule-defined cost is charged **exactly once at its canonical rule boundary** as part of the durable resolution/event transaction; retries reuse the same command/event identities and cannot charge twice. If a specific SRD rule spends a cost on declaration/cast rather than on later effect resolution, that spend occurs at the accepted rule event defined for that mechanic—not at client-side confirmation. No later presentation sequence may reorder these authority boundaries.

## 10.3 Clarification

The system asks a clarification only when different interpretations would materially alter state.

Good clarification:

> “Do you want to strike the guard beside the door or the wounded guard near the stairs?”

Bad clarification:

> “Can you provide more detail?”

When the action can be safely interpreted, the interface shows the interpretation and allows quick correction.
