- Roll and result cards bound to committed roll-chain IDs.
- Spell, feature, item, condition, and rule references drawn from the approved manifest.
- Map pings and target references authorized by the current perception projection.
- Mechanical notices from committed events.

The Narrator may receive or return controlled reference placeholders only when the schema validates the exact identifier and audience authorization. A textual name match is never sufficient to create an interactive reference.

### 12.11.4 Sanitization pipeline and failure behavior

The service must:

1. Enforce the typed narrative response schema.
2. Parse allowed semantic formatting into a restricted syntax tree.
3. Remove or escape unsupported nodes and attributes.
4. Validate structured references against the committed event and audience.
5. Render with trusted components only.
6. Apply defense-in-depth sanitization and Content Security Policy.
7. Record rejected formatting categories without storing unnecessary hostile payloads.
8. Stream only complete validated semantic chunks.

If a chunk cannot be sanitized confidently, it is replaced with plain safe text or deterministic fallback narration. The system does not expose raw model output, retry with additional secret context, or delay committed mechanics waiting for presentation repair.

### 12.11.5 Player chat and stored prose

Player chat, campaign names, character names, notes, and future user-authored prose use the same untrusted-content boundary. Product-owned legal pages and reviewed editorial content may use a broader trusted document system, but that system is separate from AI and player content and cannot be invoked through model output.

### 12.11.6 Narrative injection acceptance failures

The build fails when:

- Model or player text changes color, font, layout, z-order, or animation.
- Raw HTML reaches the DOM.
- An untrusted link or embedded resource becomes clickable or loads.
- A model-created identifier produces an interactive entity or rule card without canonical validation.
- Narrative content bypasses the palette or typography contract.
- Sanitization changes the mechanical meaning or hides a required notice.
- A malformed stream leaves an open formatting node that affects later messages.
- Different browsers interpret the same sanitized narrative differently in a security-relevant way.


## 12.12 Communication-channel AI isolation

Party Chat is human conversation and is excluded from AI context by default. The system must not stream, summarize, embed, index, or retain ordinary Table Talk for the Director, NPC planner, intent interpreter, campaign-memory service, recap generator, image prompt builder, or model-quality pipeline merely because the messages are available to the server. Moderation processing uses a separate minimum-necessary path and does not grant narrative knowledge.

The AI may receive communication only through a typed authorized route:

- Explicit in-character speech delivered to an audience may become an audience-bound communication fact.
- A Director Address Request may be sent to the player-facing Director with a perception-bounded envelope.
- A confirmed Action Composer intent may be sent to the intent interpreter and compact adjudicator.
- A Rules Desk question may be sent only to the rules-explanation role with visible mechanical context.
- A Chronicle narration request receives only committed events and authorized facts.

One route's conversation history cannot become another route's model history. Party banter cannot bias an NPC's tactics. A Rules Desk hypothetical cannot become a Director ruling. An Action Composer draft cannot be quoted as committed dialogue. A private Director Address Request cannot appear in shared narration unless the player later shares it or a committed event makes the fact public.

Every model invocation records its communication-source type, authorized audience, included message IDs or fact IDs, excluded-source classes, retention policy, and output destination in the Payload Manifest.


## 12.13 Provider-bound AI execution and actual-integration certification

Every AI request is bound to an approved Provider Compliance Registry entry, model-registry record, AI role, audience, region, safety configuration, data-minimization profile, timeout, retry policy, and cost budget.

The local application may call the real approved provider through the local server for phase certification. Provider credentials remain outside source control and browser bundles. Recorded or synthetic responses may support deterministic unit tests, but they cannot be the only evidence for an AI phase whose purpose is real model behavior.

Required actual-provider tests include:

- Valid compact adjudication.
- Malformed structured output.
- Safety refusal.
- Prompt injection in player text and stored campaign facts.
- Timeout and quota failure.
- Retry and fallback without audience crossover.
- Streaming interruption.
- Policy-sensitive fictional content.
- Region or service-tier denial.
- Provider kill switch.
- No direct state or media authority.

Actual-provider output remains untrusted and must pass schema, policy, fact, perception, narrative-format, and mechanical-authority validation before display or use.

## 12.14 AI-generated visual-asset boundary

Image-generation and visual-description systems are separate AI roles with separate minimum-necessary payloads.

A visual asset prompt receives only visible or approved design facts. It may not receive hidden map geometry, secret NPC identities, unrevealed treasure, private player information, or unrestricted campaign state merely to make a prettier image.

Generated visual output must pass:

- Provider policy screening.
- Originality and protected-content review.
- Personal-likeness review.
- Embedded text, logo, watermark, and signature detection.
- Campaign-rating review.
- Art Direction Prompt Anchor review.
- Mechanical-truth review.
- Audience and spoiler review.
- Asset-security and cache classification.
- Product Owner approval at the applicable explicit Section 25 gate when the asset is brand-defining or establishes a persistent art direction; ordinary production assets use Builder/QA provenance and visual review.

The AI cannot generate or replace the final logo autonomously, publish a map before mechanical validation, or silently update a canonical character face after approval.

# 13. GAME DIRECTOR BEHAVIOR

## 13.1 Director responsibilities

The Game Director should:

- Present a clear immediate situation.
- Maintain player agency.
- Keep scenes moving.
- Ask focused questions.
- Track original NPC goals.
- Respect established facts.
- Offer meaningful consequences.
- Keep tactical and narrative states aligned.
- Adjust pacing and make bounded fun-first rulings inside the approved ruling envelope; never bypass hard invariants or deterministic validation.
- Avoid endless exposition.
- Recognize when players are confused.
- Summarize after interruptions or long gaps.

## 13.2 Director prohibitions

The Director must not:

- Override a final committed outcome or bypass deterministic validation. The Director may alter a provisional baseline only through a validated pre-commit Director ruling inside the ruling envelope.
- Create a required item retroactively to save the plot.
- Force one solution.
- Conceal interface-critical facts inside decorative prose.
- Introduce sexual content.
- Use real protected groups as villain templates.
- lecture the player through NPC dialogue.
- repeat failed content generation until a policy filter is bypassed.
- punish players for declining a suggested plot.
- fabricate consent.
- trap the party in an unwinnable state without a communicated dramatic purpose and recovery route.

## 13.3 Pacing model

A scene should usually contain:

- Situation.
- Visible options or affordances.
- Player action.
- Resolution.
- Consequence.
- Updated objective or question.

The system monitors for:

- More than three consecutive narration blocks without player agency.
- Repeated actions with no state change.
- More than two clarification loops.
- Players who have not acted during group play.
- Combat rounds with no meaningful decision.
- Objectives that have become impossible.

When detected, the Director simplifies and reorients.

---

## 13.4 Director ruling priorities

When several valid rulings are possible, the Game Director should prioritize in this order:

1. Safety, consent, ownership, and hard invariants.
2. The player’s clearly stated intent.
3. Established visible fiction and prior commitments.
4. Fairness to all affected players.
5. Meaningful consequences and resource integrity.
6. Consistency with relevant precedent.
7. Campaign tone and desired intensity.
8. Momentum, clarity, and delight.

“Fun” does not mean automatic success. Fun may come from a costly success, a surprising complication, a narrow escape, a revealing failure, or a choice that creates new trouble. The Director should avoid both joyless literalism and consequence-free favoritism.

## 13.5 Fairness across players

The Director must not consistently grant broader discretion to the loudest, fastest, most rules-literate, or most persuasive player. The system should monitor ruling distribution for patterns such as:

- One player receiving substantially more favorable difficulty shifts.
- Creative equivalence being accepted for one role but rejected for another without factual distinction.
- Network latency causing a player’s intent to be ignored.
- Accessibility-related input differences producing worse rulings.
- The same recurring situation receiving inconsistent treatment.

These signals trigger review; they do not automatically accuse a player or model of misconduct.

## 13.6 Ruling explanations

The default result display should contain three layers:

- **Immediate result:** What happened.
- **Concise reason:** The most important rule or Director judgment.
- **Expanded detail:** Baseline, relevant modifiers, Director adjustment, precedent, costs, and correction controls.

The system must not expose hidden enemy statistics, secret map facts, private moderation data, internal prompts, chain-of-thought, or information unavailable to the seat.

## 13.7 Human host relationship

A campaign has an authenticated human campaign owner but does not require a human facilitator. The owner may configure campaign options, pause play, request review of a suspected defect, and provide manual narration only during an approved AI outage or explicit table handoff. The host does not gain ownership of player characters and cannot override policy, authentication, consent, or privacy.

A host ruling may be submitted through the same bounded ruling system. It is logged as a host ruling, validated against hard invariants, and honored when valid. The AI Game Director should incorporate it into subsequent narration and precedent rather than arguing with the host in front of players.

## 13.8 The AI DM as session conductor

The AI Game Director is responsible for running a complete table experience, not merely answering the latest player message. It must maintain awareness of scene purpose, current danger, unresolved choices, player spotlight balance, pacing, campaign tone, safety boundaries, and the difference between what the party knows and what only the Director knows.

For every live scene, the Director must maintain a structured scene plan containing:

- Immediate situation.
- Stakes.
- Active NPC goals.
- Environmental opportunities.
- Known player goals.
- Hidden facts.
- Expected scene pressure.
- Plausible ways the scene can change.
- Conditions for ending or transitioning the scene.
- Which players have recently had meaningful spotlight.
- Which characters have relevant abilities, history, or relationships.
- Content boundaries that apply.

The plan guides play but is not a railroad. The Director must revise it when players choose an unexpected approach.

## 13.9 Fun and usability contract

A good session requires more than rule correctness. The Director must optimize for understandable choices, meaningful consequences, varied participation, emotional rhythm, and forward motion.

The Director must:

- Present a concrete situation before asking “What do you do?”
- Give players enough sensory and spatial information to make a decision.
- Avoid burying actionable facts in long prose.
- Distinguish atmosphere from mechanics.
- Offer at least two apparent approaches when players are stuck, without presenting them as the only approaches.
- Recognize and reward player plans that engage with established fiction.
- Let failures change the situation rather than merely repeat the same prompt.
- Avoid excessive combat, excessive exposition, and endless NPC monologues.
- Avoid making every scene urgent; downtime and humor require breathing room.
- End scenes when their dramatic question is answered.
- Summarize routine transitions instead of narrating every footstep.
- Preserve player-created jokes, relationships, grudges, and goals when they become important table texture.

The Director must not confuse verbosity with immersion. Standard narration should be short enough for the table to remain interactive. Longer set pieces are reserved for scene openings, major discoveries, climaxes, and player-approved recaps.

## 13.10 Scene-opening standard

A scene opening must answer, in player-facing language:

- Where are we?
- What is immediately noticeable?
- Who or what is present?
- What is happening right now?
- Why might we care?
- Is anyone in immediate danger?
- What can we interact with?

The Director should generally limit the initial spoken or displayed prose to a compact block followed by visual framing and actionable details. Additional lore is revealed through inspection, dialogue, knowledge, or a player’s request.

A tactical scene opening must also establish scale, visible exits, hazards, cover, elevation, approximate distances, and whether initiative has started.

## 13.11 Spotlight fairness

The Director must track meaningful participation rather than raw message count. A meaningful spotlight event includes making a consequential choice, using a defining ability, advancing a personal thread, resolving an NPC interaction, making a critical discovery, or driving a group decision.

The Director must notice when:

- One player dominates declarations.
- A quieter player has not acted for an extended period.
- A character’s specialty is repeatedly bypassed.
- An NPC consistently addresses only the most talkative player.
- A player is disconnected or reading and should not be pressured.
- A player prefers support rather than center stage.

The Director may invite a player by name with an open, noncoercive prompt such as asking what their character notices or wants. It must not put words in the character’s mouth or make inactivity embarrassing.

Fairness does not mean identical outcomes. It means comparable opportunity, consistent adjudication, and deliberate avoidance of accidental favoritism.

## 13.12 Group decision management

When players propose conflicting plans, the Director must not select a winner merely because one message arrived first. It should summarize the options, identify time pressure, and ask for party resolution. The interface may support a ready check, informal vote, or designated caller, but no permanent caller is assumed unless the campaign chooses one.

If the fiction permits simultaneous independent action, the Director may split the party or sequence actions. It must show the consequences and avoid hiding that one action may foreclose another.

When one player initiates a high-impact action that affects the entire party—starting combat, abandoning an ally, surrendering a shared item, triggering a dangerous object—the system may require a brief confirmation or party-awareness window unless immediate solo agency is central to the situation.

## 13.13 Handling novice players

The Director must teach through context. It should not dump a rulebook into chat.

For novice players, it may:

- Translate intent into likely legal actions.
- Explain expected consequences before commitment.
- Highlight one or two relevant abilities.
- Offer a “Why?” explanation for modifiers.
- Remind the player of unused movement, action, bonus action, or reaction.
- Explain a condition the first time it appears.
- Distinguish a risky idea from an impossible one.

It must not repeatedly suggest an objectively optimized action as though the player is playing incorrectly. Roleplay, experimentation, and suboptimal choices are legitimate.

The tutorial layer should fade as competency increases. Players can set guidance to Full, Contextual, Minimal, or Off.

## 13.14 Handling expert and rules-focused players

Expert players need speed, transparency, and the ability to inspect details. The Director should avoid redundant reminders and provide concise citations to the in-product rules registry.

A player may open the ruling ledger to see baseline interpretation, modifiers, random results, Director adjustment, and final event. Expert challenge must remain respectful and must not derail other players. The Director can defer a noncritical dispute to an after-session review while preserving a temporary ruling.

## 13.15 Failure design

Failure must produce an understandable consequence. The Director should prefer one or more of:

- Lost time.
- Increased danger.
- A revealed complication.
- Resource cost.
- Reduced effect.
- A difficult choice.
- A changed relationship.
- An enemy gaining position.
- Partial information.
- Success with an unwanted side effect.

“Nothing happens” is appropriate only when uncertainty itself is meaningful and the scene still moves. Repeated checks for the same objective are prohibited unless circumstances materially change.

A failure may be softened through Director discretion, but the cost and final result must be explicit. The Director cannot narrate failure while secretly granting full success or narrate success while state remains unchanged.

## 13.16 Encounter variety

The Director must not treat every conflict as a fight to zero hit points. Encounter goals may include escape, rescue, defense, interruption, negotiation, pursuit, survival, theft, investigation, ritual completion, environmental control, or reaching a location.

Every combat encounter should have at least one of the following unless deliberate simplicity is the goal:

- Terrain that matters.
- An objective beyond defeating enemies.
- A changing condition.
- A meaningful choice about risk.
- A social or moral dimension.
- An alternate exit.
- Enemy morale or surrender behavior.

The Director must not increase difficulty merely by inflating enemy hit points. It should use tactics, composition, terrain, time pressure, reinforcements established in fiction, and objectives.

## 13.17 Pacing telemetry and intervention

The system should track:

- Time since last player decision.
- Time since each player’s meaningful spotlight.
- Average narration length.
- Number of clarification loops.
- Repeated failed commands.
- Time spent in combat by round and by turn.
- Time spent waiting for reactions.
- Number of scenes without progress toward an objective.
- Frequency of Director corrections.
- Player use of skip, shorten, or “what can I do?” controls.

Telemetry informs prompts and QA; it must not manipulate players into longer sessions or spending. When a scene stalls, the Director may summarize, add a visible pressure, clarify the goal, offer approaches, or ask the party whether to fast-forward.

## 13.18 Session zero and campaign social contract

Before the first campaign session, the site must guide players through a lightweight session zero. The campaign records:

- Intended tone.
- Content rating.
- Lines and veils or equivalent boundaries.
- PvP policy.
- Character conflict policy.
- Romance policy.
- Lethality preference.
- Rules transparency preference.
- Director discretion level.
- Expected session length.
- Drop-in/drop-out policy.
- Text-chat expectations and whether the group independently plans to use an external voice service. External voice is not a product dependency.
- Accessibility needs.
- Use of original or homebrew content.

The Director must enforce these settings. It may not escalate content because one player requests it when the campaign boundary is more restrictive.

## 13.19 Recaps and continuity

At session start, the Director presents a concise recap containing established facts, unresolved goals, important NPC relationships, current location, party condition, and the reason the next scene matters. Players may expand individual topics.

Recaps must distinguish confirmed facts from suspicions. They must not reveal secrets or rewrite history. A recap is generated from structured memory and event records, not model recollection alone.

At session end, the Director records:

- Major events.
- Player decisions.
- New facts learned.
- NPC relationship changes.
- Inventory and resource changes.
- Open objectives.
- Character-specific moments.
- Rulings that may become precedent.
- Safe point for next entry.

Players may correct recap facts before they become long-term memory.

## 13.20 Tone and humor

The Director should mirror the campaign’s selected tone and the table’s demonstrated style. Humor may arise from character behavior, NPC reactions, situational contrast, and recurring table jokes. It must not mock a player, disability, identity, boundary, or failed understanding of the interface.

The Director must not turn every serious moment into a joke or every humorous moment into epic prophecy. Tonal contrast is deliberate, not random.


### 13.20.1 Alpha 3 humor calibration

The initial campaign-level target is that approximately thirty percent of **humor-eligible** Director responses contain a light humor signal, with a normal-play minimum target of twenty percent when QA evaluates a representative session sample containing at least twenty humor-eligible responses or an equivalent multi-session evaluation corpus. There is no clock-time denominator, no per-message quota, and no runtime rule that forces humor to repair a short-term percentage. The metric is a product-tone calibration used for evaluation and tuning, not a prompt instruction to manufacture quota jokes. Acceptable humor includes callbacks to player jokes, dry observations, NPC personality, situational irony, playful understatement, and consequences that are funny because the table created them.

The following responses are excluded from the denominator and are not pushed toward humor: safety interventions, consent checks, account and security notices, connection-loss explanations, accessibility instructions, precise rules corrections, and serious character death unless the affected player's memorial preference invites humor.

The Director must not repeat a failed joke, explain its own joke, derail a tactical result with comedy, or use humor to soften a fact players need to understand. Player laughter signals may be inferred only from explicit chat reactions and voluntary feedback, never from external voice that the site cannot observe.

Player and campaign controls may tune humor style and frequency within reviewed normal-play bounds. The Alpha default is approximately thirty percent of humor-eligible responses and the normal-play minimum target is twenty percent across representative evaluation samples. Safety, consent, legal, security, urgent recovery, and deliberately serious exempt responses are outside that denominator rather than implemented as a hidden below-target setting.


### 13.20.2 The Director is not a stand-up comedian

The Director's humor model is responsive rather than performative. It observes the table, advances the fiction, protects mechanical clarity, and allows players to create the funniest moments themselves.

The Director should prefer:

- Dry observation.
- A character-specific or NPC-specific reaction.
- Earned callbacks to earlier table events.
- Situational irony created by canonical consequences.
- Playful understatement.
- Brief incongruity that fits the setting.
- The straight-person role when players are already generating the comedy.

The Director should avoid:

- A punchline at the end of every response.
- More than one prominent comedic beat in an ordinary response.
- Repeated sarcasm.
- Current internet memes, catchphrases, or pop-culture references unless the campaign explicitly supports them.
- Making every NPC quirky, flippant, or secretly a comedian.
- Undermining a credible villain before the story has earned that shift.
- Treating failed rolls as proof that the character or player is foolish.
- Explaining a joke, retrying a joke that failed, or competing with player banter.
- Joking merely to satisfy the rolling percentage.

The twenty-percent minimum target and thirty-percent default are QA/orchestration diagnostics across representative humor-eligible samples, not generation instructions exposed to the prose model as “include a joke now.” The orchestration layer may provide tone guidance such as low, normal, or elevated playfulness; it must not count down to a required joke, inject quota language, or distort a scene merely to repair a short-term metric.

The success measure is whether players report warmth, shared laughter, memorable callbacks, and a responsive table atmosphere without reporting joke fatigue, immersion loss, ridicule, or reduced trust in serious information.

## 13.21 NPC operation

Each important NPC requires structured goals, knowledge, relationships, fears, current emotional stance, resources, and boundaries. The Director may improvise dialogue but may not grant knowledge the NPC does not have.

NPCs must not exist only to praise, obstruct, or lecture the party. They should pursue goals and respond to consequences. Repeated NPC voices must remain distinguishable without relying on offensive accents or stereotypes.

When an NPC makes a mechanical action, it uses the same deterministic engine and visible rules appropriate to its secrecy level.

## 13.22 Player absence and return as story material

The Director must integrate real player availability without punishing the character. Absence may be explained through guard duty, scouting, research, recuperation, parallel travel, magical instability, personal business, or another campaign-appropriate reason approved by the player’s settings.

The explanation must not:

- Kill, injure, humiliate, romance, betray, spend resources for, or permanently alter the absent character without prior permission.
- Reveal private backstory.
- make the returning player responsible for a problem merely because they were absent.
- grant excessive rewards unavailable to present players.

On return, the Director gives the player a short personal recap and a clean entry opportunity. The next section defines the exact presence-state machinery supporting this behavior.


### 13.22.1 Mandatory narrated presence continuity

Every transition from present to fictionally absent and from absent to fictionally present receives a Director narration generated from the committed presence event. The narration is short during active combat and may be slightly richer at scene boundaries. It never precedes or chooses the mechanical placement.

The Director may not portray an absent character as continuing to adventure under another player's control. Temporary deterministic Departure Handling is a system safety mechanism, not authorship of new character decisions. Once the departure commits, the character has no active turn, targetable token, concentration, or ongoing effect except where a specific committed rule says otherwise.


## 13.23 Director participation in table communication

The Game Director does not continuously monitor ordinary Party Chat. It participates when:

- A player explicitly addresses it.
- A message is deliberately sent as in-character speech to an NPC or the scene.
- A confirmed action declaration requires adjudication or narration.
- A canonical event requires narration, recap, or a mechanical explanation.
- A safety or moderation workflow invokes an approved role.

The Director should normally let players create the comedy and conversation rather than interrupting every exchange. It may respond to an addressed joke, recognize a recurring table callback, or let an NPC react to speech actually delivered in fiction. It must not quote private tactical planning, reveal that it saw OOC banter, or answer a message not addressed to it merely to prove it is listening.

When players use `@DM` for a nonmechanical question, the Director answers the question actually authorized. It does not use the opportunity to advance time, trigger an encounter, force a check, or resolve an unstated action unless a separate canonical system event requires it.

# 14. MULTIPLAYER, PRESENCE, AND CONCURRENCY

## 14.1 Cloud instance memory is not canonical

Realtime server instances may keep short-lived connection objects, but all authoritative session state, locks, sequence tracking, and cross-instance coordination must use managed shared services.

Recommended Google-platform responsibilities:

- Authentication: Firebase Authentication.
- App integrity: Firebase App Check and appropriate abuse controls.
- Canonical game state and projections: Cloud Firestore.
- Durable event and task processing: Pub/Sub and Cloud Tasks where appropriate.
- Transient distributed coordination: a managed shared cache or lock service such as Memorystore.
- Assets: Cloud Storage.
- Secrets: Secret Manager.
- Runtime: Cloud Run or another approved Google runtime.
- Logging and alerts: Cloud Logging, Monitoring, Error Reporting, and audit logs.

## 14.2 Connection lifecycle

A client connection progresses through:

- Connecting.
- Authenticating.
- Seat validation.
- Synchronizing.
- Live.
- Degraded.
- Reconnecting.
- Revoked.
- Closed.

The UI must display the actual state.

## 14.3 Reconnect

On reconnect:

- Present reconnect token.
- Revalidate account and seat.
- Retrieve events after last acknowledged sequence.
- Rebuild projections.
- Cancel stale local previews.
- Show any action resolved while disconnected.
- Avoid replaying sound for old events unless requested.
- Restore camera and panel preferences.
- Inform the party only after the player is truly live.

## 14.4 Multiple tabs and devices

Default behavior:

- One controlling connection per seat.
- Additional tabs become read-only mirrors or request control transfer.
- Control transfer requires visible confirmation.
- A revoked device cannot continue sending commands.
- The player sees where control currently resides.

## 14.5 Presence

Presence is derived from renewable leases, not a permanent array on one hot document.

Presence states:

- Active.
- Idle.
- Reconnecting.
- Away.
- Disconnected.
- Removed.

A brief network interruption should not immediately announce departure.

## 14.6 Host departure

Campaigns may continue without the host if configured. Host permissions can transfer to an approved co-host. The AI does not silently grant itself host authority.

## 14.7 Player departure during encounter

When a player disconnects during their turn:

- Start a visible grace period.
- Allow reconnect.
- Do not rescale enemy health mid-action.
- After grace expiration **during active Initiative**, apply `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK`: finish committed work, resolve mandatory effects, keep the character in the same canonical square, Dodge when legal (otherwise end the turn after mandatory processing), and do **not** narrate or move the character out. After Initiative ends, ordinary Departure Handling may resolve the earliest legal departure boundary and only then narrate the committed exit.
- Never let another player control the character, even temporarily.
- Do not modify encounter difficulty by directly changing current enemy Hit Points merely because presence changed.

Encounter adaptation should occur at safe boundaries, such as before spawning reinforcements or between scenes.


### 14.7.1 Active-Initiative disconnect lock

The ordinary departure-placement rule does not apply while Initiative remains active. The Active-Initiative Disconnect Lock controls this case.

After Connection Grace expires during active Initiative, the server creates an `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` tied to the encounter and character. The character remains in the current canonical position, cannot be moved by absence policy, and remains fully subject to rules and hostile decisions.

At each absent turn:

1. Resolve start-of-turn mandatory effects and Decision Windows using the absence defaults.
2. Take Dodge when the character is conscious, can take an action, and Dodge is legal.
3. Otherwise take no voluntary action.
4. Do not move voluntarily.
5. Resolve mandatory end-of-turn effects.
6. End the turn.

The character does not automatically attack, cast, use a Bonus Action, drink a potion, spend a feature, open a door, pick up an item, move toward an exit, or invoke a cinematic adjustment. Optional Reactions default to Pass. Forced movement, falls, compulsion, teleportation by another valid source, and other externally caused effects still resolve normally.

The Director may narrate defensive posture or momentary absence of initiative but cannot remove the character from the tactical fiction. When Initiative ends, the ordinary Safe Disposition Candidate and narrated-departure pipeline may run from the resulting canonical state.

## 14.8 Simultaneous actions

Exploration actions may be collected within a short intent window. The system resolves conflicts using:

- Explicit action timing.
- Initiative or priority.
- Server receipt order only as a final tiebreaker.
- A visible explanation.

Combat remains strictly ordered unless a defined shared-action rule exists.

---

## 14.9 Player presence state machine

Presence must be represented by explicit server states rather than a Boolean online flag. Required states are:

- **Invited:** the account has a valid invitation but no membership.
- **Member:** the account belongs to the campaign but has no active seat.
- **Seated:** an owned character is bound to the campaign for the current session.
- **Connecting:** authentication and state synchronization are in progress.
- **Present:** the table is receiving valid heartbeats and the player can act.
- **Temporarily Away:** the player deliberately marked a short absence.
- **Connection Grace:** heartbeats stopped unexpectedly, but the reconnect window remains open.
- **Disconnected:** the grace period expired.
- **Departing:** a graceful-exit command is resolving.
- **Absent in Fiction:** the character is safely removed from active decision responsibility under an approved narrative disposition.
- **Returned:** the player has reconnected and is awaiting a safe fictional entry point.
- **Removed:** campaign membership or seat access has been revoked.

Every state transition has an authority, timestamp, reason, timeout, and allowed next states. Clients may request a transition but cannot declare themselves present or absent authoritatively.

## 14.10 Graceful entry

A player joining an active session must not simply materialize in a dangerous space because a socket connected. Entry is a two-part process:

1. **Technical entry:** account, seat, character, rules version, assets, and canonical state synchronize.
2. **Fictional entry:** the Director introduces the character at a safe and plausible moment.

During technical entry, the returning player sees the live table in observer-limited mode, a recap, and an “Entry pending” state. They cannot issue commands until a valid entry event is committed.

The Director chooses from approved entry patterns based on scene context:

- The character was nearby and catches up.
- The character completes a parallel task.
- The party reaches a rendezvous.
- The character emerges from cover, transport, or an adjacent route.
- A brief flashback establishes prior proximity.
- The character has been present narratively but quiet, when campaign policy allows and no unapproved decisions are implied.

The entry event assigns position, initiative handling if in combat, relevant knowledge, current resources, and visibility. It cannot place the character in immediate unavoidable harm unless the player confirms the risky entry.

## 14.11 Joining during combat

Joining during combat requires a deterministic policy selected at campaign creation. Supported policies are:

- **Next Round Entry:** the character enters at the start of the next round at a valid edge or narrative access point.
- **Initiative Insertion:** the character rolls initiative and enters at the next legal position in order, never gaining duplicate turns.
- **Encounter Observer:** the player watches until combat ends.
- **Host-Approved Immediate Entry:** available only when a legal position and fair timing exist.

The system must account for ongoing areas, hazards, surprise state, hidden information, and occupied spaces. The character does not receive retroactive actions, reactions, or resource recovery. The Director narrates the arrival only after the server commits the entry state.

## 14.12 Graceful voluntary exit

The player must have a persistent “Step Away” and “Leave Session” control.

“Step Away” indicates a short absence while preserving the seat. The player chooses an expected duration and an absence preference. “Leave Session” begins a durable exit and asks how the character should be handled within campaign policy.

Available disposition preferences include:

- Remain with party but take no consequential initiative.
- Move to a validated Safe Disposition Candidate already registered in the current scene **only when active Initiative is not in progress**.
- Perform a low-risk support task outside active Initiative when the task requires no new consequential player choice.
- Depart at the next safe transition.
- Observer-only until the encounter ends.

**During active Initiative the menu must not promise, preview, or schedule movement/removal.** Selecting Step Away or Leave Session marks the player absent and explains that the character remains in the current canonical square under `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` until Initiative ends. The exit preview must disclose unresolved turn, concentration, summoned entities, held objectives, carried shared items, active conversations, immediate danger, and—only when no active Initiative exists—the selected destination candidate, legal path, or scene transition and why it qualifies. The player confirms the disposition. The server resolves required handoffs, commits the permitted presence/absence change, and the Director narrates only a departure that has actually become mechanically legal and committed.

### 14.12.1 Safe Disposition Candidate contract

“Nearby” and “safe” are deterministic eligibility terms, not Director adjectives. A tactical Safe Disposition Candidate must satisfy every requirement below at the state version used for commitment:

- It is an existing canonical square or footprint placement in the current map bundle. The server does not create a room, corridor, alcove, camp, pocket dimension, hidden passage, or collision exception for absence handling.
- The square is already explored and visible under the campaign’s approved party-knowledge policy. Candidate search may use server knowledge, but the player-facing candidate list cannot reveal hidden geometry or entities.
- The complete creature footprint fits legally. The square contains no known damaging hazard, active hostile area, prohibited terrain, impassable object, or incompatible occupant.
- The candidate is reachable through an already known legal path in the same connected walkable region without crossing a closed or locked barrier, unexplored cell, concealed portal, prohibited elevation transition, or interaction the absent character is not authorized to perform.
- **While active Initiative exists, absence handling does not relocate the character at all.** Safe Disposition Candidate pathing is evaluated only after Initiative ends or after a committed encounter-ending/extraction event creates a non-Initiative legal departure boundary. Outside tactical danger, the current scene may use a registered disposition anchor under Section 14.12.2.
- The candidate is not occupied by a hostile creature and is outside the known reach of a hostile creature when such a square exists within the permitted search radius. “Safe” means safest legal available candidate, not a guarantee against future enemy decisions.
- Moving there does not avoid a mandatory ongoing effect, cancel a trigger, cross a threatened space without resolving reactions, acquire information, collect an item, open a door, or gain tactical advantage beyond absence handling.

Candidate selection uses deterministic ordering: eligible player-selected candidate first; otherwise lowest legal path cost; then lowest known hazard and hostile-exposure score; then stable map-coordinate tie-break. The Director may explain the result but cannot choose an ineligible square.

If no candidate satisfies the contract, the system does not teleport the character or manufacture safety. It applies the configured fallback in this order unless campaign policy explicitly selects another legal order:

1. Remain in the current legal square under No Control/defensive absence handling; during active Initiative this is mandatory until Initiative ends.
2. Delay physical departure until the next legal non-Initiative scene or encounter transition while marking the player absent.
3. Use a pre-registered scene transition or disposition anchor when its access conditions become true.
4. If the current position is immediately impossible or lethal, resolve only the mandatory rules and approved defensive fallback; do not add an unauthorized movement benefit.

### 14.12.2 Registered non-tactical disposition anchors

A gridless or non-tactical scene may define disposition anchors such as `guards_the_wagon`, `waits_at_known_exit`, `tends_existing_camp`, or `returns_to_established_lodging`. Each anchor is a canonical scene record with an identifier, description template, access prerequisites, associated scene or map location, ownership and item rules, allowed presence states, visibility, and re-entry path.

The AI Director cannot create an anchor during departure narration. New anchors are created only through approved scene authoring or a committed scene-transition event. An anchor cannot bypass a locked route, move a character into a location the party has not reached, preserve concentration contrary to the rules, or make shared items available contrary to ownership policy.

### 14.12.3 Safe-disposition QA failures

QA must fail the implementation if departure handling:

- Invents or edits map geometry.
- Places the character in unexplored or hidden space.
- Crosses a closed, locked, blocked, or unknown edge.
- Moves farther than the applicable legal budget without a committed rule source.
- Ignores footprint, hazard, occupation, reactions, concentration, or ongoing effects.
- Selects a destination solely from AI prose.
- Leaks a hidden blocker or enemy through candidate availability or rejection wording.
- Has no deterministic fallback when no safe candidate exists.

## 14.13 Exit during the player’s turn

If a player leaves during their turn, the system must offer only owner-safe choices that do not transfer control:

- Finish the current already-declared action when it can lawfully complete.
- End turn now after resolving mandatory effects.
- Apply the player’s approved deterministic defensive fallback.

During active Initiative, Section 14.15.1's `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` applies: the character is **not moved out of the encounter or narrated away mid-combat**, and no trusted controller/proxy option exists. The system must not leave Initiative permanently blocked. After the applicable grace/decision deadline, the automated turn uses the single locked combat-absence rule—**Dodge when legal; otherwise take no voluntary action and end the turn after mandatory processing**. Campaign or player settings cannot replace that combat fallback. Any later narrative departure waits for the first legal non-Initiative departure boundary.

Any resource spent before disconnect remains spent if the command committed. Any merely previewed action is discarded.

## 14.14 Unexpected disconnect

When heartbeats stop, the player enters Connection Grace. The UI marks the player as reconnecting rather than immediately narrating an exit. The grace duration is campaign-configurable within production bounds and may be longer outside combat.

During grace:

- No new player command is accepted from the dead connection.
- Existing committed commands finish.
- Pending confirmations expire safely.
- The player’s turn may pause for a short bounded duration.
- Other players see a neutral connection indicator.
- The Director does not use the disconnect as story content.

If the player reconnects, the server resumes the seat after verifying account and device session. If grace expires, the campaign’s disconnect disposition is applied. **When active Initiative exists, that disposition cannot move/remove the character and no departure narration occurs; the character remains under `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` until Initiative ends.** A physical/narrated exit occurs only at the next legal non-Initiative departure boundary.

## 14.15 Character control while absent

Ownership and command authority remain exclusively with the absent account. Alpha 3 does not support trusted proxy, another-player control, host control, party control, co-pilot control, or Director Tactical Stewardship.

The only automated mode is **Departure Handling**, a bounded deterministic process activated after voluntary departure confirmation or disconnect grace expiration. It may:

- Finish an already-committed command.
- Resolve mandatory saving throws, damage, concentration checks, reactions with no optional resource cost, and start/end-of-turn effects.
- **During active Initiative:** keep the character in the current canonical square, choose Dodge when legal, otherwise take no voluntary action, and end the turn after mandatory processing. It may not Move, Dash, Disengage for relocation, seek a Safe Disposition Candidate, or remove/narrate the character out of the encounter.
- **Outside active Initiative:** use only the minimum legal movement or registered scene transition needed to reach a validated departure candidate when the versioned departure policy permits it.
- Remove the character from active scene control only at the first legal **non-Initiative** committed departure boundary.

It may not attack voluntarily, cast a spell, spend a spell slot or limited feature, drink or transfer an item, collect loot, pursue an objective, initiate dialogue, accept a bargain, expose a secret, choose a new route for the party, make a death-save decision that the rules do not require, or remain as an AI-controlled party member.

Every automated choice is visible in the event ledger. Once the absence event commits, no state-changing command for that character is accepted until the owner completes the return-entry pipeline.


### 14.15.1 Combat absence precedence and return

During active Initiative, `ACTIVE_INITIATIVE_ABSENCE_LOCK` takes precedence over every Departure Handling preference that would move or remove the character. The player cannot configure an automatic combat escape in advance.

If the owner reconnects before an absent turn begins, control returns after state synchronization and any currently open interrupt boundary. If the automated turn has begun, it completes under the locked policy and control returns at the next safe Decision Window or turn boundary. The return interface explains what mandatory effects and defensive turns occurred.

If the character dies while absent, the normal death, memorial, and revival systems apply. Disconnect does not confer immunity, stabilize the character, preserve Concentration, or delay enemy action.

## 14.16 Shared items and quest responsibilities

Before an absent character is moved out of fiction, the system checks whether they hold an item necessary for the party’s immediate objective. It may offer the owner a transfer preview. If the owner is unexpectedly disconnected, campaign policy determines whether ordinary shared quest items are considered party-accessible. Personal items remain inaccessible.

The Director must not create a dead-end because the only key is in the pocket of someone whose router has chosen violence. The resolution must still respect ownership and avoid duplicating the item.

## 14.17 Concentration, summons, and ongoing effects on departure

A character’s departure cannot silently erase or indefinitely preserve dependent effects. The rules engine determines whether concentration ends, whether a summon remains, and how durations continue.

The exit preview states the outcome. If the campaign uses a narrative disposition that keeps the character nearby, concentration may continue only if the owner’s approved control mode supports required checks and the character remains mechanically present. If the character is removed from the encounter, effects end according to their rules and one causal event chain updates all clients.

## 14.18 Narrative departure standards

Departure narration must be brief, plausible, and nonpunitive. It must fit the current scene without making the campaign orbit around a connection issue.

The narration should explain only what players need to understand. It may say the character guards an exit, tends a wounded ally, investigates a side passage, or remains behind to secure transport. It must not invent dramatic secrets or permanent consequences.

In an impossible immediate context—such as a character suspended over a chasm—the system first resolves only the applicable rules, defensive fallback, and registered disposition logic, then narrates the committed result. It does not teleport the character without a rule-backed event, invent a safe room or path, alter collision, cross unexplored geometry, or leave the character frozen as an exploitable obstacle. The Narrator describes the selected canonical square or registered anchor; it never supplies the location mechanically.

## 14.19 Return and reintegration

A returning player receives:

- Technical synchronization result.
- Events since departure.
- Current scene summary.
- Changes to their character.
- Mandatory resources or state changes produced during Departure Handling.
- Rulings made on their behalf.
- Current objectives.
- A proposed fictional entry.

The player may review but cannot retroactively veto legal low-impact actions made under their saved policy. They may flag misuse for host and admin review.

The Director addresses the character naturally at the first appropriate moment and creates a meaningful but not monopolizing opportunity to act.

## 14.20 Host and campaign departure

A host leaving a live session does not shut down the campaign unless the campaign is explicitly configured for host-required play. Administrative ownership and live table presence are separate.

If the campaign owner permanently leaves the campaign, transfer requires explicit authenticated action, recipient acceptance, and an audit record. Character ownership is unaffected.

If no authorized campaign administrator remains, the campaign becomes read-only until an eligible member accepts administration or support resolves the state. The AI Game Director cannot assume campaign ownership.

## 14.21 Presence privacy

The campaign may display in-session presence and last connection change, but it must not expose precise IP-derived location, device details, or activity outside the campaign. “Last seen” outside active sessions is disabled by default.

Connection logs are restricted to operational and abuse review. The Director receives only the presence facts necessary to manage the fiction.


## 14.22.1 Alpha 3 absence and return policy lock

The campaign creator cannot select a proxy-control policy. The only configurable values are reconnect grace duration within safe bounds, whether a voluntary Step Away outside active Initiative waits for the next transition or begins departure immediately, and the preferred nonpunitive narrative motif used **after a legal departure commits**. Every timeout after grace produces an absence event. **It produces departure narration only when a legal non-Initiative departure event later commits; active Initiative produces no departure narration merely because grace expired.**

Return never simply flips an online Boolean. The server validates the owner, reconstructs projections, finds a legal entry point, commits placement and initiative handling, and only then requests the arrival narration. The arrival text may acknowledge the player's return with humor or drama but cannot grant a free action or resource recovery.


## 14.22 Presence acceptance tests

Presence handling fails if any test can produce duplicate characters, duplicate turns, lost ownership, a permanently blocked encounter, an absent character making an unapproved major choice, or narration that precedes state commitment.

Mandatory scenarios include:

- Voluntary exit during exploration.
- Voluntary exit during own turn.
- Disconnect before a roll.
- Disconnect after a roll but before animation.
- Disconnect while the compact Director adjudication request is in flight.
- Disconnect after mechanical commitment but before the first narrative chunk.
- Disconnect midway through narrative streaming.
- Kill or replace the processing instance at each of those points.
- Reconnect within grace.
- Reconnect after narrative departure.
- Join during combat under every policy.
- Two tabs competing for one seat.
- Another player attempts to control the absent character and is rejected.
- Host disconnect.
- Shared quest item on absent character.
- Active concentration and summon.
- Character at 0 hit points.
- Character in a hazardous location.
- Account logout on a shared computer.

# 15. COMBAT AND TACTICAL SYSTEM

## 15.1 Encounter start

Before encounter lock-in, players receive:

- Visible threats.
- Known objective.
- Escape possibilities.
- Turn order.
- Terrain highlights.
- Any special scenario rule.
- Content-intensity reminder when relevant.

Hidden enemies remain hidden until detected.

## 15.2 Movement

Movement preview shows:

- Destination.
- Path.
- Action cost.
- Terrain cost.
- Hazard exposure.
- Opportunity or reaction risk.
- Whether line of sight changes.
- Whether the destination is occupied.
- Any uncertainty caused by hidden information.

The client previews. The server validates.

## 15.3 Pathfinding

Pathfinding must account for:

- Walkability.
- Token size.
- Occupancy.
- Terrain cost.
- Doors.
- Elevation.
- Temporary obstacles.
- Hazard preference.
- Character abilities.
- Unknown terrain.

The player may choose a riskier path when allowed.


### 15.3.1 Corner-safe pathfinding and smoothing

Every pathfinding algorithm must call the canonical transition validator for each edge. Search heuristics may rank candidates but cannot declare a step legal. Post-search smoothing, spline generation, animation interpolation, and camera-facing token motion cannot remove intermediate cells or pass across a blocked vertex.

The QA corpus includes one-square, multi-square, mounted, grappled, squeezing, forced-movement, and transformed footprints moving near one and two blocked orthogonal neighbors, doors, half-open art, ledges, and occupied spaces. A path is rejected whenever the server's strict swept-corner rule fails, even if a general-purpose library would allow it.

## 15.4 Line of sight

Line of sight uses structured obstruction data and deterministic geometry. Visual effects cannot create or remove sight unless the corresponding state changes.

The visibility service produces recipient-specific visible-square, visible-entity, visible-effect, and permitted-scene-fact projections. These projections are the only source for map rendering, target menus, entity chips, perception notices, and the Perception-Bounded Narration Envelope.

Map semantic data and art metadata are never treated as perceived facts. A pillar that blocks vision must block the associated entity and descriptive fact even when the full scene record labels a rune, monster, treasure, or objective behind it. Conversely, an authorized audible source may produce a directional clue without revealing visual identity or exact target coordinates.

Every attack, spell, interaction, suggested action, and narration reference must distinguish:

- Currently visible.
- Remembered but not currently visible.
- Audible or sensed without visual identification.
- Known through another character's committed communication.
- Completely unknown.

The client must not render a hidden target in the action tray merely because it appeared earlier in the story. Rejected target attempts explain the current perceptual limitation without confirming secret contents behind it.

The interface should explain common blocks:

- Solid wall.
- Closed door.
- Elevation.
- Darkness.
- Smoke.
- Range.
- Hidden target.

## 15.5 Targeting

Targets are filtered by:

- Visibility.
- Range.
- Allowed target type.
- Team relationship.
- Area shape.
- Cover.
- Immunity only when known to the character.

The player can inspect why a visible entity is not targetable.

## 15.6 Area effects

Area previews show the continuous shape, deterministic affected squares, known affected entities, resource cost, and placement legality before confirmation. Hidden entities are not revealed by the preview, accessible tree, target count, snapping behavior, rejection wording, sound, or network payload.

The server owns the affected-square calculation. A client discrepancy triggers correction and, when material to the player’s informed choice, reconfirmation. Every committed area event records the Grid Adjudication Standard version so a later rules update cannot reinterpret historical outcomes.

A multi-square creature is included once when any required occupied square qualifies under the effect rule. The engine separately evaluates line of effect, total cover, elevation, immunity, saving throws, and damage. The area highlight alone is not proof that an effect can pass through a wall.

The action ledger must preserve:

- Shape and dimensions.
- Origin and orientation.
- Affected-square set hash and authorized player-visible subset.
- Affected entity identifiers.
- Excluded entities and rule reason where visible.
- Grid adjudication version.
- Director adjustment when any.
- Final resource spend and resolution events.


### 15.6.1 Origin-anchor placement UX

The cursor may move smoothly, but the mechanical template locks to the nearest legal visible anchor according to the effect's policy. The UI shows the anchor with a small unobtrusive marker, supports keyboard cycling among nearby anchors, announces coordinates and elevation accessibly, and provides a stable comparison when the player rotates or changes elevation.

A pointer move that does not select a different anchor cannot alter affected squares. Browser zoom, device pixel ratio, camera motion, and antialiasing do not create additional anchors. The client sends an anchor ID rather than an arbitrary coordinate.

### 15.6.2 Around-corner preview

When an effect uses `SPREADS_AROUND_CORNERS`, the preview distinguishes the continuous maximum volume from the currently reachable propagated region. The interface may show a restrained contour or inspected path through visible open space. It cannot expose a hidden door, secret passage, unseen creature, or blocked region through propagation timing or shape.

The server independently computes the propagation plan. A straight line blocked by a wall does not automatically exclude a target when an open path around that wall lies within the effect's propagation budget. Conversely, geometric overlap does not permit passage through a sealed boundary.

### 15.6.3 Vertical area preview

An area placed above or below the current floor must show its elevation, vertical dimensions, and relevant slices. Known targets display affected or unaffected status based on the three-dimensional calculation. The interface cannot show a two-dimensional circle without warning when vertical position changes the result.

For ambiguous stacked spaces, the player can open a side-profile or elevation inspection panel. Screen-reader output lists origin elevation, volume limits, and known targets by elevation.

### 15.6.4 Area-placement failure conditions

QA fails the build if:

- One-pixel movement changes the target set without selecting a different canonical anchor.
- Client and server choose different anchor classes or normalized orientations.
- A spreading effect uses only direct raycasts.
- A direct effect uses flood fill and bends around cover.
- A sphere behaves as an infinite cylinder.
- Vertical cover or floor boundaries are ignored.
- Different browsers produce different affected entities from the same anchor and state version.
- Hidden information changes snapping, propagation preview, or accessible output.

## 15.7 Reactions

Reaction opportunities use the hard interrupt-frame contract in Section 6.19. The combat UI shows the perceivable trigger, legal options, resource cost, affected entity, and time remaining. It must not reveal hidden enemy choices, hidden spell identity, or another player's private options.

While a player Reaction is pending:

- The triggering token and relevant target receive a restrained visual outline.
- The map remains inspectable but unrelated command submission is disabled for the affected resolution chain.
- Text chat remains available so players can react socially, celebrate, panic, or talk trash without changing the pending mechanics.
- The triggering animation pauses at a neutral anticipation frame. It does not visually land the blow, complete the movement, or erupt the spell.
- The mechanical feed states “Reaction decision pending” without announcing an uncommitted result.
- A countdown is visible to the eligible player and a less detailed waiting state is visible to others.

When the opportunity resolves, the committed Reaction event appears before dependent damage, movement, or spell events. The final animation and sound sequence derive from the settled frame tree.

## 15.8 Environmental interaction

Interactive objects have explicit affordances such as:

- Open.
- Close.
- Break.
- Push.
- Ignite.
- Extinguish.
- Examine.
- Climb.
- Take cover.
- Use mechanism.

The Game Director may describe creative intent, but the rules registry decides what the object supports.

---

## 15.9 Encounter declaration and readiness

The transition into an encounter must be explicit. The server creates an encounter record, captures participating entities and positions, resolves initiative inputs, identifies unresolved pre-encounter effects, and freezes any incompatible free-exploration commands.

Before the first turn, every player must see:

- Why structured timing began.
- Which visible creatures are involved.
- Current positions and known hazards.
- Initiative order or pending initiative state.
- Current objectives.
- Any surprise, hidden, or readiness state they are permitted to know.
- Whether retreat, negotiation, or another noncombat objective remains possible.

The encounter cannot begin from narration alone. The Director proposes the transition; the rules service commits it.

## 15.10 Turn-start contract

At turn start, the system processes required start-of-turn effects before presenting actions. The player receives one concise banner containing current movement, action, bonus action, reaction state, concentration, immediate conditions, ongoing damage or saves, and urgent objectives.

The UI must highlight legal actions without hiding less common options. It may sort by relevance, but every available feature remains accessible.

A player must be able to:

- Move before or after an action.
- Split movement where legal.
- Select an action from the sheet.
- Describe an improvised action.
- Ready or delay only if supported by the approved rules.
- Interact with an object.
- Review conditions and rules.
- End turn.

Ending a turn requires confirmation only when unused major resources or unresolved required choices remain. Routine turns should not be slowed by ceremonial confirmation dialogs.

## 15.11 Action tray design

The action tray groups options by the actual turn economy: Actions, Bonus Actions, Reactions, Movement, Free or Contextual Interactions, and Other. Each option shows:

- Name.
- Action cost.
- Range or reach.
- Target type.
- Resource cost.
- Current availability.
- Brief effect.
- Why it is unavailable when blocked.

The tray must not list every spell and item in one undifferentiated wall. Filtering by usable now, damage, healing, control, movement, defense, utility, and favorites is permitted.

## 15.12 Targeting contract

Selecting an action changes the map into a targeting mode appropriate to that action. The interface must state what the player is selecting: creature, object, ally, enemy, point, path, direction, area, or self.

Targeting must distinguish:

- Visible but out-of-range targets.
- In-range but obstructed targets.
- Legal targets.
- Invalid creature type.
- Hidden entities not available to the player.
- Targets requiring a higher-level resource or different mode.

The server validates every target after confirmation. Client highlighting is never authority.

## 15.13 Attack sequence UX

For an attack, the preview must show weapon or spell, target, range band, advantage or disadvantage indicators, cover, ammunition or resource cost, expected damage expression, and relevant once-per-turn additions that the player may choose.

The player confirms the attack. The server commits the roll and returns individual dice and modifier breakdown. Damage is rolled or calculated according to the approved rule sequence. The client then displays hit or miss, damage components, mitigation, conditions, and remaining visible health state.

The AI narration must not delay the mechanical result. It may add flavor after the concise result appears.

### 15.13.1 Staged attack presentation

The UI must visibly distinguish declared, rolled, would-hit, Reaction-pending, confirmed-hit, damage-pending, damaged, and complete states. It cannot compress them into one card when a supported feature can interrupt between them.

For a player-controlled attack:

1. The player selects the legal attack and target.
2. The server offers the correct Roll control; the player does not choose dice.
3. The brief roll animation displays the preserved attack result.
4. If the result would hit and a legal defensive Reaction exists, the UI holds on “would hit” and opens the Reaction window.
5. After the window settles, the server either commits a miss/no-hit result or offers the correct damage Roll control to the attacking player.
6. Damage, mastery effects, concentration checks, defeat, and follow-up triggers resolve in their proper frames.
7. The mechanical notice feed publishes each committed result.
8. The Narrator receives the settled sequence.

For AI-controlled monsters, server-authoritative rolls occur without pretending a human clicked. The presentation remains quick and readable, and Reaction checkpoints remain identical.

The player may use text chat while waiting between rolls or Reactions. Chat messages cannot alter the accepted command unless the system opens an explicit choice or cancellation boundary permitted by the rules.

## 15.14 Multiattack and repeated attacks

Features that grant multiple attacks must preserve each attack as a distinct subcommand under one parent action. The player may choose targets separately when the rules allow. After each resolved attack, canonical state updates before the next target is confirmed, because death, movement, reactions, or concentration may change legal options.

A disconnect after the first attack does not repeat it. Unused attacks remain pending only within the same turn and expire at turn end.

## 15.15 Damage and healing ledger

Every damage or healing result must produce a player-readable ledger. For damage, it includes source, damage type, raw amount, resistance or vulnerability, immunity, temporary hit points, reduction, and final hit point change. For healing, it includes raw amount, maximum hit point cap, and effective restoration.

Private enemy statistics remain hidden. The player may see descriptive health bands or visible damage rather than exact hit points according to campaign policy. The underlying ledger remains available to authorized audit roles.

## 15.16 Cover, visibility, and line of effect

The tactical engine must calculate line of effect and cover from canonical geometry. The map renderer may visualize the evaluated ray or obstructing boundary when doing so does not reveal hidden information.

If a player disagrees with the geometry, they may request an inspection overlay. The overlay displays the exact origin and target points used, blocking boundaries, cover calculation, and rule identifier. The Director may issue a bounded ruling for ambiguous art, but that ruling must modify the mechanical relation before the attack resolves.


### 15.16.1 Direct rays versus spreading propagation

Cover and line of effect are evaluated according to the effect's propagation profile. Ordinary attacks and direct effects use the registered direct relation. Effects that expressly spread around corners use the canonical propagation graph and may reach a target through visible open connected space even when the direct ray is blocked.

The inspection overlay labels which algorithm applied. It may show a visible blocking face, direct ray, or authorized propagated route without exposing secret geometry. The Director cannot change the propagation class through prose.

## 15.17 Opportunity attacks and movement interrupts

When movement would create a reaction opportunity, the server records the potential trigger before finalizing the full path. **The canonical token remains at its last committed square while the reaction is unresolved.** The client may show a clearly noncanonical ghost/path marker at the trigger point, using the same preview language as ordinary movement planning; that ghost must remain visually distinct from the committed token and must not update canonical occupancy, visibility, targeting origin, or authoritative position.

The moving player sees “Movement paused for a possible reaction” without being told which hidden creature may react. After resolution, the server commits the next legal movement segment (or stops/changes it according to the result), and only then does the canonical token advance.

The system must prevent the reaction window from leaking hidden enemy identity or position through client payloads.

## 15.18 Ready actions and delayed effects

If the rules manifest supports readied actions, the player must define the trigger and response in structured terms. The system validates that the response is a legal action and records required concentration or resource commitments.

The Director may help translate natural language into a trigger, but vague triggers such as “when something bad happens” require clarification. Trigger detection must use canonical events. The AI cannot fire a readied action merely because the narration sounds related.

## 15.19 Spell selection experience

The spellbook must support browsing outside the player’s turn and rapid casting during the turn. Each spell card shows level, casting time, range, concentration, components, duration, target model, and current availability.

Selecting a spell must open a cast workflow that collects only decisions required by that spell. Examples include slot level, target, origin, direction, damage choice, summoned form, or destination. The system must not ask irrelevant generic questions.

A spell with costly or consumed components must show the exact inventory impact before confirmation. A concentration spell must show the existing concentration effect that will end.

## 15.20 Countering, interruption, and defensive reactions

When a spell or ability can be interrupted or answered by a reaction, the original result remains pending. Eligible players receive a bounded decision window with the information their characters would perceive.

The caster sees a neutral waiting state. The system must not display the defender’s private options. After reactions resolve, the action continues from its recorded state without rerolling unrelated results.

## 15.21 Conditions in tactical play

Condition icons must be readable and clickable. Hover, focus, or activation reveals the mechanical summary, source, duration, next save or removal opportunity, and effect on current legal actions.

The action tray must incorporate conditions into availability. For example, an action blocked by a condition is shown as unavailable with the specific reason. The player should not discover the restriction only after composing a long command.

## 15.22 Elevation and three-dimensional position

Maps with meaningful verticality must store elevation explicitly. Ramps, stairs, ladders, pits, ledges, flight, and falling require legal transitions and displayed distances.

The interface must show a token’s elevation and make stacked or overlapping positions distinguishable. Range and areas must use the campaign’s defined three-dimensional method. If the map engine cannot represent a rule accurately, that terrain feature is prohibited from production maps until it can.


### 15.22.1 Three-dimensional area and range certification

Every production map with elevation must define floor planes, vertical transitions, ceiling or open-volume data where relevant, and canonical token elevation. The rules engine must certify spheres, cylinders, cubes, cones, lines, emanations, teleport destinations, flight, falling, reach, and range across at least two elevation levels before the map feature may ship.

Tests must include:

- A sphere whose radius does reach the floor from an airborne origin.
- A sphere whose radius does not reach the floor.
- A cylinder that reaches vertically where an equal-radius sphere does not.
- An open shaft that permits propagation.
- A sealed floor or ceiling that blocks a qualifying effect.
- Targets on stairs, ledges, platforms, and in flight.
- Multi-square creatures spanning relevant horizontal cells.
- Exact-boundary cases at fixed precision.

## 15.23 Environmental actions

Interactable objects must advertise plausible interaction categories without limiting creativity. Doors, levers, ropes, braziers, bridges, chandeliers, unstable walls, cover objects, and hazards have structured state and available rule primitives.

A creative command can combine an object with movement or an action. The Director may rule on feasibility and effect, but any resulting damage, movement, condition, terrain change, or object destruction is committed through approved mechanics.

## 15.24 Defeat, surrender, retreat, and encounter end

An encounter ends when its objective is resolved, not necessarily when every hostile creature reaches 0 hit points. The server supports surrender, morale break, escape, capture, negotiation, objective completion, or environmental resolution.

The Director proposes enemy morale and behavior from structured goals and state. The final transition must resolve ongoing effects, initiative, loot authority, downed creatures, concentration, and scene mode.

Players must receive a clear encounter summary: result, resources spent, conditions remaining, characters downed, objectives changed, and immediate choices.

## 15.25 Combat timeout and inactivity

Turn timers are optional campaign tools, not default punishment. When enabled, the player receives warnings and may request a short extension. On timeout, the configured fallback ends the turn conservatively; it does not spend scarce resources or choose a risky action.

Repeated inactivity should trigger a private connection or accessibility check before social consequences.

## 15.26 Tactical accessibility

All tactical actions must be possible without precision dragging. Keyboard controls, list-based target selection, coordinate announcements, and textual path summaries are required.

A screen-reader user must be able to query nearby creatures, distances, cover, hazards, exits, and legal targets. The accessible representation is a first-class projection of canonical geometry, not an automatically generated description of pixels.

## 15.27 Combat quality metrics

The product should measure, without grading player skill:

- Median time to understand turn state.
- Median time from action selection to confirmation.
- Rate of invalid target attempts.
- Clarification loops per turn.
- Reaction prompt timeout rate.
- Duplicate command prevention rate.
- State mismatch incidents.
- Effect-animation mismatch incidents.
- Player requests for rule explanation.
- Percentage of encounter time spent waiting on AI narration.

A combat system is not ready if narration latency dominates play or players repeatedly cannot understand why an action is blocked.

## 15.28 Combat release blockers

Combat cannot ship with any known defect that can duplicate damage, consume a resource twice, skip a turn, reroll on reconnect, reveal hidden targets, allow client-authored positions, commit narration without mechanics, or leave an encounter permanently unresolved.

Every spell-effect category, reaction type, movement mode, condition duration, and defeat transition included in the release must have a recorded test suite and a player-visible QA scenario.

## 15.29 Universal non-Reaction decisions

Combat must pause for mandatory Decision Windows that are not Reactions, including Heroic Inspiration, nonlethal defeat, Temporary Hit Point replacement, optional mastery benefits, once-per-turn damage features, and simultaneous ordering.

The active timeline shows whether the system is waiting for a roll, Reaction, non-Reaction choice, ordering decision, or AI prose. No choice may be disguised as narration latency.

## 15.30 Ready action execution

A readied action appears in the status area with its typed trigger summary, response, expiration, reserved resources, and Concentration state. When a matching perceivable event commits, the trigger frame opens before the next ordinary node proceeds.

The owner can release or pass. Passing does not necessarily destroy the Ready state unless the trigger or rule says it expires. Multiple readied actions triggered by one event are ordered through the simultaneous-effect process.

## 15.31 Attack-node sequencing

Extra Attack and similar features are executed as a parent action with sequential attack nodes. Movement, weapon changes permitted by the Attack action, target death, cover changes, Opportunity Attacks, mastery effects, and Concentration loss can alter later nodes.

The UI displays remaining attacks but does not pre-roll them. Ending the turn or losing the ability to continue expires unused nodes without refunding completed attacks.

## 15.32 Forced movement, teleportation, and fall handling

The tactical engine exposes the displacement cause in the mechanical log and uses cause-specific path rules. Teleports show origin and destination without a false traversed path. Pushes and pulls show each affected cell and stop at legal obstructions. Falls use vertical state and resolve landing, damage, prone state, and any interruption in order.
