Opportunity Attack previews must never appear for displacement causes that do not legally provoke. Hazard and area triggers use whether squares were actually traversed or entered under the specific rule.

## 15.33 Grapple tactical UX

A grapple displays a visible relationship line or paired status indicator that remains readable without relying on color. The grappler's occupied hand or body part and the target's speed restriction appear on their sheets.

Dragging previews both footprints and movement cost. Any step that would clip a wall, exceed reach, violate a doorway, or place either token illegally is rejected before commitment.

## 15.34 Stealth, invisibility, and target uncertainty

Combat projections are audience-specific. A player may receive a precise token, a special-sense token, a last-known marker, an audible directional cue, a suspected area, or no marker. These states have different targetability.

The action tray must calculate Advantage, Disadvantage, target visibility requirements, and legal point targeting from the same perception relation used by narration and fog of war.

## 15.35 Concentration and repeated damage

Each damage instance produces its own Concentration checkpoint when required. The UI groups checks beneath the source action for readability but does not merge them mechanically.

If Concentration breaks, the map, status chips, areas, summons, and target legality update before the next attack or effect. Later nodes visually acknowledge the changed state.

## 15.36 Forms and footprint transitions

Transforming a creature previews the new size, footprint, movement modes, senses, and available actions. The server validates the resulting footprint and any required placement before commitment.

The interface clearly distinguishes base statistics from current-form statistics and allows the player to inspect what is replaced, retained, or suppressed. Ending a form reverses only the declared layer.

## 15.37 Shared-roll and per-target damage presentation

When one area effect uses one shared damage roll, the animation and log show that roll once. Each target then receives an individual resolution line for save outcome, immunity, Resistance, Vulnerability, reduction, Temporary Hit Points, and final Hit Point loss.

The Narrator receives the shared roll and final per-target outcomes. It cannot quote a universal damage total when targets actually suffered different amounts.

## 15.38 Revival in tactical and immediate post-combat play

When a revival effect is attempted, the UI validates the dead target, elapsed fictional time, remains, components, caster resources, and soul-consent requirement before commitment. A valid spirit-consent Decision Window is private to the character owner.

A successful revival returns the character at the location and state specified by the effect, then recalculates Initiative participation, prone state, equipment, conditions, and current turn legality. It does not erase the death event or memorial entry.

## 15.39 Server-issued timing authority in tactical play

Active Initiative is controlled by Timing Authorities, not by browser focus, token selection, a disabled toolbar, or a client-reported active character.

At the start of a turn, the server issues Active Turn Authority to the active character's authenticated seat. The authority exposes only command types currently possible in principle; individual commands still undergo complete deterministic validation.

When the active character spends an Action, Bonus Action, movement, Reaction, item interaction, spell slot, or other resource, the authority projection narrows immediately. The client does not retain stale controls simply because it has not received an animation or narrative update yet.

When a rules-defined interrupt opens:

- The parent frame and relevant Active Turn Authority are suspended as required.
- Eligible recipients receive separate scoped authorities.
- Noneligible players receive no indication that a hidden option exists.
- Only the response types allowed by the opportunity are accepted.
- Pass, timeout, duplicate response, nested interrupt, disconnect, and worker replacement follow the durable Decision Window rules.
- Completing the interrupt never grants the responder an ordinary turn.

Non-active players remain able to chat, inspect, plan, pan, zoom, and use noncanonical previews. Their previews cannot alter canonical position, visibility, resource availability, target reservations, path reservations, object state, or initiative.

Macros and natural-language drafts are inert until the player reviews them under a current authority. A draft made two turns earlier may be reopened, but targets, path, range, resource cost, visibility, and legality are recalculated. It never auto-fires.

The server rejects out-of-authority interaction with a stable machine-readable reason and a player-safe explanation such as **It is Mara's turn. You can plan, chat, or review your sheet until you receive a reaction or decision prompt.** Rejection text must not reveal a hidden interrupt, invisible actor, secret trigger, or exact state unavailable to the player.

Turn Authority Gate behavior must remain correct when:

- Two tabs for the same player race one command.
- A stale tab submits after Initiative advances.
- A command is delayed by network latency until a later turn.
- A player reconnects with an old action tray.
- The active player disconnects during a Decision Window.
- Multiple players receive the same public Reaction opportunity.
- One hidden NPC and one visible player are both eligible.
- A Ready action releases outside its owner's turn.
- Simultaneous effects require ordering.
- A player is compelled and receives only bounded choices.
- An encounter ends while authorities remain outstanding.

The encounter cannot advance past an unresolved mandatory timing opportunity. It also cannot remain permanently blocked by an expired optional opportunity; the typed timeout policy resolves it safely and durably.

# 16. SOUND DESIGN — NO MUSIC

## 16.1 Scope

Hallucinated Dungeons uses non-musical sound only.

Allowed categories:

- Interface confirmation.
- Dice and random-resolution sounds.
- Footsteps and movement.
- Weapon and ability impacts.
- Door, lever, container, and object sounds.
- Weather.
- Fire.
- Water.
- Cavern drips.
- Wind.
- Forest wildlife.
- Crowd murmur without intelligible copyrighted material.
- Creature vocalizations created for the project.
- Spatial warning cues.
- Optional disclosed synthetic narration.

No score, songs, melodic loops, licensed tracks, or background music are included.

## 16.2 Sound is supplementary

No player must rely on sound to understand:

- Turn changes.
- Damage.
- danger.
- Connection state.
- incoming chat.
- target selection.
- countdowns.
- policy warnings.

Every sound event has a visual equivalent.

## 16.3 Playback consent

Browsers often require user interaction before audio. The first-run flow includes an explicit “Enable Sound” control with preview and volume.

Failure to initialize audio must not produce repeated prompts.

## 16.4 Mix priorities

Priority order:

1. Critical alert.
2. Player action confirmation.
3. Turn cue.
4. Nearby tactical effect.
5. Environmental ambience.
6. Decorative interface sound.

Environmental sound automatically ducks beneath narration and critical cues.

## 16.5 Spatial audio

Spatial audio may communicate direction but not exclusive information. Players using mono audio or no audio receive directional visual indicators.

## 16.6 Sound originality

Every sound requires provenance. Generated or recorded sounds must not imitate recognizable film, game, celebrity, or franchise audio.

## 16.7 Sensory controls

Provide:

- Master volume.
- Interface volume.
- Effects volume.
- Ambience volume.
- Narration volume.
- Mute on background tab.
- Reduce startling sounds.
- Disable spatial audio.
- Subtitle descriptions for significant sounds.

---

## 16.8 Audio event authority

Sound plays from committed or safely anticipated event states. A hit sound, healing completion, door opening, spell impact, condition removal, or creature defeat must not play before the corresponding authoritative outcome. A neutral windup sound may begin after command acceptance when cancellation behavior is defined.

Every audio event contains source event identifier, category, spatial anchor, volume group, priority, maximum concurrency, accessibility text equivalent, and fallback behavior.

## 16.9 Environmental sound zones

Maps may define non-musical environmental zones such as wind, rain, water, fire, machinery, insects, distant crowds, cavern resonance, or structural creaks. Zones must crossfade smoothly and respect player volume settings.

Ambient effects must not imitate urgent mechanical cues. A decorative growl cannot sound identical to a hidden-creature reveal. Important cues have distinct patterns and are always duplicated visually or textually.

## 16.10 Combat sound hierarchy

When many events occur, the mix prioritizes:

1. Player’s own urgent reaction cue.
2. Confirmation or rejection of the player’s command.
3. Major resolved event affecting the player’s character.
4. Turn and danger alerts.
5. Nearby combat impacts.
6. Environmental interaction.
7. Background ambience.

Concurrency limits prevent a multi-target spell from producing twenty deafening identical impacts. The system may aggregate sounds while the mechanical ledger preserves individual outcomes.

## 16.11 Player-optional speech input/output — required Alpha 3 feature

Game Director and NPC narration are canonically stored and displayed as text. By Phase 4, the product must allow each player to independently enable **text-to-speech playback** of approved player-visible narration and **speech-to-text dictation** into text composers. Both features may default off; implementation of both features is required.

Text-to-speech uses the campaign's selected Game Director identity. Veyra uses the approved female voice family and Garrick uses the approved male voice family. The player may select an approved compatible voice variant where available, plus speed, volume, and autoplay. Spoken narration cannot add information, change personality, change mechanics, reveal hidden facts, or become the only carrier of a clue or rule. It starts only after the corresponding text is approved for that audience and must not delay mechanical feedback.

Speech-to-text activates only through an explicit player control. The transcription appears as an editable, unsent draft in the currently selected composer. It uses the exact same submission, moderation, intent-intercept, authorization, and accessibility path as typed text. Dictation cannot auto-submit an action, send chat, answer a Reaction, confirm a choice, or switch composer meaning.

Alpha 3 still excludes passive microphone use, stored player voice messages, voice conferencing, spatial voice chat, a party push-to-talk channel, and voice cloning. Raw dictation audio is not retained by Hallucinated Dungeons by default. Failure of speech input or output falls back to ordinary text without blocking play.

## 16.12 Loudness and hearing safety

Audio assets must be normalized to reviewed loudness ranges. Sudden peaks, prolonged high-volume noise, and sharp high-frequency cues are prohibited. Master volume defaults conservatively after the player enables audio.

The player has independent controls for master, interface, effects, and ambience. Mute is immediate and persistent as a preference.

## 16.13 Audio acceptance tests

Testing must verify:

- No sound before consent.
- Mute and category volumes persist.
- Mechanical events have visual or textual equivalents.
- Spatial sound does not reveal hidden entities.
- Reconnect does not replay stale sounds as new events.
- Duplicate broadcasts do not duplicate audio.
- Reduced sensory mode removes nonessential layers.
- Microphone permission is requested only after an explicit dictation action; denied permission leaves ordinary typed text fully usable. Optional text-to-speech obeys the player's settings and falls back cleanly to text.
- Audio remains understandable with several simultaneous events.
- Asset failure produces no repeated error noise.

# 17. CHARACTER SHEET AND PLAYER READABILITY

## 17.1 Summary-first design

The default sheet uses familiar SRD terminology and shows:

- Character identity.
- Class and level.
- Background and Species.
- Current and maximum Hit Points, plus Temporary Hit Points when present.
- Armor Class (AC).
- Speed.
- Initiative and Proficiency Bonus.
- Current conditions.
- Applicable class resources and Spell Slots using their actual SRD names.
- Core actions.
- Current objective.
- Important inventory.

Detailed statistics remain available but do not dominate novice play. Flavor labels may supplement these terms but may not replace them.

## 17.2 Ability presentation

Every ability displays:

- Name.
- Purpose.
- Cost.
- Range.
- Target.
- Roll.
- Result.
- Cooldown or limit.
- Visual example.
- Common reason it may be unavailable.

## 17.3 Condition presentation

Conditions display:

- Icon and text.
- What it changes.
- Duration.
- Source.
- How it can end.
- Whether the player can act.

## 17.4 Inventory

Inventory separates:

- Equipped.
- Ready.
- Carried.
- Quest items.
- Consumables.
- Valuable.
- Archived.

A player cannot accidentally consume, discard, or transfer an important item without confirmation.

## 17.5 Character continuity

A character’s appearance, pronouns, dialogue style, relationships, known facts, injuries, equipment, and progression persist across sessions.

Narrative memory must not overwrite player-authored identity.

---

# 18. CAMPAIGN, SCENE, QUEST, AND MEMORY MODEL

## 18.1 Campaign state

Campaign state includes:

- Membership.
- Roles.
- Content profile.
- World seed.
- Current chapter.
- Active scene.
- Objectives.
- Factions.
- Locations.
- Time.
- Party resources.
- Safety settings.
- AI model configuration.
- Asset manifest.
- Archive status.

## 18.2 Scene state

A scene includes:

- Scene type.
- Location.
- Time.
- Weather.
- Lighting.
- Visible entities.
- Hidden entities.
- Interactable objects.
- Tactical map reference.
- Ambient sound zones.
- Objective.
- Exit conditions.
- Failure transitions.
- Content tags.
- Memory summary.

## 18.3 Objective design

Every active objective has:

- Player-facing description.
- Completion conditions.
- Failure conditions.
- Optional status.
- Known location.
- Related characters.
- Time pressure.
- Alternative paths.
- Current feasibility.

The system must detect and repair impossible objectives.

## 18.4 Memory layers

- **Immediate memory:** Current scene and recent actions.
- **Session memory:** Major events from the current session.
- **Campaign memory:** Canonical facts and unresolved threads.
- **Character memory:** Facts known to a particular character.
- **NPC memory:** Facts known or believed by an NPC.
- **Player preference memory:** Tone, pacing, accessibility, and boundaries.

Memory entries require source events and visibility rules.

---

## 18.5 Session lifecycle and save points

A campaign session is a named, time-bounded play interval with participants, start state, active scenes, and an explicit end state. The system creates a session record when the first authorized player starts or resumes play. It does not create a new session merely because a browser reconnects.

A session must support:

- Scheduled start.
- Ad hoc start.
- Players joining late.
- Players leaving early.
- Temporary pause.
- Suspension during an unresolved technical incident.
- Deliberate end with recap.
- Automatic safe suspension when everyone disconnects.

The system continuously creates recoverable canonical checkpoints through events and projections. A “save point” is a player-facing marker indicating that no command is pending, all current events are committed, and the scene can be resumed cleanly. It is not a separate local save file.

Before session end, the Director should seek a natural stopping point when possible. If players must stop immediately, the system records current initiative, pending choices, reactions, ongoing effects, positions, and narrative context without pretending the scene concluded.


## 18.5.1 Persistent tactical scene resume contract

When the last player leaves or the campaign deliberately pauses, the server creates a suspension checkpoint after all accepted commands reach terminal states or are represented by durable pending records. The checkpoint references canonical event sequence and projection versions; it is not a screenshot or client save.

An active tactical scene persists:

- Exact map bundle and version.
- Art, mask, and effect asset hashes.
- Grid dimensions and calibration.
- Cell, edge, collision, elevation, cover, door, object, and hazard state.
- Token identity, anchor, footprint, facing where mechanically relevant, health, conditions, and visibility.
- Initiative order, active turn, round, resources, reactions, concentration, summons, transformations, and persistent areas.
- Per-seat fog, exploration, known facts, and hidden-information partitions.
- Scene clock, weather, lighting, environmental sound configuration, objectives, and narrative delivery state.
- Every unresolved choice, prompt, and command lifecycle record.

Resume loads the stored bundle and replays or rebuilds projections through the last committed sequence. It never asks an image model to recreate the active map. If a required asset hash is unavailable, the scene enters a truthful recovery state and uses a mechanically complete neutral fallback rendering of the same canonical geometry; it does not generate different walls, doors, terrain, or art and pretend continuity.

A map-content version transition after a campaign has used the map requires an explicit version transition plan, before-and-after geometry comparison, preserved event compatibility, rollback, and independent QA. Cosmetic art replacement may not move mechanical anchors or reveal hidden space.

Required resume tests suspend and restore during exploration, mid-turn, after movement, after a door opens, with active fog, with a persistent spell zone, with summons, after an object is destroyed, during narration streaming, after a worker dies, and after all clients remain offline longer than normal cache lifetimes.


## 18.6 Exploration presentation

Exploration must be visually and mechanically useful without forcing combat-style turns for every hallway. The map can remain visible while the party moves as a group, scouts, searches, listens, manipulates objects, or chooses routes.

The interface should provide:

- Party position and marching order where relevant.
- Visible exits and interactable objects.
- Time and light status.
- Active travel pace or caution mode.
- Group stealth or similar mode when supported.
- Current objectives and unresolved observations.
- A clear way to split the party deliberately.
- A clear way to regroup.

Routine movement may be submitted as a party intention such as “continue to the next junction cautiously.” The rules engine expands it into time, path, and relevant checks. The Director narrates meaningful discoveries and summarizes uneventful distance.

The system must never auto-walk the party through a newly revealed hazard, hostile encounter, irreversible transition, or meaningful choice without stopping.

## 18.7 Search and investigation UX

Search actions must identify scope and method. “Search the room” is often too broad for a useful result. The Director may ask whether the player focuses on the desk, walls, floor, magical traces, sounds, or another approach when that choice affects outcome.

The UI may highlight visible areas that can be examined, but highlights must not reveal hidden objects. A search result distinguishes:

- Clearly visible fact.
- Discovered hidden fact.
- Inference.
- Unconfirmed suspicion.
- Nothing found.

Repeated searches by different characters are allowed only when a different method, ability, knowledge, tool, or changed circumstance could matter. The Director must not invite every player to roll until somebody succeeds.

## 18.8 Traps and hazards

A trap or hazard has structured trigger, detection, disarm or avoidance methods, effects, reset behavior, and visibility. It may be represented visually only to characters who can perceive relevant signs.

The system must separate:

- Player moving the pointer over a map element.
- Character observing it.
- Character detecting it.
- Player understanding its exact mechanics.

A hazard cannot trigger from a client-side hover or art-layer mistake. It triggers from a committed movement, interaction, time, or event condition.

When a player proposes a reasonable mitigation not listed in the default options, the Director may issue a bounded ruling using existing mechanics. The result must update the hazard state.

## 18.9 Social-scene interface

During social play, the map may shift to a scene illustration or portrait arrangement while preserving spatial facts when they matter. The interface must show active NPC names known to the party, speaker cues, relationship summaries available to the character, and important visible emotional changes without reducing roleplay to a reputation meter.

Players may speak in character, describe intent out of character, or combine both. The system should distinguish quoted dialogue from instruction to the Director. It must not assume that text entered in first person is necessarily a binding mechanical command when ambiguity exists.

A social action preview may show objective, approach, relevant skill or ability, known leverage, and possible risk. It must not reveal the NPC’s secret target number or hidden motive.

## 18.10 Party text chat and external voice boundary

Alpha 3 provides accessible text communication. The stable player-facing names are:

- **Party Chat — Table Talk:** table-wide human conversation and planning outside the fiction.
- **Party Chat — Speak as Character:** deliberately committed in-fiction speech; it may create only the approved audience-bound communication fact.
- **Rules Desk:** explanatory rules questions only.
- **Director Address:** private/shared nonmechanical communication to the Game Director where moderation handling is complete.
- **Action Composer:** the separate mechanical action-proposal/declaration surface; it is not Party Chat and is the only conversational/prose path that can lead to a command after required review/confirmation.

System messages and Chronicle entries are application-produced outputs rather than player chat channels. Private player-to-player messaging is excluded from Alpha 3. Players who need private or voice conversation may use Discord or another external service independently. Hallucinated Dungeons does not integrate those accounts, ingest external messages, rely on them for game state, or claim to moderate them.

Channel/surface identity must be unmistakable before send. The Director receives only the in-product surfaces appropriate to its role and must not infer external speech. A player who does not use external voice must still receive every rule, choice, recap, and social cue needed to participate fully.


### 18.10.1 Top-level Communication Dock

**Party Chat** is the top-level human-chat destination within the Communication Dock. It is not a submenu of the Rules Desk. Chronicle, Party Chat, and Rules Desk remain peer destinations because they answer different player needs: what happened, what the humans are saying, and how the rules work.

**Table Talk** and **Speak as Character** are the only player-facing Party Chat mode names. Director Address is separate and may not be treated as a private action command. Mechanical action declarations use the Action Composer even when phrased as prose.

### 18.10.2 Social knowledge and communication facts

When a character deliberately speaks in fiction, the server records the lawful audience and may update audience-specific knowledge with the fact that the statement was heard or otherwise received. The record does not certify the statement as true. OOC Party Chat never changes character knowledge.

A player may explicitly share a private observation with the party through in-character speech or another valid communication action. The shared fact becomes available only after the communication event commits and only to recipients who could receive it. Discord or external speech never updates canonical knowledge automatically.

### 18.10.3 Communication continuity

Party Chat, Chronicle, and Rules Desk resume independently after reconnect. The player sees the last confirmed message cursor, any failed unsent message, unread counts, and whether a Director or Rules Desk response is still pending. Reconnect cannot duplicate a chat message, replay an old `@DM` request, resend an action draft, or place a human message into the Chronicle.

## 18.11 Puzzles and player reasoning

Puzzles should support actual player reasoning without requiring pixel hunting or inaccessible visual acuity. Every visual puzzle requires a text-accessible representation that preserves the challenge rather than giving away the answer.

The Director may provide hints in escalating levels:

1. Restate observed facts.
2. Clarify the objective.
3. Point to a relevant relationship.
4. Offer a strong directional hint.
5. Allow bypass with a cost or alternate approach.

The campaign may configure hint generosity. The system should not trap a session indefinitely behind one answer imagined by the AI.

## 18.12 Downtime

Downtime is a structured scene type for recovery, crafting where supported, research, training, shopping, relationship development, and personal goals. Players may act independently without requiring everyone to wait through each interaction in real time.

The Director gathers each player’s intent, resolves low-risk actions in batches, and brings the table together for decisions or consequences that affect the group. Time, cost, resources, and results are committed through events.

Shopping must use an approved inventory and pricing source or campaign module. The AI cannot invent a permanent magic item sale in narration and then add it to inventory without validation.

## 18.13 Rest workflow

A rest request must state intended type, location, watch or security plan where relevant, and any preparations. The interface previews expected resource recovery and unresolved risks.

The Director may introduce interruption only before the rest completion event. If interrupted, the system records elapsed time and any partial effects allowed by the rules. If completed, recovery is committed atomically and the Director narrates the result.

Players must not have to manually click every regained slot or hit point. The ledger explains what recovered and why.

## 18.14 Travel and world movement

Travel uses a world or regional map distinct from tactical maps. The party chooses destination, route, pace, and relevant precautions. The system estimates game time and known resource demands without revealing unknown encounters.

Travel resolution may include weather, navigation, foraging, fatigue, random or planned encounters, discoveries, and changes in world state. Random tables are deterministic content records with preserved rolls when used.

The Director must not narrate arrival before travel events, time, and resources commit. If travel is interrupted, the tactical or scene map opens at the correct location and time.

## 18.15 Objectives and quest clarity

Objectives must remain understandable without forcing players to follow them. Each objective record contains description, source, status, known location, known deadline, related NPCs, dependencies, and whether it is party-wide or personal.

Statuses include Rumor, Available, Active, Blocked, Completed, Failed, Abandoned, and Superseded. Failure and abandonment are not hidden; consequences become campaign events.

The objective panel must distinguish what characters know from system metadata. It cannot reveal the “correct” path or hidden completion conditions.

## 18.16 Loot and distribution

Loot appears only after a validated discovery or reward event. The loot interface distinguishes party items, personal items, currency, consumables, and unknown or unidentified objects.

Distribution supports claim, offer, vote, random allocation if the party chooses, and leave-behind. The system must prevent double-claiming under simultaneous input.

The AI Director may recommend distribution based on character utility only when players request it. It cannot assign another player’s item without consent.


## 18.16.1 Chapter renewal and indefinite campaign continuity

A campaign skeleton stores pressures and possibilities, not a fixed railroad. At the conclusion of a major arc, the system performs a Chapter Renewal:

1. Freeze and summarize completed objectives, resolved NPC arcs, changed factions, locations, losses, rewards, and outstanding consequences.
2. Preserve all canonical events and produce retrieval indexes rather than dumping full history into every model call.
3. Ask the players what goals or directions matter next.
4. Generate several plausible original chapter pressures grounded in current world state.
5. Let the party choose, combine, reject, or create another direction.
6. Build only the next needed layer of scenes and validated maps.

The campaign never ends solely because the initial outline reached its expected conclusion. A campaign may be archived by its owner, become inactive under quota policy, or close through account administration, but the story engine itself supports continuing play.


## 18.17 Session recap verification without retcon

At end of session, the Director generates a recap from committed events and structured memory. Players may flag a recap sentence that contradicts those records, exposes private information, misattributes a speaker, or uses an inappropriate tone.

A verified recap repair changes only the summary so it matches canonical history. It cannot erase a choice, reverse a relationship change, resurrect a character, recover a resource, reveal a different roll, or create party consensus that did not occur. Mechanical discrepancies follow the narrow defect-correction process in Section 10.7; player regret does not qualify.

The verified recap becomes the default opening summary for the next session and remains linked to the event range it summarizes.

## 18.18 Fun and friction review after every session

After a session, the product may ask a small optional set of questions:

- Did you understand what your character could do?
- Did your choices change what happened?
- Did anyone wait too long for a turn or response?
- Did the Director make a ruling that felt inconsistent?
- Was any content uncomfortable or outside expectations?
- Did technical issues interrupt play?
- What moment was most enjoyable?

Responses are used for product and campaign improvement, not to evaluate or rank players. The Director may receive aggregated campaign-level signals but not private criticism attributed to a player unless the player chooses to share it.

## 18.19 Canonical time and rest persistence

Every scene and encounter references the campaign clock. Session pause stores the exact fictional timestamp and all relative duration counters. Real-world absence never advances poison, spell, rest, travel, death-revival windows, or dawn-based recovery unless the campaign explicitly advances time.

Rest progress is canonical and resumable. If the table pauses during a rest, resume shows the same progress and interruption state. A model-generated recap cannot declare a rest complete without the required completion event.

## 18.20 Death, revival, and memorial continuity

Campaign memory stores death, memorial, revival eligibility, revival attempts, owner decisions, and successful returns as distinct facts. NPCs and recaps may remember the death even after revival. The Director must not treat a revived character as though nothing happened or as a newly owned copy.

A permanently retired character remains part of campaign history but cannot be reactivated through narration or administrative convenience.

# 19. DATA AND AUTHORITY MODEL

## 19.1 Principles

- Authentication identity and game identity are distinct.
- User input never directly becomes canonical state.
- Client state is a cache.
- Large or unbounded arrays are avoided.
- Hot shared documents are avoided.
- Private information is partitioned by seat.
- Event history is append-only.
- Projections can be rebuilt.
- Schema changes are versioned.

## 19.2 Core records

Required conceptual records include:

- User profile.
- Terms and age-attestation record.
- Accessibility profile.
- Safety profile.
- Character.
- Character ability.
- Character inventory item.
- Campaign.
- Campaign membership.
- Seat.
- Scene.
- Map.
- Map cell or region metadata.
- Entity.
- Token.
- Objective.
- Command.
- Event.
- Projection.
- Chronicle entry.
- AI request audit.
- Safety incident.
- Asset.
- Asset provenance.
- Invitation.
- Presence lease.
- Report.
- Moderation action.

## 19.3 Character ownership record

Every player-character record must contain an immutable normal-operation owner account identifier established by the server. Ownership authorization is resolved from the verified authentication context on every sensitive operation.

The ownership model must enforce:

- One active owner account per player character.
- No client-created ownership claims.
- No ownership derived from email text, display name, campaign role, device, or local storage.
- No host override of ownership.
- No AI ability to change ownership.
- No control seat unless the authenticated owner matches.
- Audited exceptional version transition only through approved account-recovery or merge operations.
- Ownership-aware privacy-data access, deletion, suspension, and retention behavior; no playable export or import.
- Private character fields visible only to the owner and specifically authorized system roles.

Ownership and control are different records. Ownership persists across sessions. Control is temporary, scoped, revocable, and represented by a seat.

## 19.4 Ruling and precedent records

A state-changing action that reaches adjudication must preserve enough information to reproduce and review the result:

- Baseline ruling identifier and version.
- Input facts used by the baseline.
- Fixed random results.
- Director acceptance or adjustment.
- Adjustment category and magnitude.
- Director reason.
- Ruling-envelope version.
- Validation result.
- Final ruling.
- Precedent scope and key.
- Player-visible explanation.
- Narration reference.
- Correction links.

Precedent records must be compact, structured, and scoped. Raw narrative prose is not a reliable precedent key.

## 19.5 Privacy partition

Player-private notes, hidden information, and per-character visibility must not share the same broadly readable record as public scene state.

## 19.6 Retention

The product must define separate retention for:

- Account profile.
- Campaign content.
- Chat.
- Audio-generation inputs.
- Image-generation prompts.
- Safety logs.
- AI prompts and outputs.
- Operational logs.
- Deleted accounts.
- Backups.

Players must receive a clear deletion and legally required privacy-data access flow. Alpha 3 does not provide a portable gameplay export or re-import format. Provider-side retention and abuse-monitoring behavior must be disclosed accurately.

---

## 19.7 Authoritative service boundaries

The production system must use explicit service boundaries. Implementation agents may not move authority into a convenient client component merely because it makes a demonstration easier.

**Web presentation service:** Serves the hosted application shell, authenticated pages, accessible DOM, and static assets. It renders projections and submits commands. It does not calculate authoritative game outcomes.

**Authentication and session service:** Exchanges verified Firebase identity for the application session, manages renewal and revocation, and supplies authenticated account identity to HTTP and WebSocket entry points.

**Game command service:** Validates authorization, command schema, state version, rules version, idempotency, and timing. It invokes deterministic rules and creates canonical events.

**Rules service or package:** Contains versioned rule primitives and approved SRD data. It has no direct access to browser state and no authority to authenticate users.

**Realtime gateway:** Maintains ephemeral WebSocket connections, subscribes to shared event notifications, and sends player-specific projections. It does not own canonical campaign state.

**AI orchestration service:** Builds minimum necessary model context, applies safety policy, validates structured outputs, requests Director rulings and narration, and submits approved proposals to the command service. It cannot write game state directly.

**Asset service:** Processes, scans, sanitizes, stores, versions, and serves approved maps, portraits, tokens, effects, and sounds.

**Administration service:** Provides privileged review through separate authorization, audit, and interface boundaries.

**Outbox dispatcher:** Reliably publishes committed event notifications from shared storage to cross-instance messaging. It is idempotent and independently monitored.

## 19.8 Canonical write model

All game state changes originate as commands and produce immutable events. Current-state documents are projections maintained for efficient reads. The event record is the audit source for how state changed; the projection is the current answer for what state is now.

The canonical commit must atomically establish:

- Command receipt or idempotency record.
- State-version precondition.
- Event or event batch.
- Updated authoritative projection fields required for the next command.
- Transactional outbox record.

If the database cannot atomically support the complete batch at the chosen granularity, the architecture must use a recorded resolution plan with resumable steps. It may not update hit points and later hope to remember that a condition should also have been applied.

## 19.9 Event envelope

Every canonical event must include:

- Globally unique event identifier.
- Campaign identifier.
- Scene and encounter identifier where applicable.
- Aggregate or entity identifiers affected.
- Parent command identifier.
- Causation identifier.
- Correlation identifier for a multi-step action.
- Acting account and controlled entity.
- Event type and schema version.
- Campaign rules version and engine release.
- Prior and resulting state versions.
- Server commit timestamp.
- Visibility classification.
- Mechanical payload.
- Rule references.
- Director ruling reference if used.
- Random result references if used.
- Correction or reversal reference if applicable.

Events are append-only. Sensitive player-private payloads may be partitioned or encrypted separately, but the existence and causal structure of the event remain auditable.

## 19.10 Projection classes

The system must maintain separate projections rather than send one full campaign object to every client.

Required projection classes include:

- Public campaign invitation preview.
- Campaign-member dashboard.
- Player table projection.
- Character-owner private sheet.
- Director omniscient scene state.
- Moderator safety view.
- Administrative operational view.
- Accessible spatial projection.
- Reconnect delta and full snapshot.

A projection is generated from authorization and visibility policy. Hidden content is omitted server-side, not hidden with CSS.

## 19.11 Core record inventory

At minimum, the data model requires versioned records for:

- Accounts and profile preferences.
- Authentication sessions and device sessions.
- Characters and character-choice derivations.
- Character ownership and optional transfer history.
- Campaigns, memberships, roles, invitations, and bans.
- Session instances and seat bindings.
- Presence transitions.
- Rules manifests and content entries.
- Campaign modules and precedents.
- Scenes, maps, geometry, environmental state, and visibility.
- Encounters, initiative, turns, reactions, and deadlines.
- Tokens and entities.
- Commands, resolution plans, random rolls, events, and outbox records.
- Inventory items, containers, transfers, and entitlements.
- Spells, ongoing effects, conditions, concentration, and summons.
- Chat, narration, recaps, and structured memory.
- NPC knowledge, goals, relationships, and secrets.
- Assets and provenance.
- Safety settings, reports, blocks, moderation actions, and appeals.
- Usage budgets, AI calls, policy decisions, and model registry.
- Audit and administration events.

Each record requires an owner or authority, retention policy, visibility policy, schema version, and version transition strategy.

### 19.11.1 Additional timing and state-control records

The following durable or reconstructable records are required:

#### Resolution Frame

Tracks one staged mechanical checkpoint, its parent and child frames, source command, rule checkpoint, input projection version, pending effect, current status, deadline, eligible interrupt set, final result, and resume transition.

#### Reaction Opportunity

Tracks one recipient-specific interrupt offer, legal options, costs, trigger facts, visibility scope, opening and expiration time, selected result, terminal status, and idempotency evidence.


#### Timing Authority Grant

A durable or durably reconstructible record authorizing one account-seat-character tuple to submit a bounded set of command types during one exact encounter opportunity. It stores authority class, encounter and frame references, projection and turn sequence, parameter constraints, issue and expiry times, consumption policy, parent authority, revocation state, response identity, and audit result. Player projections expose only the minimum viewer-safe response token and visible choices.

#### Action Plan and Plan Node

Tracks a player-confirmed sequence, typed branches, exact fallbacks, current node, node statuses, child commands, preserved rolls, interruption frames, and narration links. Plan records cannot contain executable predicates or free-form instructions to mutate state.

#### Equipment State Projection

Tracks canonical hand occupancy, worn gear, stowed and dropped items, item availability, mastery eligibility, ammunition, components, charges, and any state dependent on holding or releasing an item.

#### Perception Fact and Narration Envelope

A Perception Fact is a canonical bounded statement with sensory channel, source, audience, precision, event-time state, targetability, and confidentiality. A Narration Envelope is a recipient-specific immutable selection of approved fact identifiers and committed event identifiers for one generation request.

#### Mechanical Notice

Tracks a recipient-safe, model-independent explanation of a committed event or projection delta, including category, salience, plain-language template, affected entity, sequence, display surfaces, deduplication key, and accessibility behavior.

All records include schema version, campaign boundary, creation metadata, and audit linkage. Client-supplied identifiers are resolved and authorized before use.

#### Decision Window

Stores category, owner, trigger, timing boundary, visible information, options, default, deadline, state version, response, resource consequences, and closure reason.

#### Roll Chain

Stores the initial roll, approved reroll or replacement feature, Decision Window, resource use, replacement rolls, selection rule, and final operative result.

#### Ready Contract

Stores the typed perceivable trigger, response, expiration, reserved resources, Concentration requirement, trigger history, and release or pass decision.

#### Temporal Usage Ledger

Stores rule-specific once-per-turn, per-target, per-action, per-hit, and other usage keys with reset boundaries.

#### Displacement Event

Stores movement cause, origin, destination, traversed path when applicable, footprint checks, provoking status, terrain and hazard interactions, and placement procedure.

#### Grapple Link

Stores grappler, target, occupied body part, reach, restrictions, linked movement state, and termination cause.

#### Observer Perception Relation

Stores observer-target visibility, special sense, precision, last-known location, audible or suspected data, and authoritative version.

#### Form Overlay

Stores source effect, replacement and inherited fields, form Hit Points, size, footprint, senses, actions, equipment interaction, and ending procedure.

#### Campaign Clock and Duration Index

Stores fictional time, active turn and round sequences, scheduled expirations, rest progress, and world-event boundaries.

#### Damage Instance Ledger

Stores source, shared-roll relation, target, damage components, saves, adjustments, defenses, Temporary Hit Points, final damage, and dependent checks.

#### Death and Revival Record

Stores death event, remains state, revival eligibility, attempts, spirit decisions, material use, successful return, and permanent-retirement state.


### 19.11.2 Additional geometry, presentation, source, and orchestration records

The canonical model includes the following typed records where applicable:

- **Area Origin Anchor:** map coordinate-space version, anchor ID, anchor class, fixed horizontal and vertical coordinates, legal effect policies, visibility scope, and source geometry.
- **Area Placement Record:** effect version, selected anchor, normalized orientation, dimensions, three-dimensional volume policy, propagation profile, candidate and final set hashes, and expected state version.
- **Propagation Plan:** topology version, traversable faces and portals, propagation budget, shortest authorized distances, blocked relations, authorized inspection subset, and affected target identities.
- **Presentation Cue Plan:** source event, projection version, recipient scope, cue identities, visual and sound assets, milestones, timing, fallbacks, deduplication, and replay policy.
- **Active Initiative Absence Lock:** campaign, encounter, character, grace expiration, current position, automated turn policy version, lifecycle status, and release condition.
- **Source Artifact Manifest:** artifact identity, type, version, hash, authority class, inclusion reason, consumer role, and quarantine status.
- **Human Approval Checkpoint:** frozen candidate hash, evidence manifest, approver role, state, decision identity, expiry, supersession, and resume identity.
- **Dependency Change Record:** package identity, version, purpose, material security/license notes, lockfile identity, and rollback note. It is Builder-authored for ordinary engineering changes; only high-risk categories defined by Section 1.10.9 require human approval.

These records are server-authored or Builder-authored according to their boundary. A browser, Narrator, implementation subagent, or QA subagent cannot self-authorize them.

### 19.11.3 QA identity, capability, fixture, and progression records

The Local Arena requires explicit test-control records rather than hidden conventions. These records and their minting/control endpoints are test-environment infrastructure and are not exposed as ordinary Milestone or Launch Production capabilities.

#### Development Test Identity

Stores a server-minted non-production identity, stable internal account identifier, creation authority, expiration, allowed fixture scope, session status, and audit linkage. It contains no repeatable password and cannot be converted into a production Google identity.

#### QA Capability Grant

Stores a random short-lived capability identifier, hashed secret material or provider-managed credential reference, allowed operations, target fixture scope, issuer, issued time, expiry, revocation, test-run binding, rate limits, and audit status. The raw capability is never stored in source, browser local storage, character names, URLs, prompts, or ordinary logs.

#### QA Fixture Marker

Stores fixture type, owning test run, disposable status, permitted destructive operations, cleanup deadline, ordinary-player exclusion, and canonical-service requirements. A record is not a QA fixture merely because its display name starts with `QA `.

#### QA Operation Audit

Stores capability identity, operation, target, prior state, requested inputs, result, canonical event references, build hash, test-run ID, timestamp, rejection reason, and cleanup status.

#### Progression Test Setup Event

Stores a fixture-only canonical setup action such as establishing XP immediately below a threshold, generating a validated level-N fixture through approved progression replay, or restoring a named progression checkpoint. It cannot directly author derived character statistics.

#### Identity Cutover Status

Stores the current player-facing identity mode, Google Sign-In readiness, temporary-development-route state, QA automation exception state, cutover approvals, revoked capability set, and external Alpha launch eligibility.

These records are server-authored. Ordinary clients cannot read raw capability data, mark themselves as fixtures, or select a different identity mode.

## 19.12 Character aggregate

A character aggregate must preserve both chosen source facts and derived current state. It contains:

- Stable character identifier.
- Owner account identifier.
- Creation rules version.
- Current campaign bindings.
- Identity and presentation details.
- Current Experience Points, next threshold, level-availability state, pending level-up transaction, and single-class progression through level 20.
- Species, background, feats, proficiencies, languages, and other approved choices.
- Ability scores and derivation.
- Hit point derivation and current values.
- Defenses, movement modes, senses, and passive values.
- Actions and attacks derived from features and equipment.
- Spell access, preparation, slots, resources, and concentration.
- Inventory, currency, equipment, containers, and attunement where relevant.
- Conditions, ongoing effects, exhaustion-like states where included, and death-save state.
- Private notes and campaign-visible notes.
- Visual specification and approved assets.
- Revision history.

Current combat state may be stored in a session entity projection while durable character state remains in the character aggregate. The boundary must be explicit so an encounter rollback does not erase permanent advancement and a character edit does not rewrite an active turn.

## 19.13 Campaign and scene aggregates

A campaign record stores durable configuration, membership, rules version, content modules, safety agreement, Director settings, and current session pointer.

A scene record stores present location, time, environment, active NPCs, active objectives, map reference, exits, hazards, hidden facts, light, sound zones, and transition conditions.

Scene state is not a blob of AI prose. Narrative prose may describe it, but structured fields control rules, visibility, and future consistency.

## 19.14 Encounter aggregate

The encounter aggregate contains:

- Status.
- Objective.
- Participants.
- Initiative method and order.
- Round and active turn.
- Turn-resource states.
- Pending reaction opportunities.
- Pending resolution plans.
- Token positions and elevations.
- Ongoing areas and environmental effects.
- Victory, defeat, escape, and suspension conditions.
- Connection and absence policies applied.
- Event-version cursor.

Only one command may advance the same encounter version successfully. Competing commands are rejected or serialized through deterministic ordering.

### 19.14.1 Encounter timing-authority index

The Encounter aggregate maintains a canonical index of current, suspended, consumed, expired, and revoked Timing Authorities. The index supports:

- One Active Turn Authority per ordinary active actor unless a specific rule creates another structure.
- Multiple scoped Reaction or Decision authorities when several actors are independently eligible.
- Parent-child linkage for nested interrupts.
- Viewer-safe opportunity projections.
- Atomic consumption and Initiative advancement.
- Recovery after process replacement without reopening choices or accepting stale commands.
- Revocation when an encounter, turn, frame, seat, character state, target, resource, or rules predicate changes.

The authority index is not stored only in WebSocket memory, React state, a PixiJS object, local storage, or a disabled control map.

## 19.15 AI memory records

Memory must be structured by scope:

- Global campaign canon.
- Scene facts.
- NPC-private knowledge.
- Party-known facts.
- Individual-character-known facts.
- Player-private preferences and boundaries.
- Open objectives.
- Resolved history summaries.
- Unconfirmed theories.

Every memory has source events, confidence or confirmation status, visibility, created date, and invalidation or supersession links. Model-generated guesses cannot become facts without an event or explicit human confirmation.

## 19.16 Data version transitions

Every schema change requires:

- Forward version transition.
- Validation query or equivalent verification.
- Rollback or compensating plan.
- Staging rehearsal on representative data.
- Compatibility window for old clients during deployment.
- Monitoring for rejected or unknown schema versions.
- Backup and restore point.

AI coding agents must not mark a version transition complete because the script ran. They must provide before-and-after counts, invalid-record counts, sampled records, and application smoke tests.

## 19.17 Snapshot and reconnect protocol

A reconnecting client submits its last confirmed event cursor and local presentation version. The server returns either:

- An ordered delta of authorized events and projection changes; or
- A complete fresh snapshot when the cursor is missing, invalid, too old, or incompatible.

The client replaces obsolete optimistic state, applies data in order, and acknowledges the resulting version. It must never merge stale local hit points, positions, or inventory into the server snapshot.

## 19.18 Data lifecycle and deletion

Account deletion requires a preview of characters, campaigns owned, campaigns joined, private uploads, and records that must be retained for security, payment, legal, or shared-campaign integrity.

Shared campaign history may retain an anonymized actor reference when deletion would otherwise corrupt other players’ records. Private profile data and inaccessible assets are deleted according to policy. The system must explain this distinction before confirmation.

Campaign deletion enters a recoverable grace period before permanent deletion. Active sessions are stopped first. Backups age out according to documented retention rather than pretending immediate physical erasure.


### 19.18.1 Acceptance-history privacy disposition

The `/users/{userId}/termsAcceptances/{acceptanceId}` history is append-only while the account exists and no approved privacy disposition is active. Account deletion does not permit ordinary code to edit a record in place. Instead, a privileged deletion workflow performs one atomic or recoverably staged disposition:

- Freeze new acceptance writes for the deleting account.
- Resolve legal holds, fraud or security retention, shared-record obligations, and regional policy through the approved retention rules.
- Delete the private acceptance/eligibility summary and revoke access immediately.
- If no retention basis exists, delete the per-user acceptance records under the live-data and backup-aging schedule.
- If a bounded basis exists, create a minimal restricted compliance-retention record with a random opaque identifier, copy only fields approved by the retention schedule, remove direct and indirect account links, and then delete the original user-namespaced records.
- Destroy any temporary account-to-retention mapping as soon as the legal basis permits.
- Produce a non-identifying disposition receipt and verify that ordinary account, campaign, analytics, search, and support systems can no longer resolve the retained proof to the deleted player.

No stable hash, encrypted UID, email digest, or device fingerprint is automatically considered anonymous. Retention and anonymization must be verified against the approved privacy standard and reviewed when techniques or law change.

## 19.19 Data-integrity invariants

Automated integrity checks must detect:

- Character without owner.
- Seat bound to a character not owned or permitted.
- Duplicate active seat for one character where prohibited.
- Event version gaps.
- Projection version behind committed event cursor.
- Negative or impossible resources.
- Item in multiple containers.
- Ongoing effect without source or expiration model.
- Concentration linked to multiple exclusive effects.
- Token referencing missing entity.
- Hidden entity leaked into a player projection.
- Pending reaction past deadline.
- Encounter with no valid active-turn path.
- Outbox record permanently unpublished.
- Asset without provenance.
- Rule record without source.

Critical integrity failure places the affected campaign into safe read-only recovery rather than allowing further mutation.

## 19.19.1 Integrity incident classification and scoped freeze

A failed invariant creates a durable `IntegrityIncident` with severity, affected campaign, detected event cursor, projection cursor, rule or security invariant, detection source, evidence references, and recovery status.

The system applies the smallest safe freeze:

- A broken private projection may freeze only that projection and its affected commands.
- A shared combat-state mismatch freezes campaign mutation.
- A suspected hidden-information leak freezes affected delivery and rotates or invalidates cached projections.
- Unknown canonical corruption freezes the campaign and associated background workers.

Read-only mode must preserve text explaining that the campaign is protected, not deleted. Players may view only information already authorized for them, inspect the recovery status, and leave safely. They cannot continue mutating gameplay through an alternate route, stale socket, second device, direct API call, or queued background command.

## 19.19.2 Recovery state machine

Each incident moves through explicit states:

1. `detected`
2. `contained`
3. `forensic_snapshot_captured`
4. `classified`
5. `recovery_plan_ready`
6. `awaiting_required_approval`
7. `recovering`
8. `verifying`
9. `resynchronizing_clients`
10. `resolved`
11. `escalated`
12. `abandoned_with_campaign_preserved_read_only`

Transitions are idempotent, audited, and lease-protected. A worker replacement, deployment, or retry cannot run two competing recoveries.

## 19.19.3 Recovery strategies

### Projection rebuild

When canonical events are valid, delete or quarantine only the affected derived projection, replay authorized events from the last verified cursor, regenerate viewer-specific state, compare invariants, and publish one fresh snapshot version. No gameplay event changes.

### Outbox and delivery repair

When a valid event was committed but not delivered, repair or replay the original outbox entry using its existing idempotency identity. The process must not repeat a roll, damage application, narrative generation, visual effect, sound, resource cost, or chat entry.

### Canonical recovery branch

When the event chain itself is invalid:

- Preserve the damaged chain and forensic snapshot as restricted evidence.
- Identify the last verified checkpoint through deterministic invariants and tamper-evident, hash-bound cursor evidence.
- Create a recovery branch.
- Replay every subsequent event proven valid and authorized.
- Exclude only a record proven corrupt, duplicated, unauthorized, or impossible.
- Recompute projections after every replayed boundary.
- Append a typed `CampaignRecoveryEvent` describing the incident class, excluded event identities, restored cursor, verification report, and player-visible summary.
- Promote the branch only after independent verification.

The process does not rerun random rolls. Fixed random results remain fixed unless the event itself was never validly created, in which case the recovery follows the approved defect-correction policy and cannot be chosen to benefit a player.

### Backup restoration

A backup is used only when canonical replay cannot recover the intended truth. Restoration must identify data lost after the backup, attempt event-log reconciliation, and require heightened operator review. The UI must not describe a backup restore as exact if verified later events could not be recovered.

## 19.19.4 Campaign-owner recovery experience

The owner-facing interface shows:

- Incident reference and detection time.
- Plain-language affected system.
- Whether canonical events, projections, delivery, visibility, or security are affected.
- Last verified event and campaign time.
- Whether characters, maps, and campaign history remain safe.
- Proposed recovery strategy.
- Whether owner authorization, operator approval, or no human approval is required.
- Current progress and final verification result.
- A support or escalation route.

The owner may request diagnosis, authorize an approved non-discretionary recovery, or leave the campaign paused. The owner cannot select an arbitrary prior round, event, roll, death, inventory state, or narrative branch. Recovery controls are not exposed as “undo,” “rewind,” or “restore to my preferred point.”

## 19.19.5 Recovery completion and client resynchronization

Before mutation resumes:

- Every relevant integrity invariant passes.
- Canonical cursor, projection cursor, outbox cursor, and campaign clock agree.
- Ownership, seats, conditions, resources, inventories, fog, and hidden-information partitions are revalidated.
- The recovery plan and result are attested in tamper-evident evidence by the responsible automated service or reviewer; no custom cryptographic signing service is required unless the security architecture independently requires one.
- Connected sockets are invalidated or instructed to discard local state.
- Every client receives a fresh authorized snapshot and new projection epoch.
- Pending commands against the prior epoch are rejected or reconciled safely.
- A visible mechanical/system notice explains that a technical recovery occurred without exposing secrets.

A campaign that fails verification remains read-only and escalates. It cannot silently reopen because a timeout elapsed or the owner refreshed the page.

## 19.19.6 Recovery evidence and acceptance failures

Certification requires fixtures for projection corruption, outbox loss, duplicated delivery, unauthorized event insertion, event-gap corruption, stale snapshot promotion, hidden-information leakage, interrupted recovery, worker replacement, and failed verification.

The build fails when:

- A campaign can remain read-only with no incident status, recovery path, or escalation.
- An owner can choose an arbitrary rollback point.
- Recovery deletes or rewrites the original event chain in place.
- A reroll or duplicate mechanical effect occurs during recovery.
- A repaired projection leaks information to an unauthorized viewer.
- A stale client can submit commands after recovery without receiving the new epoch.
- The UI claims exact restoration without evidence.


## 19.20 Architecture acceptance evidence

The implementation phase must produce architecture diagrams, authority tables, command sequence traces, failure sequence traces, schema registry, version transition plan, and threat model. QA must demonstrate through black-box use that client tampering cannot alter ownership, rolls, damage, inventory, targets, or visibility.

Ordinary independent QA must compare observed behavior to event and projection evidence. In Phase 6, Phase 7, or an earlier explicit risk trigger, the separate Independent QA Judge also challenges that evidence. A polished UI with an unverifiable backend does not pass.


## 19.21 Communication Dock records and projections

Communication data is separated by authority and retention purpose. Required record classes include:

- **Chronicle Entry:** trusted audience-filtered presentation linked to canonical event, narration, mechanical notice, or system record.
- **Party Chat Message:** human-authored nonmechanical message with sender, selected mode, audience, moderation state, delivery state, and retention classification.
- **Communication Fact:** canonical audience-scoped record that a specific in-fiction statement or signal was delivered; it does not certify truth.
- **Rules Desk Request and Response:** nonmutating question, approved visible context references, cited rules, and response state.
- **Director Address Request and Response:** nonmechanical addressed question or note, audience, perception-envelope version, response, and optional Action Draft Suggestion.
- **Action Draft:** noncanonical player-owned draft with source, visible-state version, selections, expiry, privacy class, and no mutation authority.
- **Action Draft Suggestion:** server-produced bridge from a nonmechanical request into the Action Composer; it cannot be accepted as a command directly.
- **Communication Dock Projection:** viewer-specific tabs, unread cursors, message states, pending responses, and urgent-priority metadata.

These records use separate identifiers and cannot be retyped in place. A Party Chat Message does not become a Command; a new Action Draft or confirmed Command is created through the appropriate path. A Rules Desk Response does not become a Ruling; a later Director ruling references its own canonical inputs.

Typing indicators, draft-presence hints, and ordinary online indicators are ephemeral and noncanonical. They are never supplied to the AI Director as evidence of player intent, hidden activity, or character knowledge.

Communication projections are audience-filtered. Private Director Address content, moderation evidence, hidden-character speech, and staff annotations cannot enter shared feeds, recaps, notifications, exports, accessibility descriptions, or model payloads outside their authorized purpose.

## 19.22 Local emulator data domain

Local emulator data is a separate non-production authority domain.

- Emulator Authentication users are development identities, not live accounts.
- Emulator Firestore, Storage, Functions, and related records are disposable or explicitly versioned seed fixtures.
- Local document paths may mirror production schemas so tests remain realistic, but local records never establish production ownership, legal acceptance, campaign membership, entitlements, or audit proof.
- No automatic synchronization, replication, version transition, backup restore, export, or copy operation may move emulator data into the live project.
- Production snapshots may not be imported into local QA unless a separately approved sanitization process irreversibly removes player identity, secrets, private chat, hidden campaign content, and regulated data.
- QA reset operations carry an emulator-environment proof and fail when the target project, host, or credential does not match the Local Stack Manifest.
- The local event log, projection store, outbox, session store, and asset metadata must be complete enough to test recovery and persistence without contacting production.
- A local campaign resume test must stop and restart the local stack, re-import or retain the intended baseline, and prove the exact map, tokens, events, visibility, chat, and turn state return.

Local fixtures are evidence tools, not shortcuts. They must still traverse the same canonical command, event, projection, ownership, and progression services used by the production candidate unless a test explicitly targets a lower-level unit contract.


## 19.23 Holistic product, provider, brand, visual-scene, and quick-start records

The data and configuration model includes:

### Provider Compliance Registry Record

Stores provider, service, model or SDK, purpose, data classes, terms and policy identities, effective and review dates, age and region restrictions, service tier, retention and training controls, safety configuration, attribution, branding, cost and quota, approval, fallback, and kill-switch status.

### Brand Clearance Record

Stores product name or mark, asset hashes, jurisdictions, search scope, reviewer, conflicts considered, restrictions, approval status, and next review date.

### Brand Asset Manifest

Stores primary and variant logo assets, wordmark text, vector sources, size and color rules, accessibility labels, animation treatment, favicon, hashes, provenance, and approval.

### Quick-Start Character Template

Stores immutable template identity, supported Class and level, selected Background and Species, plain-language role description, complete mechanical creation choices, derived-stat expectation, optional neutral/class preview-art references, accessibility description, rules-manifest version, and approval. It contains no player name, pronouns, personal portrait/token identity, or account ownership. Selection copies the mechanical choices into a draft; the account-owned character and its final visual specification are created only after the player completes Identity & Final Review.

### Visual Scene Manifest

Stores stage mode, approved background or map asset bundle, lighting, ambient loops, motion budget, token and portrait set, fog policy, visible interactables, accessible description, reduced-motion alternative, low-effects alternative, sound-zone references, and version.

### Player-Safe Map Asset Manifest

Stores player-safe base assets, secret asset partitions, region or tile identities, audience rules, cache policy, reveal requirements, and asset hashes. The client projection references only authorized entries.

### Visual Identity Specification

Stores the canonical description and approved assets for one character or persistent NPC across portrait, avatar, token, dialogue, initiative, form, memorial, and accessibility uses.

All records are versioned, audience-aware, candidate-bound where applicable, and included in version transition, backup, privacy, security, and resume tests.

# 20. SECURITY AND ABUSE PREVENTION

## 20.1 Identity

- Verify authentication tokens server-side.
- Derive user identity from verified credentials.
- Never trust a client-supplied user identifier.
- Require recent authentication for account deletion, email change, and security-sensitive actions.
- Revoke sessions after password or security changes.

## 20.2 Authorization

Every command checks:

- Campaign membership.
- Seat.
- Character control.
- Role.
- Scene.
- Turn.
- Target visibility.
- Resource permission.
- State version.

## 20.3 Invitation protection

Use long random invitation tokens or rate-limited short codes backed by:

- Expiration.
- Attempt limits.
- IP and account abuse detection.
- Revocation.
- Host approval.
- No public metadata leakage.

## 20.4 App and API abuse

Use:

- App integrity checks.
- Rate limits by account, device, IP, campaign, and operation.
- Quotas for AI and asset generation.
- Payload limits.
- Upload scanning.
- Request timeouts.
- Circuit breakers.
- Bot and credential-stuffing protection.
- Audit logging.
- Alerting for unusual generation or invitation patterns.

## 20.5 Secrets

No API key, service credential, prompt secret, moderation rule, or internal endpoint belongs in client-delivered code.

## 20.6 Player reporting

Players can report:

- Another player.
- AI content.
- Uploaded assets.
- Harassment.
- Sexual content.
- Hate content.
- Threats.
- Impersonation.
- Intellectual-property concerns.
- Privacy concerns.
- Technical exploitation.

Reports preserve relevant evidence under restricted access and notify the reporter of status without exposing private enforcement details.

---

## 20.7 Security architecture baseline

Security must be designed to an application-security verification standard appropriate for an authenticated multi-user service. The project should target OWASP ASVS Level 2 controls unless a documented risk assessment requires stricter treatment. Security acceptance is based on verified behavior, not the presence of a library or a checkbox in a cloud console.

The production architecture must enforce:

- HTTPS and WSS only.
- Server-side verification of authenticated sessions.
- Deny-by-default authorization.
- Message-level authorization for every real-time command.
- Origin validation for WebSocket upgrades.
- CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated state-changing HTTP routes.
- Strong content security policy.
- Output encoding and sanitization for all user and AI text.
- Rate and size limits for HTTP, WebSocket, uploads, and AI requests.
- Secret storage outside source code and browser bundles.
- Least-privilege service accounts.
- Immutable audit records for privileged actions.
- Dependency, container, and artifact scanning.
- Backup, recovery, and incident-response procedures.

## 20.8 Authentication sessions

The browser must not treat a client-readable token in local storage as the primary long-lived session. The preferred web session uses a secure, HTTP-only, same-site cookie created and verified by the backend after Firebase authentication. Cookie duration, renewal, revocation checks, and reauthentication requirements must be documented.

High-risk actions require recent authentication, including account deletion, ownership transfer where supported, campaign administration transfer, email or identity-provider change, privacy-data access requests, and security-setting changes.

Logout must revoke or invalidate the active application session and clear browser-local sensitive state. “Log out all devices” must revoke all application sessions after a confirmation and recent authentication.

### 20.8.1 Temporary development identities

Temporary development identities exist only inside the Local Arena to support internal development and automated QA. They may continue to exist locally after the external Google-only cutover because the cutover governs hosted player authentication, not local engineering. They must:

- Be minted server-side through an approved test service.
- Use stable internal account identifiers.
- Exercise normal session, ownership, authorization, seat, command, event, and projection paths.
- Contain no user-selected password.
- Be visibly classified in restricted diagnostics and audit records.
- Be barred from conversion into ordinary production identities.
- Expire or be revoked under test-run and cleanup policy.

The public client cannot choose development identity mode. A discovered route without a valid QA capability returns no usable session and no instructions for obtaining one.

### 20.8.2 Google-only external Alpha cutover

Before any external Alpha player invitation is activated:

- Google Sign-In is the only player-facing identity provider.
- Email/password, anonymous, magic-link, development-login, and alternative social-provider player paths are disabled unless a later Product Owner-approved blueprint revision authorizes them.
- The backend verifies Firebase identity and issues the secure application session.
- Google passwords never enter Hallucinated Dungeons systems.
- Temporary development identities cannot access ordinary player campaigns.
- Existing test fixtures are not silently transitioned into player accounts.
- Cutover, rollback, provider outage, shared-computer, revocation, and account-deletion behavior are tested.

A provider outage may display a clear degraded-state message and preserve invitation intent, but it cannot fall back to a hidden password or development login.

### 20.8.3 Local-Arena QA capability security

Automated QA may continue after Google cutover without a Google account only inside the Local Arena through a machine-only capability path. The same capability must be rejected by Milestone and Launch Production.

A QA operation requires all of the following:

1. A server-controlled harness-enabled state.
2. A valid short-lived, revocable capability bound to one test run.
3. An allowlisted operation.
4. A target explicitly marked as a disposable QA fixture.
5. Canonical production services for the tested behavior.
6. Complete immutable audit evidence.
7. Rate, quantity, and cleanup limits.

The capability cannot alter ordinary accounts, ownership, campaign membership, adult-acceptance records, security roles, arbitrary Firestore fields, or non-fixture campaigns. It cannot be stored in the repository, blueprint, client bundle, local storage, character name, route query, or chat. A rejected request does not reveal how to gain access.

## 20.9 Account recovery and identity changes

Account recovery must not create a second owner identity for existing characters. Characters remain attached to the stable authenticated account identifier.

Changes to email, display name, provider, or password must preserve ownership. Account merges are prohibited until a human-reviewed merge process can prove control of both identities and reconcile characters, campaign memberships, entitlements, audit logs, and safety actions.

Support staff cannot manually reassign a character based only on an email request. Recovery actions require verifiable identity evidence and produce an audit event.

## 20.10 Authorization matrix

Every server action must map to an explicit permission. Roles alone are insufficient; permissions must consider resource ownership, campaign membership, seat state, entity control, scene visibility, and action timing.

At minimum, the matrix distinguishes:

- Public visitor.
- Authenticated account.
- Campaign invitee.
- Campaign member.
- Seated player.
- Character owner.
- Campaign moderator.
- Campaign owner.
- Support reviewer.
- System administrator.
- Security administrator.
- Automated service identity.

A campaign owner does not automatically own player characters. A system administrator has only the explicit Admin capabilities authorized to that account and does not automatically gain gameplay secrecy bypass or character control. A support role does not gain gameplay visibility unless needed for a specific reviewed case. A service identity may perform only its assigned function.

Authorization is checked at command receipt and again immediately before state mutation if relevant state could have changed.

## 20.11 WebSocket security

The WebSocket endpoint must authenticate during upgrade or through an immediately required authenticated initialization message bound to the verified server session. Client-supplied user identifiers, character identifiers, campaign roles, and ownership claims are untrusted.

The server must validate:

- Secure transport.
- Allowed origin.
- Session validity and revocation.
- Campaign membership.
- Seat binding.
- Message schema.
- Message size.
- Command type permission.
- Referenced entity visibility and control.
- State version.
- Idempotency key.
- Rate limit.

Connections receive short-lived server connection identifiers. Reauthentication or reconnect occurs before the Cloud Run request timeout. Session affinity may improve continuity but cannot be relied on for security or canonical state.

Malformed or unauthorized messages receive bounded errors and security telemetry. Repeated abuse closes the connection and may suspend the account or source according to policy.

## 20.12 Cross-instance real-time design
